1.name: Thúy Vi Tông
1.look: Twin summits rise out of the blue-green haze of the hills, their slopes stepped with herb terraces and white-walled halls under green-glazed roofs. Around the higher summit a broad path of white stone winds in a spiral from the haze to the peak, and on misty mornings only its pale upper turns show above the clouds.
1.lore: Thúy Vi Tông, the Sect of the Emerald Haze, is a righteous (chính đạo) great sect of alchemists whose herb terraces climb its slopes in green stripes. Its founder came into these hills when the last master of Không Sơn Viện gave them away, and the sect still leaves that old academy untouched. Its head Ngu Lam Sơn walked in the haze for a hundred days before giving his first order, and new disciples now walk the white spiral path, the Haze Walk, from dawn to dusk before they take their vows.
1.history: In 500 Phùng Yên Hà founded Thúy Vi Tông in the blue-green mist of the north-western hills, the same year Thôi Bất Kiến of Không Sơn Viện, having no heir, gave Thanh Loan Lĩnh, his whisk and his only student to Phùng Yên Hà. In 505 the sect opened the green jade mine that Không Sơn had forbidden, and when Thôi Bất Kiến died in 520 it left his academy unlocked and unlooted. The sect took the cape of snow and fire in 560 and founded the ports of Yên Ba Thành in 590 and Mục Ca Thành in 700. In 668 Tùng Đào Cung marched on its Cold Ford coast without a writ, took it in 672, and the Pivot let the seizure stand. Thúy Vi waited, and in 901, holding the Pivot's writ, marched to take it back, retaking the Cold Ford in 905, more than two centuries after losing it. In 1000 Phùng Yên Hà died at 640; Ngu Lam Sơn became head, took the White Cloud Whisk, and walked in the haze for a hundred days before giving his first order.
levels: A new hall of pill furnaces rises on the eastern summit and the herb terraces climb another band of the slope.
A tall many-roofed pagoda crowns the lower summit facing the spiral path, and covered stairs link the herb terraces of both peaks.

2.name: Tùng Đào Cung
2.look: Out of an endless sea of pines a long ridge rises, crowned with stacked halls of dark timber and blue-grey tile. Along the crest runs an open-sided roofed gallery so long that it follows the ridge out of sight, and the wind through the pines sounds in it like surf.
2.lore: Tùng Đào Cung, the Palace of the Pine Waves, is a righteous great sect of spell cultivators (pháp tu) of Wood and Water, lord of the pine sea, the great river basin and the northern lake. Its disciples sit in the long gallery and learn to hear the pine waves before they are taught a single art, and pilgrims still climb the ridge only to listen. Thôi Khinh Hồng, the founder's first disciple and its second head, lives in the retreat beside the seat, and the palace lowers its voice near it.
2.history: In 200 Kỳ Tùng Ẩn founded Tùng Đào Cung among the endless pines, with his first disciple Thôi Khinh Hồng beside him. The palace raised Tùng Gian Thành below it in 240, took the river basin of Cửu Khúc Xuyên in 260, and extended its rule to Lãnh Nguyệt Lâm and the long lake in 330. In 270 Kỳ Tùng Ẩn and Chung Hoài Cực drank for three days at Thạch Kiều Thành, a peace that held until 502, when he broke it to march on the heart with Lạc Hà Tông. The War of the Pivot ended in defeat in 509, the iron chain of Thiết Tỏa Quan lying on the river bed. In 672 the palace took the Cold Ford coast from Thúy Vi without a writ and held it until 905. Kỳ Tùng Ẩn died in 690 at 620 and Thôi Khinh Hồng became the second head; in 900 she retired to the retreat by the seat, and her disciple Đàm Tùng Lại took the headship. The palace kept the long lake in the arbitration of 944, and fought Lạc Hà over the river tolls on the Ngư Ca border in the Ferry War, which ended in 1175 with neither side forgiving.
levels: A second terrace of halls climbs the far end of the ridge and the gallery gains a bell pavilion at its midpoint.
A tall many-roofed pagoda rises at the gallery's far end, and a broad stone stair road is cut down through the pines toward the city below.

3.name: Băng Tâm Các
3.look: Out of red badlands at the desert's edge rises a tall white pavilion of stacked celadon-glazed roofs, pale stone terraces climbing to it. Even at midsummer frost rims its eaves, and a thin cold mist spills from the round well-house at its foot, where the water keeps ice all year. Far beyond, the snow ranges of Ngọc Hồ Sơn stand white against the sky.
3.lore: Băng Tâm Các, the Pavilion of the Ice Heart, is a great sect (đại tông môn) of sword cultivators (kiếm tu) and lord of the desert and the ice mountains; its name comes from the old line that the ice heart sits in the jade vessel. Sở Ngọc Hồ has led it since 1010 as keeper of the Jade Vessel, with Tiết Hàn Mai as first elder and Sở Hàn Y as her disciple. Disciples at the seat drink only its well water, and a newcomer who flinches at the cup is told to stay until they no longer do.
3.history: In 440 Tần Ngưng Sương founded Băng Tâm Các in the cold north-east, a pavilion for the ice heart, on the high badlands between the desert and the ice fields. In 445 Tần Ngưng Sương made the well water of the desert seat cold enough to keep ice all summer. The sect claimed the empty ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn and founded Trường Vân Thành in 470, and took the frost coast from Hàn Giang Môn in the war of 492 to 498. In the Desert Road War of 722 to 728 it lost Cô Thành to Phượng Minh's fire, and in the Long Lake War of 940 to 944 won only the right to fish the northern shore of Hạo Nguyệt Hồ. Tần Ngưng Sương died in 1010, and Sở Ngọc Hồ became head and keeper of the Jade Vessel; in 1090 she joined the hunt that killed Mặc Huyết Sinh, and in 1121 Hạng Dạ Bôi knelt to her. In 1188 her claim to Tinh Tủy Mạch was rejected before the Pivot, and she returned without a word and shut herself in the seat's ice hall for a year.
levels: A second ice hall carved into the badland ridge behind the pavilion, and terraces of sword-practice grounds below it.
Twin frost-rimmed side towers flanking the main pavilion, joined by covered bridges, and a ring of cold wells mist-veiling the lower terraces.

4.name: Lạc Hà Tông
4.look: The road climbs a low swell of steppe to a sect (tông môn) of long ochre earth terraces and rose-tiled halls, every one of them turned to the west. On the westernmost terrace stands the Sunset Ring, a great round stone gate with no doors and no wall, through which the whole sect watches the sun go down each evening. Below, the river shoals of Hạc Đinh Thị shine in the low light.
4.lore: Lạc Hà Tông, the Sect of the Drifting Sunset Clouds, is one of the seven great sects and master of the western lands; its arts lean on earth and wood, and its disciples hold the hour of evening glow best for cultivation. The head Tô Vãn Chiếu carries the sword Tử Điện; its twin Thanh Sương fell on Chiết Kích Nguyên in 803, and no one has dared go back for it. The dusk of 803, when the river boats fell silent, is kept each year as an evening of mourning, and the head's youngest disciple Tô Mộ Vân is the sect's brightest hope.
4.history: Nhan Cô Vụ founded Lạc Hà Tông in 290 in the western lands where the sun goes down, and a market soon grew on the river shoals below. In 360 the sect forged the twin swords Tử Điện and Thanh Sương for its armoury. It lost the War of the Pivot beside Tùng Đào and lived under the North Star Compact from then on. Its founder later swore with Phó Tiêu Tương to end the Pivot's oversight; when news of the battle on Chiết Kích Nguyên reached the seat in 803, the fishing boats did not sing at dusk for the first time in six hundred years. Nhan Cô Vụ died in 940 and Trầm Tịch Dương became the second head; in 1160 he stepped down for his disciple Tô Vãn Chiếu, who took Tử Điện. In 1176 Tô Mộ Vân was born on the day the evening glow filled the whole sky.
levels: More terraces climb the rise, a second ring of rose-tiled halls stands around the Sunset Ring, and a covered stair runs down toward the river market.
The terraces crown the whole swell; a tall many-roofed pagoda rises behind the Sunset Ring, and banners of rose silk hang along every terrace wall.

5.name: Thiên Xu Tông
5.look: High on a bare mountain above the heart of the continent, seven terraced halls step down a curving ridge in the bent line of the Northern Dipper, each a little lower than the last. The first and highest, the Pivot Hall, carries a slender black-iron spire that catches the last light long after the valleys are dark. Around the seat the slopes are strangely green for such a height, the mark of the Bắc Thần Phúc Địa.
5.lore: Thiên Xu Tông, the Sect of the Heavenly Pivot, is the oldest great sect and the enforcer of the North Star Compact; its arts lean on metal and earth, and its formation (trận pháp) masters are the finest on the continent. Its head Doãn Ngọc Hành keeps the Bắc Thần Ấn, while the former head Đỗ Tinh Hà sits as first elder. Scented wood from Mộc Hương Thôn burns in the Pivot Hall day and night, beside the old stones of Thạch Kiều Thành's bridge.
5.history: Chung Hoài Cực founded Thiên Xu Tông in 120 under the stars of the Northern Dipper, and the ground around his seat grew rich as the sect gathered, becoming the Bắc Thần Phúc Địa (blessed land). In the Age of First Gates the sect won the ore miners of Ngọc Hành Sơn with fair weights rather than swords and fixed its northern borders for good. It destroyed Cửu Thiều Cung in the War of the Nine Shao, beat Tùng Đào and Lạc Hà together in the War of the Pivot without taking land, and set the North Star Compact at Thạch Kiều Thành. Chung Hoài Cực died in 760 and Đỗ Tinh Hà became the second head; in 785 he named Quý Trường Kích war marshal and gave him the Thiết Mã banner and its tally. Under Đỗ Tinh Hà the Pivot called the Pirate Purge, crushed the rebel Phá Quân Môn and judged one vein war after another. In 1150 he stepped down for his disciple Doãn Ngọc Hành, who became head and keeper of the Bắc Thần Ấn and soon brought the sect into the war at Đan Sơn Mạch on Phượng Minh's side.
levels: Covered stairs join the seven terraces, and a walled formation yard with stone array discs opens below the lowest hall.
Each terrace gains a tall pagoda so the Dipper line reads from far off, and a ring of warding pillars stands around the whole ridge.
projects: grand warding formation around the seat

6.name: Phượng Minh Cung
6.look: High on the ridges of Thê Ngô Lĩnh, a palace of red-lacquered halls and stacked golden-brown pagoda roofs climbs around one colossal ancient wutong (ngô đồng) tree, whose broad green crown rises above the highest roof. Wutong groves fill the terraces below.
6.lore: Phượng Minh Cung, the Palace of the Phoenix's Call, is the great sect of fire and wood in the south, founded on the empty lands of the fallen Cửu Thiều Cung. It holds the rice plain of Triêu Dương Nguyên, whose granaries carried the south through the drought of 649, and since 590 the fire coast of Đan Huyệt Châu. Its head is Hoa Triêu Dương, with the first elder Vu Ngô Đồng at her side. The palace keeps the old court music of the ridges in its rites, but its elders grow uneasy when any tune is played too long, and there are whispers that the palace keeps something of Cửu Thiều's that it never shows.
6.history: Ngô Thê Đồng founded Phượng Minh Cung in 480 on the lands left empty since the fall of Cửu Thiều Cung, and in 485 a market of the Shao music opened at the foot of the new palace. In 520 the palace took the rice plain of Triêu Dương Nguyên, and in the decades after it founded Lai Nghi Thành and its gulf port Thanh Khê Thành. In 584 it asked the Pivot for a writ against Xích Thành Môn, which had burned eleven villages, and won the first writ of the Compact; in 590 it destroyed that sect, took Đan Huyệt Châu and hung the Xích Hà Kỳ in its hall. It fought Băng Tâm Các over the Desert Road from 722 and broke Cô Thành in 726, until the Pivot imposed a truce in 728. In 1040 it went to war with Thính Vũ Lâu for the Kinh Lôi vein, and in 1046 the Pivot's judgement left the vein with Thính Vũ. Ngô Thê Đồng died in 1100 and Hoa Triêu Dương became head; it is whispered in the palace that the dying founder gave her something with a warning, though no one says what. From 1150 to 1158 the palace held Đan Sơn Mạch against Thính Vũ Lâu, with Thiên Xu at its side from 1154.
levels: A second ring of red halls and a covered music terrace climb the ridge around the great wutong, and a stair of red gates runs down toward Thiều Âm Thị.
A nine-roof pagoda rises beside the tree, nearly as tall as its crown, and the terraces spread along the whole ridge with a wutong planted on every step.
projects: music terrace for the dawn rites

7.name: Thính Vũ Lâu
7.look: Out of the rain forest rises a dormant volcanic cone, dark with banana groves on its terraced flanks, and on its crown a slender many-eaved tower, the tallest thing in the south. From every eave of every storey hang long bronze rain-chains, so that in a downpour the whole tower runs with water and rings like a struck bell. No lamp burns in any window.
7.lore: Thính Vũ Lâu, a great sect (đại tông môn) of the ma đạo (demonic path), is ruled by Mạnh Dạ Vũ, who holds the Tương Phi Tán. Its founder Phó Tiêu Tương built the tower so that one could listen to the rain, and its sword disciples are still taught by the sound of it. Since the masters of the ma đạo came by night after the Night Rain Edict, the Tower's lamps have never been lit. Its soul vaults are kept by Lệ Tiêu Hồn, its first elder is Quan Vũ Thanh, and its war elder is Cố Dạ Lan, who has never lost a duel; the head's ambitious disciple Mạnh Lưu Ly is his rival for the sect's future.
7.history: Phó Tiêu Tương founded Thính Vũ Lâu in the rain forests in 380. A century later, when Khải Lôi Môn fell, the Tower rose on its ground and took the thunder mountains. It won the forest half of the Petal Shore by the Pivot's judgement, then broke the Compact beside Lạc Hà in the War of Broken Halberds and lost. In 880 Phó Tiêu Tương died, and Mạnh Dạ Vũ took the headship and the Tương Phi Tán; in 905 he proclaimed the Night Rain Edict. In 906 the ma đạo masters came by night, Cố Dạ Lan among them, and the lamps were never lit again. Beaten at Đan Sơn Mạch, the Tower had rebuilt its strength twice over by 1165, to the Pivot's unease. In 1185 its first elder Quan Vũ Thanh went in secret to Phượng Minh to talk of peace, and came back without an answer.
levels: New halls stack up the cone's flank on black stone terraces, each roof hung with its own rain-chains, and a covered stair climbs from the lake.
A second, lower tower rises on a shoulder of the cone, joined to the first by a roofed bridge; the whole slope is walled in dark stone, and still no window shows a light.

8.name: Hàm Nguyệt Trang
8.look: A low manor of dark timber and grey tile stands among birches on the lake shore, its slim piers reaching out over still water. Just off the piers a perfect ring of white stones breaks the surface, enclosing a circle of water so calm it holds the moon whole; the manor calls it the Moon Net.
8.lore: Hàm Nguyệt Trang is a small water-arts sect (tông môn) sworn to Tùng Đào Cung, living on spirit fish (linh ngư) and lake pearls. Its founder said the moon in the lake is easier to catch than the one in the sky, and novices still begin by sitting at the Moon Net until they can watch the reflection without breaking it. Its mistress Kiều Nguyệt Châu has doubled the pearl harvest since she took the manor. The manor keeps no war boats; its old ones lie on the lake bed where it sank them.
8.history: In 410 a water cultivator founded Hàm Nguyệt Trang on the long lake, saying the moon in the lake is easier to catch than the one in the sky. In 470 a fisher of Tuyết Lộc pulled a pearl the size of a fist from Hạo Nguyệt Hồ; the manor bought it and began to farm pearls, and pearls have been its wealth ever since. In 610 its disciples tracked a snow-leopard spirit beast that had taken a child from Hàn Yên Thôn for forty days across the ice. In 748 the lake froze to its bed for one winter, and the manor's spirit fish lived through it in the moon's reflection, which the disciples count as proof of their founder's words. When Tùng Đào Cung and Băng Tâm Các went to war over the lake, Băng Tâm skiffs raided the pearl beds in 942, and the manor sank its own boats rather than lose them. The arbitration that ended the war left the lake with Tùng Đào but gave Băng Tâm the fishing of the northern shore, so the manor now shares its waters with its old raiders. In 1150 Kiều Nguyệt Châu became mistress of the manor and doubled the pearl harvest within twenty years.
levels: Pearl sheds spread along the shore on both sides of the piers and the moon-viewing tower gains a fourth roof.
The manor walls take in the birch grove, a stone pearl hall rises behind the tower, and a second, smaller ring of white stones is laid in the shallows for the disciples.

9.name: Hồng Lô Cốc
9.look: A steep coastal valley of snow and black rock opens onto a grey sea, its terraces climbing to a squat red-brick furnace tower. Snow never settles in a wide ring around the tower; the bare dark ground there steams, and the stack glows at night like a coal.
9.lore: Hồng Lô Cốc is a sect of alchemists (đan sư) sworn to Thúy Vi Tông, whose furnace was lit with fire carried from the volcanic isles. Its saying is that a snowflake on the red furnace is gone at once, and novices stand catching snow by the furnace mouth until they stop flinching. Its master Đồng Hồng Lô once kept the furnace burning nine years without letting it cool. The valley also works Bích Ngọc Khoáng, the green jade mine in the hills of Thanh Loan Lĩnh.
9.history: Thúy Vi Tông took the cape of snow and fire in the Age of the North Star Compact, and its surveyors soon charted the smoking volcanic isles offshore. In 650 a company of alchemists carried fire from those isles across the water and lit a furnace in this coastal valley, founding Hồng Lô Cốc. The valley swore itself to Thúy Vi, whose own art is alchemy, and became its lord's furnace on the cape. In time it also took over the working of Bích Ngọc Khoáng, the green jade mine Thúy Vi had opened soon after its founding. In 930 Đồng Hồng Lô became master of the valley and kept its furnace burning for nine years without cooling, a feat the alchemists still toast each midwinter. In 1185 the volcanic isles smoked for a month, and Hồng Lô Cốc's alchemists sailed out to gather the ash before the rain could take it.
levels: A second, taller furnace stack rises beside the first and the snow-free ring widens over a new terrace of drying sheds.
A stacked pagoda hall of red tile crowns the valley head above the furnaces, and a curved stone breakwater shelters the ash boats.

10.name: Vân Khởi Quán
10.look: High on a mountain shoulder a small abbey of grey stone halls follows a thin stream uphill to the point where it vanishes into a cleft in the rock. Beside that spot a wooden platform juts out over the drop, and below it the clouds rise from the valleys.
10.lore: Vân Khởi Quán is a Daoist abbey (đạo quán) of mountain hermits and teachers, sworn to Thúy Vi Tông and founded by Tống Tọa Vân, the last student of Không Sơn Viện, who is still its abbot. Its teaching is to walk to where the water ends, then sit and watch the clouds rise, and a novice's first lesson is a day on the platform with nothing to do. The abbey works a small mica mine and calls the stone cloud made solid.
10.history: Tống Tọa Vân came to these hills as a boy, the only disciple Thôi Bất Kiến took after becoming master of Không Sơn Viện in 460. In 500 his master, with no heir, gave the hills, his whisk and his only student to Phùng Yên Hà of Thúy Vi Tông. In 540 Tống Tọa Vân founded Vân Khởi Quán higher on the mountain, to walk where the water ends and watch the clouds rise, and swore the abbey to Thúy Vi. In 560 its monks opened the mica mine of Vân Mẫu Khoáng and said the stone was cloud made solid. Over the centuries hermits and teachers drifted up the mountain to the abbey, and Thúy Vi took to sending its restless disciples there to learn stillness. In 1080 the mica ran thin, and the abbot said only that clouds, too, pass.
levels: A row of hermit cells is cut into the cliff beside the platform and a stone path climbs to a second, higher terrace.
A stacked three-roofed sutra tower rises above the halls, and a covered walk follows the stream from the gate to the platform.

11.name: Vạn Hác Viện
11.look: Deep in the pine sea the ground breaks into ravine after ravine. Over the deepest, on a single pillar of rock rising from its floor, stands a hexagonal pavilion, and the academy's halls step along the ravine rim around it.
11.lore: Vạn Hác Viện is an academy of sound cultivation sworn to Tùng Đào Cung, keepers of the zither Tùng Phong Cầm. Its founders were listeners: a monk played under these pines until his zither sounded like ten thousand ravines, and they stayed to learn. The academy teaches that a piece is finished only when the listener forgets why he came, and students who play on the pillar pavilion hear every note thrown back by the ravines.
11.history: Before the academy, the ravines of Thâm Tùng Hải were only a hard stretch for Tùng Đào's road wardens. In 620 a monk played the zither in the pines here until it sounded like ten thousand ravines, and his listeners founded Vạn Hác Viện around him and kept his Tùng Phong Cầm. The pavilion on the rock pillar is said to stand where he sat. Within two years its zither students were practising in Tùng Phong hamlet, where the villagers learned to sleep through anything. The academy swore itself to Tùng Đào and in time took the malachite workings of Thạch Lục Khoáng into its care. In 1080 a Vạn Hác student played so well under the pines that Thiên Xu's envoy forgot his message.
levels: A second hall of practice rooms lines the far rim and a narrow stair is cut down the side of the pillar.
A tall three-roofed hall of the zither rises on the highest point of the rim, facing the pillar pavilion across the ravine.

12.name: Thải Chi Cốc
12.look: A shallow forest valley opens off the road, its floor striped with herb beds that step down toward the river below. At the valley mouth sit four moss-grey stone hermits in a row, each cradling a lingzhi in its lap and facing the road as if judging who may enter. The air smells of bitter roots and the smoke of drying sheds.
12.lore: Thải Chi Cốc is a minor sect (tiểu tông môn) of herb growers and alchemists (luyện đan sư) sworn to Tùng Đào Cung. Its founders were lingzhi pickers who had left the world, and the valley still sings their old song of the four hermits at every planting. Since Nghiêm Linh Chi became valley-mistress in 1000, the river's orphans have worked the fields and learned their letters in the drying sheds, and many never leave.
12.history: In 480 lingzhi pickers who had turned their backs on the world settled this valley under the pines of Cửu Khúc Xuyên and founded Thải Chi Cốc, singing the song of the four hermits as they cleared the ground. Tùng Đào Cung, lord of the basin since the Age of First Gates, took the little sect under its banner. In 520 the valley planted the first spirit-herb (linh dược) fields along the river, and for a century travellers said the valley smelled of medicine before they saw a roof. The four stone hermits at the valley mouth are thought to date from those years, though no one agrees whose hands carved them. The valley kept out of its lord's wars, sending pills (đan dược) downriver rather than disciples to the field. In 1000 Nghiêm Linh Chi became valley-mistress and opened the herb fields to the orphans of the river, and the valley has been louder ever since. The riverside town of Hà Bạn Trấn answers to it today.
levels: More drying sheds and a stone furnace house with a tall chimney; the herb terraces climb further up both valley walls.
A second pagoda hall joined to the first by a covered stair, an upper grove of shaded lingzhi logs, and long orphan dormitories along the lower fields.

13.name: Lãng Đào Môn
13.look: On low wooded ground just back from the river stands a sect gate made of two great river-boat hulls, upturned and set on end so their keels meet overhead in a pointed arch. Behind it, tarred timber halls and rope sheds climb a gentle rise, and a path of crushed shell runs down toward the landing at Đào Sa Thị. The whole place smells of pitch and wet hemp.
13.lore: The ferrymen of the Nine-Bend River banded together as Lãng Đào Môn in 790, a minor sect (tiểu tông môn) under Tùng Đào Cung that carries most of the river trade. Its disciples learn water arts (thủy pháp) on a deck before they learn them in a hall, and a ferryman who retires burns his first oar at the gate of hulls. Since the Ferry War the sect counts its lost boats aloud each spring, one by one.
13.history: Before 790 the boatmen of Cửu Khúc Xuyên worked alone, each family with its own landing and its own feud. In 790, the year the War of Broken Halberds broke out on the border plain of three sects, they banded together as Lãng Đào Môn under Tùng Đào Cung, to carry the river trade as one. From 800 gold-washers gathered on the sands beside them, and the market of Đào Sa Thị gave the sect its landing. For nearly four centuries its ferries tied the river towns together while Tùng Đào took the tolls. In 1172 the quarrel with Lạc Hà Tông over the river tolls on the Ngư Ca border turned to war, and Lãng Đào's ferries burned; in 1173 Lạc Hà raiders fired its boats at the Đào Sa landing. The Ferry War ended two years after that raid with the tolls split and no land changed, and neither side forgives. Giang Cửu Khúc heads the sect today, and its slipways have not been quiet since.
levels: A covered slipway and a second hall for rope-makers; the watch pagoda gains a lantern storey to signal ferries at night.
A stone dock of its own on the river bend with rows of rebuilt ferries drawn up, and a four-roof pagoda rising behind the gate of hulls.

14.name: Cửu Cao Phái
14.look: Out of a reed marsh rise slender red-lacquered crane-roost towers, each topped with a broad platform of woven reed where the great birds stand and preen. Behind them, terraced halls climb a low wooded rise to a four-roof pagoda. The cry of cranes overhead never quite stops.
14.lore: Crane riders who tamed the first cranes of the nine marshes founded Cửu Cao Phái in 700, a minor sect (tiểu tông môn) of beast tamers (ngự thú sư) sworn to Thiên Xu Tông. Its riders carried the Pivot's messages over Phá Quân's fort in the rebellion, and now circle Tinh Tủy Mạch day and night. In 1197 its head Ung Hạc Minh tamed a crane king that will let no one else ride it, and the young riders compete for the honour of grooming it.
14.history: In 700 crane riders tamed the first cranes of the nine marshes in Dao Quang Lĩnh and founded Cửu Cao Phái; the old line runs that the crane cries in the nine marshes and is heard in the sky. That same year the cranes were first seen landing at Hạc Quy Thôn on the same day every year, and the school has ridden the first of them since. When Phá Quân Môn rose against Thiên Xu, the crane riders stayed loyal, and in 872 they carried the Pivot's messages over the rebel fort. At the war's end in 874 Thiên Xu gave Cửu Cao Phái the rebels' holdings. In 1010 Ung Hạc Minh was born in Hạc Quy Thôn, the year the cranes stayed a month longer, and Ung Hạc Minh now heads the school. After Băng Tâm's claim to Tinh Tủy Mạch was rejected by the Pivot, the school's cranes were set to circle the vein day and night. In 1197 Ung Hạc Minh tamed a crane king that will let no one else ride it.
levels: More roost towers out across the marsh and a long crane stable hall on the lower terrace.
A tall roost tower for the crane king beside a five-roof pagoda, and a stone landing terrace where riders come down from the sky.

15.name: Lê Hoa Am
15.look: A small hermitage of white-plastered halls climbs a steep slope beside the ice fields, inside an orchard of old pear trees whose branches are white with rime most of the year. From below, the rimed orchard looks like a hillside in full blossom even in deep winter. A single three-roof bell pagoda stands above the trees.
15.lore: Lê Hoa Am is a hermitage (am) of ice cultivators, a minor sect (tiểu tông môn) sworn to Băng Tâm Các, and it takes only women. It was founded in 600 by a nun who came after a snow fell like pear blossom overnight in the eighth month. Thái Lê Tuyết has been abbess since 1020, and when Chúc Long Sơn rumbled in 1199 the nuns prayed all winter.
15.history: In 600 a snow that fell like pear blossom overnight in the eighth month brought a nun to the ice fields of Ngọc Hồ Sơn, and she founded Lê Hoa Am where it had fallen. The hermitage swore itself to Băng Tâm Các, which had held the empty ice for more than a century. Its nuns planted pear trees around their halls, and the rime on the branches gave the place the look of its name. The Tiêu family's village of Hòe Âm below came to answer to the hermitage. In 1020 Thái Lê Tuyết became abbess. In 1150 the Tiêu clan sent its first son to the gate; he was turned away for being a son, and became a hunter. In 1199 Chúc Long Sơn rumbled under the ice for the first time since the eruption that buried Hồ Thiên Phái, and the nuns prayed all winter.
levels: A meditation hall cut into the ice field edge and a wider ring of rimed pear trees.
A second bell pagoda higher on the slope, a covered stair between the two, and a walled guest court below for pilgrims.

16.name: Dạ Quang Môn
16.look: A squat fort of rammed red earth sits on the open steppe, ringed by horse lines and sabre racks. Over its gate, on a pillar, stands a great stone cup carved from a pale stone that glows faint green after dusk. Around it the steppe is trampled bare by hooves.
16.lore: Hạng Dạ Bôi gathered the desert raiders and founded Dạ Quang Môn in 970, a minor sect of the demonic path (ma đạo) known for its blood sabres. Since Hạng Dạ Bôi knelt to Sở Ngọc Hồ in 1121, its riders have guarded the very caravans they used to rob. Lately the young blades drink from the night-glowing cups again, the old raiders' rite before a ride, and Băng Tâm's elders pretend not to see.
16.history: Hạng Dạ Bôi was born in 870 to a caravan guard's family in Trường Vân Thành. In 970 Hạng Dạ Bôi gathered the desert raiders and founded Dạ Quang Môn on the steppe beside the caravan road, bound to no lord. For a century and a half its blood sabres preyed on the caravans of Băng Tâm's desert, and the raiders' camp hardened into a fort. In 1119 Băng Tâm Các marched on it. In 1121 Hạng Dạ Bôi knelt to Sở Ngọc Hồ, and Dạ Quang Môn became a vassal of Băng Tâm, and does not forget; its raiders were made to guard the caravans they used to rob. The lotus village of Liên Đường Thôn, on the caravan road, answers to it. In 1194 its young blades drank from the night-glowing cups again, and Băng Tâm's elders pretended not to see.
levels: A second ring of earth walls with stables, and a feasting hall with a dark tiled roof.
A tall watch pagoda over the caravan road and a row of glowing stone cups on the outer wall.

17.name: Trạc Anh Đài
17.look: A low wooded rise above a clear, cold stream, its halls stepping up in grey-tiled tiers among birch and fir. At its foot lies the terrace that gives the sect its name: a broad granite platform running out into the water, strung with long bamboo poles where rows of dyed hat strings hang drying in the wind.
17.lore: Fishers and sea hunters of the frost coast keep this small sect (tông môn) of body cultivators (thể tu), sworn to Băng Tâm Các; its head is Đoàn Thanh Lãng, born in Liên Giang Thành. Every new disciple washes the strings of a reed hat on the terrace on the day they join, after the old fisherman's song: when the water is clear, wash your hat strings in it. When a thaw muddies the stream, no oath is sworn until it runs clear again.
17.history: Until 498 the frost coast belonged to Hàn Giang Môn, whose fishers cultivated alone in the snow on the cold river. When Băng Tâm Các took the coast that year, the fishers stayed and worked on under the Pavilion's flag, keeping the old habits but no sect of their own. In 830 fishers and sea hunters of the frost coast founded Trạc Anh Đài on this rise, sworn to Băng Tâm Các as their lord. The founders chose the place for its stream, which runs clear even in the spring floods, and built the washing terrace before any hall. They trained the body rather than the sword, hardening hunters for the winter sea and the ice floes. The woodcutters of Tiều Lộ Thôn came to answer to the terrace. In 990 Đoàn Thanh Lãng was born in Liên Giang Thành during a cold rain that joined the river by night; he leads the terrace now.
levels: A second terrace is cut lower into the stream, a covered hall rises at the crest, and smokehouses for seal meat line the path up the rise.
The halls reach the crest under a tall watch pavilion, a stone stair joins every terrace, and the drying poles stretch in long bright rows down both banks.

18.name: Bình Thủy Môn
18.look: A sect seat on a low green headland over the strait, its halls rising in grey-tile tiers to a single high hall. On the point stands a tall mast hung with green lanterns, lit every dusk to mark the crossing, and below it the ferries come and go from the market quay.
18.lore: Strangers far from home, meeting on the island by chance like duckweed on water, founded this sect in 520 and live by sea trade, ships and the strait crossing, sworn to Lạc Hà Tông. Every disciple must have been born somewhere else, and gives the name of their home village at the gate; it is written on a green lantern, and the mast carries the homes of all who have served. Under Bùi Phiêu Bình, head since 1110, the crossing runs every day of the year.
18.history: A generation before the sect, Cô Vụ Đảo became Lạc Hà Tông's land when Giang Bích Không swore Cô Phàm Các to Lạc Hà in the Strait Oath. In 520 strangers far from home, who had met on the island like duckweed on water, founded Bình Thủy Môn on this headland. In 525 a market of chance meetings, Tương Phùng Thị, grew up at the quay below the seat, and the sect's ferries made it the island's door to the mainland. When the fleet of Cô Phàm Các was lost at sea in the Age of the North Star Compact, Bình Thủy's ferries became the island's surest ships. In the Age of Vein Wars Wave Rock split at Lãng Thạch Thôn, one of the sect's villages, and gave up a sea cave of old Cô Phàm charts; some say the best of them are kept in the seat's archive. In 1110 Bùi Phiêu Bình became head, and under him the strait crossing runs every day of the year, storm or calm.
levels: A ferry hall rises by the quay, and a second tier of halls climbs the headland behind the main hall.
The headland is terraced to the point, a covered stair runs down to a stone pier, and the lantern mast is doubled with a second mast across the cove.

19.name: Mục Vân Trang
19.look: A manor seat on a low rise near the coast of the open plain, its halls climbing in tiers to a tall stable tower under a sweeping grey roof. Around the foot of the rise runs a great oval racing track of packed earth, and on it pale spirit horses (linh mã) move like clouds.
19.lore: Herders of the open plain founded Mục Vân Trang in 740 to raise spirit horses that run like clouds under the endless sky of Trường Thiên Nguyên. It is sworn to Lạc Hà Tông and its body cultivators train with their beasts, riders and horses together. Its head, Khấu Mục Vân, was born in Thanh Điền the same night as a spirit foal that would let no one else ride it. Its horses won every race at the Lạc Hà festival of 1185, and Kim Vạn Lý, who bet on them, lost anyway; how is still argued in every tavern on the plain.
19.history: Lạc Hà Tông extended its rule over the open grassland of Trường Thiên Nguyên in the Age of Seven Seats, and the herders of the plain kept their flocks under it. In 740 herders founded Mục Vân Trang to raise spirit horses that run like clouds. As its herds grew, the manor took the villages of Thanh Điền, Điền Viên and Chu Tân under its hand. In 940 Khấu Mục Vân was born in Thanh Điền, and a spirit foal born the same night would let no one else ride it; he leads the manor now. Its horses became the pride of the plain, ridden by Lạc Hà's couriers across the grassland. In 1185 Mục Vân Trang's horses won every race at the Lạc Hà festival, and Kim Vạn Lý bet on them and lost anyway. The track below the manor has never been busier.
levels: A second stable hall and a long covered viewing gallery rise beside the track.
The manor climbs to a high riders' hall above the stable tower, and a second track loops out toward the coast with stone stands.

20.name: Thiên Bảo Trai
20.look: A tall sect seat on a dry steppe rise above the bay, its stacked pagoda roofs ridged in gilt bronze that burns in the evening sun. Around its base a ring of refining furnace chimneys trails thin smoke in green, copper and violet.
20.lore: Founded in 350 as a refiners' workshop beside the bay, Thiên Bảo Trai refines artifacts (luyện khí) and runs the treasure market of Thu Thủy Loan, sworn to Lạc Hà Tông; its sign still reads that the riches of the land are heaven's treasures. Since Phan Vật Hoa became mistress in 1050 it holds a treasure auction every season. Buyers sit behind screens and bid by bell, so no one knows who bought what.
20.history: Thiên Bảo Trai was founded beside the bay in 350 as a refiners' workshop, its sign declaring the riches of the land heaven's treasures. In 360 red gold was found at Xích Kim, and the workshop bought the mine before Lạc Hà's stewards heard of it. By 500 a market for the land's riches, Vật Hoa Thị, had grown beside it. In 700 its refiners were washing their finest work in the clear brooks of Khê Đầu and Khê Thanh. When Kim Cốc Viên collapsed and its city burned, the Trai hired, in 1004, the ruined merchants who could still count. In 1050 Phan Vật Hoa became mistress and began a treasure auction every season. In 1180 a buyer from Thiên Bảo Trai bought a white bear brought alive out of Vô Tung Lâm at Mộc Lan Thành, and the Trai's reach now runs from the frost coast to the bay.
levels: An auction hall with a gilded double roof rises on a new terrace, and the furnace ring grows a second row.
The pagoda gains a higher tier with a gilt spire, and a walled treasury court with its own gate faces the market road.

21.name: Nam Phố Đường
21.look: Under old forest near the southern shore stands one long hall whose beams and rafters are painted, end to end, with drifting clouds, so that through the open doors the roof seems to float. Lines of yellow paper hang drying between the trunks, and the smell of cinnabar ink and pine soot carries far down the road.
21.lore: Nam Phố Đường, the Hall of the Southern Shore, is a minor sect of talisman (phù lục) makers and scribes sworn to Lạc Hà Tông, founded in 880 by scribes who painted the clouds of the southern shore. Its hall-mistress Châu Phi Vân, born in Tang Ma Thành, keeps the hall and the maple town and brook village in its care. Every new scribe must paint one cloud on the hall's beams before selling a single talisman, so the ceiling grows a little denser every year. The scribes still wince at the talisman contest of 1190 at Hạc Đinh Thị, which they lost to a girl of fourteen.
21.history: In the Age of First Gates Lạc Hà Tông's founder planted maples on this shore, and the forest here became the sect's quiet hinterland. Through the long North Star Compact, scribes came to paint the clouds of the southern shore and drifted into the habit of selling charms to Lạc Hà's disciples. In 880 they founded Nam Phố Đường as a minor sect under Lạc Hà, and raised the cloud-painted hall. The maple town of Phong Lâm Trấn and the brook village of Hoa Khê came into the hall's keeping. In 930 Châu Phi Vân was born in Tang Ma Thành, and in time she rose to be hall-mistress. When the Ferry War came to the Ngư Ca border, the hall's ward talismans went north with Lạc Hà's disciples. In 1190 its best scribes lost the talisman contest at Hạc Đinh Thị to the fourteen-year-old Tô Mộ Vân.
levels: A second painted hall rises behind the first, joined by a covered gallery, and a walled yard of paper-drying lines spreads under the trees.
A three-roof scripture pavilion with cloud-painted beams rises above the forest canopy, ringed by scribes' cells and a small ink-grinding mill on a brook.

22.name: Củng Tinh Quán
22.look: On a high open shoulder of the plain, beside a round mountain lake, stands a quiet abbey (quán) of low walls and dark tile. In the middle of its main court, on a raised stone platform open to the sky, turns a great bronze armillary of nested rings, green with age, that follows the Northern Dipper through the year.
22.lore: Củng Tinh Quán, the Abbey of the Bowing Stars, is a minor sect of formation masters and star-diviners sworn to Thiên Xu Tông, named for the stars that bow to the pole. Its head Thẩm Bắc Thần keeps the Tuyền Cơ Nghi, the armillary finished in 180, and the abbey reads the Dipper both in the sky and in the still water of Tinh Lạc Hồ; it also keeps the star-iron mine at Vẫn Tinh. In 501 the armillary warned of war and no one listened; since then the star-readers send every omen to the Pivot in writing, sealed, so that no one can say again that they were not told.
22.history: Star-readers founded Củng Tinh Quán on the high plain in 150, a vassal whose very name honours its lord, the Heavenly Pivot. In 155 they found that the high lake Tinh Lạc Hồ holds the Dipper at night as clearly as the sky, and by 160 they were keeping the mine at Vẫn Tinh, where iron from a fallen star is dug. In 180 they finished the Tuyền Cơ Nghi, an armillary that follows the Northern Dipper through the year. In 501 it showed the Dipper's handle turned toward the heart, and the abbey warned of war; no one listened, and the War of the Pivot began the next year. In 789 the armillary went dark for a whole night, and the star-readers burned incense and waited; the War of Broken Halberds broke out the next year. Since then the abbey has served the Pivot as its watchers of the sky, and Thẩm Bắc Thần heads it now.
levels: A second court with a star-map paved into its floor opens beside the armillary, and a covered walk leads down to the lakeshore.
A tall three-roof observation tower rises over the abbey, its open top deck facing the pole, and the walls take in the near shore of the lake.

23.name: Thối Tinh Môn
23.look: On a steep mountain flank, a sect of soot-dark stone halls climbs beside a stream led through a long cascade of stone quenching troughs, each spilling into the next. White steam bursts from the troughs whenever a blade is plunged, and the whole slope seems to smoke.
23.lore: Thối Tinh Môn, the Gate of the Quenched Stars, is a minor sect of weapon forgers (luyện khí) sworn to Thiên Xu Tông; its smiths quench star iron in mountain water and name their work after their lord's stars. In 600 it forged the halberd Trầm Sa Kích for the young officer Quý Trường Kích, and the forge where it was made is kept swept and cold, never used again. Its head Cát Lưu Quang forged a blade from the star that fell near Thanh Bách.
23.history: Smiths who quenched star iron in the mountain river founded Thối Tinh Môn in 330 under Thiên Xu, and in 335 they claimed the Mine of the Iron from Beyond the Sky, saying its ore fell with the stars. Through the Age of Seven Seats they armed the Pivot's disciples, and the War of the Pivot kept every trough steaming. In 600 they forged the halberd Trầm Sa Kích from star iron for a young officer of Thiên Xu, Quý Trường Kích. Two centuries later he fell as war marshal on Chiết Kích Nguyên and was laid under the Vạn Cốt Trủng with the halberd, whose iron has not worn away. The smiths count that as the proof of their quenching. In 1050 Cát Lưu Quang became head and forged a blade from the star that fell near Thanh Bách.
levels: A second cascade of troughs and a walled ore yard open beside the first, and the forge hall gains a third roof.
A tall smoke tower of black stone crowns the seat, and a covered stair runs from the forges down to the mine road.

24.name: Phất Y Cốc
24.look: In a high green valley ringed by grey peaks, a modest sect of plain timber halls stands behind a tall stone gate whose name board is left deliberately blank. Swordsmen pass in and out beneath the empty board without a word.
24.lore: Phất Y Cốc, the Valley of the Brushed Sleeve, is a minor sword sect sworn to Thiên Xu Tông that hires out its swordsmen; its name comes from the poem of the swordsman who, deed done, brushes his sleeve and goes, hiding body and name. Its swords are forged from the ore of Can Tương, as its founder began. Disciples carve their names on nothing and take no credit for any deed, and the blank board over the gate is the sect's only boast. Its head Thang Vô Tạ fought Tư Không Hạc Niên to a standstill on Cùng Mục Phong in 1130, and will not speak of it.
24.history: In 560 a swordsman who brushed his sleeve and left after every deed founded Phất Y Cốc in this high valley, and dug the ore of Can Tương for its swords. He left no name on the gate, and none has been added since. The valley grew into a sword sect sworn to Thiên Xu, hiring out its swordsmen across the heart through the long Compact, often on errands no sect would put its own name to. In the Age of Vein Wars its blades were wanted on every border, and its swordsmen took pay from either side but, by the valley's rule, never crossed swords with one another. In 1130 its head Thang Vô Tạ dueled Tư Không Hạc Niên on Cùng Mục Phong for three days; neither won, and Tư Không Hạc Niên left without a sect. From 1131 Thang Vô Tạ would not speak of the duel, and his disciples began to climb the peak to see the sword marks.
levels: A walled practice yard of raked sand and a row of guest lodgings for hiring patrons stand below the gate.
A tall sword pavilion of three plain roofs rises at the valley head, with a stone stair to a meditation ledge above, and still no name carved anywhere.

25.name: Trúc Thực Viên
25.look: On a low grassy plain, terraced beds of tall golden bamboo bow under heavy tassels of seed, and between them long swept earthen floors are spread with seed drying in the sun. A plain hall roofed with split bamboo stands at the centre.
25.lore: Trúc Thực Viên, the Garden of the Bamboo Seed, is a minor sect of spirit farmers (linh thực sư) sworn to Phượng Minh Cung, founded in 760 to grow the bamboo seed the phoenix eats; it grows spirit grain and beast feed too, and keeps the coast village of Bích Lãng. Its head Ninh Trúc Thực bred a bamboo that seeds every year instead of once in sixty, and the garden's seed now goes to beast keepers across Phượng Minh's lands. Disciples carry the first seed of every harvest up Cao Cương Phong, in case the phoenix comes.
25.history: The phoenix, the saying goes, eats nothing but the seed of the bamboo, and since its founding Phượng Minh Cung had kept a few wild groves of it for its rites, though they seeded only once in sixty years. In 760 spirit farmers founded Trúc Thực Viên on the plain below the ridges to grow that seed, sworn to Phượng Minh. They added spirit grain and beast feed as the palace's needs grew, and took the coast village of Bích Lãng into their keeping. In 1050 Ninh Trúc Thực became head and bred a bamboo that seeds every year instead of once in sixty. The new seed turned the garden from a shrine into a granary, and beast keepers across the south began to buy from it. In the Cinnabar Vein War a century later its seed and grain fed Phượng Minh's war beasts and its wounded at Thanh Khê.
levels: A second terrace of seed bamboo and a woven-bamboo seed store join the garden, and a beast pen of woven bamboo stands at the edge.
A tall three-roof hall of bamboo and red timber rises over the beds, with stepped seed terraces spreading from it like a fan.

26.name: Lễ Tuyền Phái
26.look: A low rise on the open grassland by the shore of Triêu Hà Hồ carries a short stack of pale timber halls and a three-roofed pagoda. Below the pagoda a round basin of white stone brims with spring water under one enormous wutong (ngô đồng) tree, its broad leaves always beaded wet. Stoneware jars sealed with red clay stand in rows on the lowest terrace, warming in the sun.
26.lore: A minor sect (tiểu tông môn) of healers under Phượng Minh Cung, Lễ Tuyền Phái brews spirit wine (linh tửu) from the sweet spring the phoenix is said to drink from, and treats the sick with it. Its head, Mai Lễ Tuyền, keeps the lake springs and the herb gardens of Lục Dã Trấn. Disciples may not draw from the basin with metal; they use gourds, so that the spring is never cut. Since the wine first went to the Pivot's table, the jars that leave the spring carry the school's name further than its arts ever have.
26.history: In 660, in the Age of the North Star Compact, healers who brewed wine from the sweet spring founded Lễ Tuyền Phái beside the lake, under the protection of Phượng Minh Cung. Two years later, in 662, the green meadows of Lục Dã were given to the school for its herb gardens. For two centuries it stayed small, known in the rice towns for fevers cured and wounds washed clean. In 850 Mai Lễ Tuyền was born in Lục Dã Trấn, and it was said her first cry made the spring flow sweeter; she grew up to lead the school. Through the Age of Vein Wars its healers tended the wounded of their lord's short wars and took no side of their own. In 1140 its spirit wine was served at the Pivot's table for the first time, and Thiên Xu Tông set a standing yearly order for it. Envoys of the Pivot now come to the spring each year to fetch the jars.
levels: A second pagoda roof and a wine cellar dug into the rise; the spring basin gains a carved stone canopy and a covered walk runs down to the lake.
The whole rise is terraced with herb courts and a guest hall for the Pivot's envoys; a white balustrade rings the wutong and a long jar store lines the shore.

27.name: Hồng Đậu Trang
27.look: Where the rain forest meets the sea, a walled manor of red-lacquered halls rises in three terraces, half buried in glossy leaves. Its entrance is a perfect round moon gate of red lacquer, so thickly wreathed in vines of scarlet, black-eyed beans that the lacquer barely shows. A path of crushed shell leads to it from the forest road.
27.lore: Hồng Đậu Trang is a minor ma đạo sect under Thính Vũ Lâu, a house of poisons and charms behind a gracious door. Its mistress Nghê Hồng Đậu found the sword Phi Hồng in this forest and built the manor around it. The door opens to guests of every sect and the house is famous for its hospitality; it is also said that those who stay too long do not leave. Red beans grow in the south, the old poem says, and here everyone knows the lovesick bean is a deadly poison.
27.history: In the early years of the North Star Compact, Diệp Phi Hồng, sworn sister of Lạc Anh Phái's new head, kept the sword Phi Hồng when the school's founder died without naming an heir. More than a century later, long after Lạc Anh had broken apart, she carried Phi Hồng into the rain forest of Tiêu Vũ Lâm and taught its art to no one, and the sword waited there for an heir. In 800 Nghê Hồng Đậu was born in Thu Trì Thành, and red beans grew from the cracks in her mother's doorstep. In 910 she found Phi Hồng where Diệp Phi Hồng had left it, and founded Hồng Đậu Trang around it under the lordship of Thính Vũ Lâu. By 912 the manor's gracious door was open to guests from every sect, and the saying began that those who stay too long do not leave. Its poisons and charms found ready buyers once the Night Rain Market opened in Thu Trì the next century. In 1197 travellers on the forest road found red beans scattered on the path to the manor, and stepped around them; no one has said what they meant.
levels: A guest wing on stilts over the shore and a walled poison garden behind the halls; the moon gate gains a twin on the sea side.
Three walled courts climb the slope to a red pagoda where Phi Hồng is kept; the bean vines now cover the whole outer wall.

28.name: Xuyên Lâm Môn
28.look: On a high shoulder of Kinh Trập Sơn above the rain forest, a sect gate of plain grey stone stands at the head of a long stair that drops straight into the trees. Beside it an open-sided gatehouse holds racks of worn hardwood guide staffs, one taken down for every traveller led through the forest. Above the gate, small halls climb the ridge on narrow terraces.
28.lore: Xuyên Lâm Môn is a minor sect of staff fighters under Thính Vũ Lâu, who guide travellers through the rain forest and pay no heed to the rain beating the leaves. It is a chính đạo (righteous path) school under a ma đạo lord, and does not hide its dislike of the Tower's new arts. Its head, Úc Diệp Thanh, guided every traveller himself in his first year. A traveller returns the staff at the far end of the road, and the next guide carries it home.
28.history: Staff fighters who guided travellers through the rain forest founded Xuyên Lâm Môn in 690, in the Age of the North Star Compact, under the lordship of Thính Vũ Lâu. They took their name from an old line about paying no heed to the rain that pierces the forest and beats the leaves. Their footwork was trained in the bamboo of Đả Diệp Lâm below the gate, and their guides kept the forest roads open in war and peace. In 907 the school refused the arts of the Night Rain Edict, and its head walked the forest road alone for a month in protest. The Tower let the protest pass, and the school kept its own ways and its coastal town of Vọng Hải. In 1170 Úc Diệp Thanh became head and guided every traveller himself for a year. In 1199 an earthquake raised a river isle at Hà Châu, and Xuyên Lâm claimed it against its own lord.
levels: A second staff house at the foot of the stair, and a roofed rest hall halfway down for travellers.
A walled mountain gate with a training court cut into the ridge and a covered stair running the full way down into the forest.

29.name: Phần Vũ Đường
29.look: On the grassland inland from the red cliffs, a field of smoking volcanic vents opens in the ground, and around the largest a hall of red-brown stone climbs in tiers. The vent pits nearest the hall have stone sitting ledges cut into their lips, worn smooth by bodies. Above them a tall mast of black stone flies the crimson war banner Xích Hà Kỳ.
29.lore: Phần Vũ Đường is a minor sect of body tempering (luyện thể) under Phượng Minh Cung, whose disciples sit in the vents until their feathers burn and walk out reborn. Its head, Hùng Phần Vũ, born in Ngũ Thải Thành, founded it young in the vents where Xích Thành once stood. Phượng Minh lent it the Xích Hà Kỳ, the banner of the sect it destroyed, and everyone in the south reads the loan as both a trust and a warning. The mulberry town of Tang Điền belongs to it.
29.history: The vents of Đan Huyệt Châu fed Xích Thành Môn's fire arts from its founding in 250, and its banner Xích Hà Kỳ was woven from fire-silk spun in them. When Phượng Minh destroyed Xích Thành Môn under writ in 590, the vent field was left without cultivators for more than four centuries. In 980 Hùng Phần Vũ was born in Ngũ Thải Thành, and a red feather fell on his cradle. In 1020 the young Hùng Phần Vũ founded Phần Vũ Đường in the vents where Xích Thành once stood, and Phượng Minh lent it the Xích Hà Kỳ. By 1025 its disciples were sitting in the vents until their feathers burned and walking out reborn; the first of them died trying. Since then the hall has sent its tempered fighters to the Palace's wars, and its sitting ledges are worn smooth.
levels: A second tier of halls and a walled court around the sitting vents, with a stone bath for the burned.
A stepped red-stone hall rises high over the whole vent field, and the black mast stands on its top terrace.

30.name: Yên Ba Thành
30.look: A walled port city stands where a river meets the sea, its quays and lower streets often lost in a drifting blue-green mist. Above the haze rises a slender pagoda of green-glazed tile at the end of the harbour mole, and a bronze horn at its top sounds through the fog to guide the ships home.
30.lore: Yên Ba Thành is Thúy Vi Tông's port and the busiest market of its coast, where grain from the cape villages and the trade of the white sands meet. Sailors say the mist on the river waves makes a man sad, and the city answers with noise: the horn, drums at the gates, and taverns that stay open late. A protective formation (trận pháp) laid by Thúy Vi keeps the worst sea fogs out of the upper town.
30.history: A generation after Thúy Vi Tông took the cape of snow and fire, the sect needed a harbour to tie it to its hills. In 590 it founded Yên Ba Thành, a port in the mist of the river waves, at the river's mouth, and raised the horn pagoda on its mole. The city grew into the cape's market, buying fish, wool and grain from the villages around it. Through one long, hard winter early in the Age of Vein Wars it lived on grain from Hòa Thử Thôn, and its granary wardens still buy from that village first. Generations later a daughter of the Thẩm clan of Bạch Sa married into one of its merchant houses, and the white sands became a trading town tied to Yên Ba. Only a few years ago, after a poor harvest drove grain prices in Mục Ca Thành beyond the herders' reach, they came to sing their songs for coin in Yên Ba's streets.
levels: The walls extend up the river bank and a second quay with green-roofed warehouses lines the river mouth.
A great stone harbour gate spans the river behind the mole, and the upper town's green roofs climb a terraced hill clear of the mist.

31.name: Hàn Tân Thành
31.look: A walled port city of grey roofs stands on bleak tundra coast where a broad river meets the sea at a shallow ford. Across the ford march a line of tall stone pillars, each with a lamp niche, marking the safe crossing for wagons and boats alike.
31.lore: Hàn Tân Thành is the northern ford and port of the cold coast, a city of fishers and ferrymen. It has changed hands twice and remembers both: the year the Cold Ford came home, the fishers lit lamps on every boat for a month, and the lamps in the ford pillars are still lit on that month's first night each year. Old families keep a jar of pine resin by the door, a joke about the tax they once could not pay.
31.history: In 430 fishers and ferrymen built Hàn Tân Thành at the cold ford of the north coast, under the protection of Không Sơn Viện. When Không Sơn's last master gave his hills to Thúy Vi Tông's founder in 500, the Cold Ford came with them. In 668 Tùng Đào Cung marched on the Cold Ford coast without asking the Pivot for a writ, and in 672 it took the coast and the city; Chung Hoài Cực, Kỳ Tùng Ẩn's old drinking friend, let it stand, and the Compact's first crack showed. Under Tùng Đào the fishers were taxed in pine resin they did not have, and from 674 many left for the hills. In 901 Thúy Vi marched to take back the Cold Ford, this time holding the Pivot's writ. In 905 it retook the coast and Hàn Tân Thành after more than two centuries, and in 906, when the Cold Ford came home, the fishers lit lamps on every boat for a month.
levels: The walls reach the far bank and a fortified bridge-gate rises at the middle of the ford.
A tall beacon tower stands over the harbour, and a second line of pillars marks a deep channel for larger ships.

32.name: Tùng Gian Thành
32.look: A walled city at a river mouth on the coast, its grey roofs half hidden among tall pines that grow inside and along its walls. In the wall facing the palace ridge stands a huge round moon gate, and from the harbour road the moon rises framed in it among the pines.
32.lore: Tùng Gian Thành was Tùng Đào Cung's first city and is its port on the coast, with a formation laid over its walls. Its people never cut a pine inside the walls and build around the trees. On the Night of a Thousand Pines they hang a lantern on every tree around the city, and one of its great halls is roofed with beams from a single fallen pine, carved by the Lâm clan of Lộc Minh.
32.history: In 240 Tùng Đào Cung raised Tùng Gian Thành among the pines below its palace, its first city. It grew as the palace's port where the river meets the sea, with the pine sea's timber, resin and pilgrims passing through its gates. Long after the founding, the Lâm clan's woodcarvers of Lộc Minh made the beams of a new hall in the city from a single fallen pine. In 880 the city held its first Night of a Thousand Pines, hanging a lantern on every tree around it, and the festival has been held ever since. The city's formation keeps the sea storms off its trees, and townsfolk boast that no pine inside the walls has fallen since the city was founded.
levels: The walls grow to take in a new pine grove, and a carved timber hall with a double roof rises behind the moon gate.
A second moon-viewing terrace tower stands above the harbour, and a stone mole extends the port into the sea.

33.name: Đào Thanh Thành
33.look: A walled river city under endless pine, its quays set high up the bank on tall stone steps. Below them, at low water, a row of old drowned quay pillars stands in the current like a broken fence, marking where the city once met the river. When the wind turns, the forest above roars like surf, and the streets go quiet to listen.
33.lore: Tùng Đào Cung founded the city in 300 on the river below its forests, and named it for the sound of the pine waves heard from the seat above. Timber merchants, river traders and the families of Tùng Đào's outer disciples live here. On windy evenings the townsfolk climb the walls to hear the pines, and a child who sleeps through the first great wind of autumn is teased for a year.
33.history: Tùng Đào Cung took the river basin of Cửu Khúc Xuyên in the Age of First Gates, and in 300 founded Đào Thanh Thành on the river below its forests. The city grew as the palace's market and river gate, shipping timber and pine resin downstream. In 700 a great flood on the Nine-Bend River drowned three villages, and Tùng Đào moved the city's quays up the bank; the old pillars were left standing in the water. The city prospered through the long peace of the North Star Compact, and is said to have sent boats and grain north in the Long Lake War of the Age of Vein Wars. When the Ferry War burned Lãng Đào's ferries, its merchants felt it in their ledgers, and the split tolls still sour the wharf taverns. Today it is the busiest city on the river, and the pines above it are as loud as ever.
levels: A second row of wharf warehouses along the high quays and a pine-roofed listening terrace on the upper wall.
An outer wall reaching to the forest edge, a covered bridge over the river, and a five-roof bell pagoda that answers the pine waves.

34.name: Khai Dương Thành
34.look: A walled port city where the northern road meets a river mouth and the sea. Its east gate tower carries a great polished bronze disc that catches the first light before dawn, so the gate seems to burn while the streets below are still dark. Masts crowd the river quays under the walls.
34.lore: Thiên Xu Tông founded Khai Dương Thành on the northern road in 280, naming it for a star of the Northern Dipper. In 900 its gate was rebuilt to face the morning star, and travellers say the city wakes before the sun: bakers, porters and ferrymen are at work in the dark. Late sleepers are called guests here, even if they were born in the city.
34.history: A generation after Thiên Xu Tông extended its protection over Dao Quang Lĩnh, in 280, it founded Khai Dương Thành on the northern road where it reaches the sea. The city became the Pivot's northern port, shipping ore and timber by river and by sea. Through the Age of the North Star Compact it grew quietly rich, far from the wars of the south. When Thiên Xu founded Thanh Bách Thành on the same road in the first years of the Compact, Khai Dương became the road's harbour end. In the Phá Quân rebellion of the Age of Vein Wars, the city fed and shipped the Pivot's forces in the mountains above. In 900 its gate was rebuilt to face the morning star and the bronze disc was set over it; travellers say the city wakes before the sun.
levels: A stone sea mole with warehouses along it, and a second bronze disc on the river gate.
An outer harbour wall, a lighthouse tower on the mole, and a new walled quarter climbing the riverbank inland.

35.name: Trường Vân Thành
35.look: A walled harbour city at the edge of the desert, where a river reaches the sea under the snow mountains. A long roofed caravan gallery runs straight through the city from the land gate to the docks, so goods pass from camel to ship without seeing the sun. On cloudy days a faint shimmer of a ward formation hangs over the walls, and long clouds lie on the peaks behind.
35.lore: Băng Tâm Các founded Trường Vân Thành in 470 at the edge of the desert, under the long clouds over the snow mountains, and it is still the sect's door to the sea. Caravan guards, ship chandlers and Băng Tâm's officers crowd the taverns of the gallery. Hạng Dạ Bôi was born here to a caravan guard's family in 870, and the guard families of the city have never let anyone forget it.
35.history: In 470, the year it claimed the ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn, Băng Tâm Các founded Trường Vân Thành at the edge of the desert, under the long clouds over the snow mountains. The city became the sea gate of the desert road, and the sect raised a ward formation (trận pháp) over its walls. When Băng Tâm built Cô Thành on the caravan road half a century later, Trường Vân became its supply port. Through the Desert Road War the city sent water and swords to the lone fortress, until Cô Thành fell. In 870 Hạng Dạ Bôi was born here to a caravan guard's family; a century later Hạng Dạ Bôi founded Dạ Quang Môn and raided the caravans that fed the city. Since Dạ Quang Môn knelt to Băng Tâm, its raiders have guarded those caravans instead, and the gallery is busy again.
levels: A second caravan gallery branching to a new dock, and a stone caravanserai inside the land gate.
An outer wall around the docks, a lighthouse on the river mouth, and a taller ward formation pagoda at the city's centre.

36.name: Liên Giang Thành
36.look: A grey port city where a cold river meets the sea, its walls running down both banks to the harbour. Across the river mouth stretches a long roofed bridge of dark timber and grey tile, its eaves hung with racks of silver ice-fish drying in the rain.
36.lore: The fishers of Hàn Giang Môn built the city and it still smells of their trade; under Băng Tâm Các its people pay their tax in ice-fish, as they have since the frost coast fell. Cold rain comes in off the sea at night and joins the river, and locals say a child born in such a rain will never drown; Đoàn Thanh Lãng, head of Trạc Anh Đài, was born on such a night. The city's line is the first of Băng Tâm's own poem: cold rain joins the river by night.
36.history: Hàn Giang Môn founded Liên Giang Thành in 350, where the cold rain joins the river, as the harbour of its fisher cultivators (tu sĩ). For a century and a half its boats worked the cold river and the frost coast under the Gate of the Cold River. In the last years of the Age of Seven Seats Băng Tâm Các made war on Hàn Giang for the coast, and in 498 Hàn Giang fell with its last head Liễu Cô Chu; the city passed to the Pavilion with the rest of Hàn Sương Châu. From 499 the old sect's fishers kept fishing the cold river under Băng Tâm's flag and paid their tax in ice-fish, a custom still kept. Old people say the roofed bridge was raised in Hàn Giang's time so the fishers could mend nets out of the rain. In 990 Đoàn Thanh Lãng was born here during a cold rain that joined the river by night, and grew up to lead Trạc Anh Đài. Today the city is the frost coast's oldest port and Băng Tâm's door to the sea.
levels: The roofed bridge is doubled with a second span, new ice-houses line the quays, and the walls take in the fishers' quarter on the far bank.
A tall grey drum tower rises over the harbour, the quays run out in stone piers to the sea, and both banks are walled to the forest edge.

37.name: Đàm Ảnh Thành
37.look: A low walled port city on the island's grassy shore where a river meets the sea. In its heart lies a large round pool, so still that the clouds and the city's roofs lie upside down in it, ringed with open pavilions where painters set up their easels.
37.lore: Cô Phàm Các built the city in 410 and it outlived the sect; now it is Lạc Hà Tông's, and lives by fish, trade and painters. Painters come from the mainland to paint the sky upside down in the pool, and a painting made here is signed at the bottom, not the top. The blind Đoạn Thương Hải, who survived the Hóa Thần tribulation (thiên kiếp) that killed his master, has lived beside the pool since 1062 and listens to it instead of looking at it.
37.history: Cô Phàm Các, the sailors' sect of Cô Vụ Đảo, founded only a decade before, built Đàm Ảnh Thành in 410, and below it the harbour of Bích Không Cảng, from which its sails vanished into the blue. At the close of the Age of Seven Seats the Strait Oath swore Cô Phàm Các to Lạc Hà Tông. Nearly three centuries after the city's founding a storm sank the whole Cô Phàm fleet with its head Mã Viễn Ảnh, and the city lost its masters in a night; Lạc Hà's stewards took it in hand. A year later the harbour below was abandoned, and the city turned to its river quay and its pool. By 800 the pool mirrored the clouds so clearly that painters came from the mainland to paint the sky upside down. In 1060 a Hóa Thần tribulation over the island sea killed the master of Đoạn Thương Hải, who survived it blind, holding the Thương Tang Kính. In 1062 he settled in Đàm Ảnh Thành, and he has listened to the pool ever since.
levels: A painters' hall with long open galleries rises on the pool's north side, and the river quay is rebuilt in stone.
A second walled ward takes in the river's far bank, and a tall pavilion over the water is built so its reflection completes it in the pool.

38.name: Nhạn Thanh Thành
38.look: A walled city where a river meets the sea on the dry steppe coast, its grey roofs crowded around wool warehouses. Over the main gate rises a tower whose two upswept roofs spread like the wings of a goose in flight, and the wild geese pass over it in long formations each autumn.
38.lore: Lạc Hà Tông founded the city in 450 where the wild geese fly in formation, and it is the wool market of the western plain; Kim Vạn Lý, the richest merchant of the west, made his name here. Since the cold year of 1120, when archers shot the low-flying geese from the walls, no one may shoot a goose in the city. Its scholars retire to Điền Viên Thôn to farm.
38.history: Lạc Hà Tông took the open grassland of Trường Thiên Nguyên in the Age of Seven Seats, and in 450 founded Nhạn Thanh Thành on the western plain where the wild geese fly in formation. The city grew on the plain's wool and grain, shipped from its river harbour. By the Age of Vein Wars its scholars were retiring to farm the gardens and fields of Điền Viên Thôn, which fed the city. In 1040 Kim Vạn Lý bought the wool of the whole plain in one season and became the richest merchant of the west. In 1120 the wild geese flew so low over the city in a cold year that archers shot them from the walls, and the city forbade it ever after. Kim Vạn Lý still lives here, and the goose gate is the first thing the herders see when they drive their flocks to market.
levels: A great wool exchange with a long grey roof rises by the harbour, and the walls take in the dyers' quarter.
A second winged tower is raised over the river gate, and stone wool warehouses line both banks to the sea.

39.name: Tử Điện Thành
39.look: A walled port city on the bay where a river meets the sea, its grey roofs packed tight inside strong walls. Above them rises a tall armoury tower roofed in violet-glazed tile, and on clear evenings the faint violet shimmer of its ward array (trận pháp) hangs over the whole city.
39.lore: Lạc Anh Phái founded the city on the bay side of the Petal Shore in 360; Lạc Hà Tông took it by the Pivot's judgement in 620 and renamed it Tử Điện Thành for its armoury, after the purple-lightning sword Tử Điện. Its smiths and guards are the most disciplined in the bay. Old families still plant a peach tree in the courtyard for Lạc Anh, though the city's first name is all but forgotten.
39.history: Lạc Anh Phái founded a city on the bay side of the Petal Shore in 360; it would bear another name before it bore its last. The same year Lạc Hà Tông forged twin swords for its armoury, Tử Điện and Thanh Sương, after the purple lightning and blue frost of an old general's blades. Two and a half centuries later Lạc Anh Phái split over its inheritance and its last head, Khương Vọng Nguyệt, vanished. Lạc Hà and Thính Vũ Lâu both claimed the empty Petal Shore, their disciples fought in the burning orchards, and Hồng Vũ Thành burned. In 620 the Pivot's judgement gave the bay to Lạc Hà and the forest to Thính Vũ, and Lạc Hà renamed the bay city Tử Điện Thành, for its armoury; it raised a ward array so the fire would not come twice. In the War of Broken Halberds Thanh Sương fell from its bearer's hand on Chiết Kích Nguyên, and no one has dared go back for it. Late in the Age of Vein Wars Tô Vãn Chiếu became head of Lạc Hà Tông and took the sword Tử Điện.
levels: A second armoury hall with violet tile rises inside a new inner wall, and the harbour gains a war-boat slip.
The walls are doubled on the landward side with gate towers, and the ward array's shimmer brightens into a clear violet dome over the bay front.

40.name: Tinh Hán Thành
40.look: Thiên Xu's port on the inland sea sits where a river meets the shore, a walled grid of grey roofs behind a long curving breakwater. The breakwater is the reef itself: a line of great white arched ribs, the bones of the old sea-serpent, rising out of the water with stone packed between them. At night the harbour lamps and the Milky Way in the water make the city seem set among stars.
40.lore: Tinh Hán Thành, the City of the Star River, was founded by Thiên Xu Tông in 260 on the reef left by the sea-serpent a nameless swordsman killed in 15. A city formation (trận pháp) runs along its walls and the bone reef, and formation masters are common here; the freelance master Vệ Văn Cơ was born in the city and drew formations in the harbour sand before he could talk. Wheat comes from the mills of Thủy Đối and pearls from Châu Bạng, and sailors touch the nearest rib for luck before every voyage.
40.history: In 15 a nameless swordsman killed the sea-serpent of the inland sea, and its bones became a reef. In 260 Thiên Xu Tông founded Tinh Hán Thành on that reef as its port on the inland sea, packing stone between the ribs to make the breakwater. Its formation was laid along the walls and the reef against storms and sea beasts, and the Pivot's formation masters have kept it in repair ever since. In the Age of Seven Seats pearl oysters found in the shallows at Châu Bạng gave the port its pearl trade, and in the Compact years the water mills at Thủy Đối ground wheat for the whole city. Ore from Ngọc Hành Sơn and star iron from Thối Tinh Môn came down to its quays and went out across the sea. In 980 Vệ Văn Cơ was born here and drew formations in the harbour sand before he could talk.
levels: The wall runs the whole shore, a second stone quay reaches out from the bone reef, and a lighthouse tower rises at the reef's end.
A grand harbour hall with a three-roof pagoda faces the sea, the reef is armoured with dressed stone between every rib, and the formation's pillars glow faintly along the walls at dusk.

41.name: Lai Nghi Thành
41.look: A walled port city at a river mouth on the dry eastern steppe, its harbour mole curving out into the gulf. On the mole rises a terrace of nine stepped stone tiers, each crowned with a bronze bell frame, so that the whole stair glints at sunrise. A faint shimmer over the walls marks the city's guardian array (hộ thành trận).
41.lore: Phượng Minh Cung founded the city in 530 on the plain where, the old book says, the phoenix comes when the music is played nine times. Every dawn the city's musicians climb the nine tiers and play the same welcome nine times over, one tier at a time, whether or not anything comes. Harbour folk say the phoenix came once, long ago, and argue about which dawn it was. Ships of the gulf put in for rice from the plain and leave with lacquer and bronze.
41.history: Phượng Minh Cung founded Lai Nghi Thành in 530, soon after it took the rice plain of Triêu Dương Nguyên, empty since the fall of Cửu Thiều. The name came from the old line about the Shao music played nine times, and the founders raised the bell terrace before the walls were finished. In the decades that followed the city became the Palace's door on the sea, and the guardian array was set over its walls. Once Hoàng Vân Thành was built upriver the grain barges came down to its quays, and in the great seven-year drought its harbour shipped the plain's rice to the hungry south. When Thôn Hải's pirates burned Châu Lệ Cảng, the city manned its walls every night until the Pirate Purge swept the gulf clean. It has grown quietly rich on the coastal trade ever since. Old musicians say Cửu Thiều's music was never truly lost, only scattered to the four coasts, and that some of it came home here.
levels: The nine-tier terrace gains a roofed musicians' gallery and the harbour a second mole lined with warehouses.
A second wall ring takes in the river quays; the terrace is faced in red-lacquered stone and a tall ceremonial gate opens on the sea.

42.name: Thu Trì Thành
42.look: A walled port city where a river meets the sea below wooded hills, built in steps so that tiers of square stone pools descend through its streets from the upper town to the harbour. After night rain on the hills every pool brims and spills into the next, and the whole city murmurs. Over the lower terraces hang the dark oiled-paper awnings of the Night Rain Market, and a guardian array (hộ thành trận) shimmers faintly on the walls.
42.lore: Thính Vũ Lâu founded the city in 400 and named it for the old poem of night rain on the mountain swelling the autumn pools. Since 1000 it has held the Night Rain Market, which sells ma đạo pills, poisons and arts that no other city allows; it opens only after dark and only in rain, and buyers come from as far as the desert. Innkeepers here learned long ago not to ask names. Nghê Hồng Đậu and the head's disciple Mạnh Lưu Ly were both born within its walls.
42.history: Thính Vũ Lâu founded Thu Trì Thành in 400, twenty years after its own founding, as its port on the southern sea. The stone pools were cut into the slope to catch the night rain off the hills, and the forest's honey, timber and grain went out from its harbour. In 800 Nghê Hồng Đậu was born here, and red beans grew from the cracks in her mother's doorstep. After the Night Rain Edict, strangers in black came up the forest road at night for the whole of 908, and the innkeepers learned not to ask their names. In 1000 the Tower opened the Night Rain Market in the city, and its treasury doubled within fifty years. By 1005 the market was known to open only after dark and only in rain, and it drew buyers from as far as the desert. In 1060 Mạnh Lưu Ly was born here, and Mạnh Dạ Vũ took her as his disciple.
levels: The pools climb higher up the hill as the upper town grows; a second harbour basin and a long covered hall for the Night Rain trade.
