A walled upper city of dark halls looks down over the tiered pools; the market's awnings spread across three terraces and the harbour is walled in stone.

43.name: Không Mông Thành
43.look: A walled port city in a low valley mouth by the sea, almost always seen through fine hazy rain. Every street is roofed by long covered arcades of grey tile on red-painted posts, so that one can cross the whole city without getting wet. Above the arcades rise the older halls of Khải Lôi's time, their roof ridges capped in green bronze.
43.lore: Khải Lôi Môn founded the city in 200 in the hazy rain of its southern valleys, and Thính Vũ Lâu has held it since the Gate fell. Many of its families descend from the people of Lôi Trạch Thành, who came here after their own city burned. They still keep a thunder-day in spring, beating drums under the arcades when the first thunder is heard. The hills hazy in the rain are lovely too, the poem says, and painters come for it.
43.history: Khải Lôi Môn, the Gate That Opens the Thunder, founded Không Mông Thành in 200 in the hazy rain of its southern valleys, the same year Lý Thiên Cổ first beat the thunder drum Xuân Lôi Cổ. The city grew as the Gate's southern port, while Lôi Trạch Thành held the river mouth below the mountains. Nearly three centuries later Hầu Xuân Lôi was struck down by his own tribulation, and its lightning burned Lôi Trạch Thành. A year afterwards the people of Lôi Trạch moved up the valley to Không Mông Thành, and the arcades were raised over the streets to shelter the newcomers' stalls. The Gate never recovered, and Thính Vũ Lâu rose on its ground and took the city with the mountains. Through the Age of Vein Wars it has stayed a quiet trading port. Old families still whisper that the Gate's thunder inheritance lies sealed somewhere in the mountains above.
levels: The arcades reach the harbour quays, and a drum tower rises at the main crossing.
A second wall ring up the valley sides; covered bridges link the arcades across the river, and the harbour gains a stone breakwater.

44.name: Ngũ Thải Thành
44.look: A walled port city at a river mouth on the warm southern coast, its wards roofed in glazed tile of five colours, red, yellow, green, white and black, so that from the hills it looks like a bird's spread wing. A gate tower painted with a five-coloured bird faces the harbour.
44.lore: Xích Thành Môn built the city in 300 and named it for the five-coloured bird of Mount Đan Huyệt, the phoenix; Phượng Minh Cung has held it since 590. Each ward's guild keeps one colour of glaze, and quarrels between wards are settled by who repairs the most roofs. Hùng Phần Vũ, head of Phần Vũ Đường, was born here in 980, and a red feather fell on his cradle.
44.history: Xích Thành Môn built Ngũ Thải Thành in 300 on the coast of Đan Huyệt Châu as its port and market. Its potters glazed the roofs in five colours for the five-coloured bird of the old book, one colour to each ward. After Tôn Hà Khởi died, the city watched its own sect turn under Chu Liệt Nhật to burning villages. In 590 Phượng Minh destroyed Xích Thành Môn, and the city passed to the Palace with the rest of Đan Huyệt Châu. Through the pirate years it barred its harbour by night, and its ships sailed with Phượng Minh's fleet in the Pirate Purge. In 980 Hùng Phần Vũ was born here, and a red feather fell on his cradle. Since he grew up and founded Phần Vũ Đường in the old vents, the city's young walk inland to try themselves.
levels: A sixth ward of plain grey roofs for newcomers and a stone breakwater for the harbour.
A second wall ring up the river, and a five-roofed hall of the potters' guilds at the city's heart.

45.name: Lam Yên Thị
45.look: A broad stone stair climbs from the valley into the mountain haze below Thúy Vi Tông, lined on both sides with stalls under indigo cloth awnings. On misty days the awnings fade into the haze one step at a time, so the market seems to climb into cloud.
45.lore: The market grew at the foot of Thúy Vi Tông in the mountain mist and is named for it. Herbs, pill ingredients and scripture are its trade, and scholars from three sects come to buy the red-leaf bookmarks of Thu Diệp Thôn. Each stallholder hangs a small bell from the awning so customers can find the stall by ear in the fog.
45.history: Before the market, the foot of the mountain was only the place where Thúy Vi's disciples met the carters who brought up rice and herbs. In 600 a market had grown there in the mountain mist, and it took the name Lam Yên Thị. Its stair was paved step by step as each stallholder laid the stones in front of a stall, so no two steps quite match. It became the place where the sect sold the pills it did not need and bought what its herb terraces could not grow, and scholars climbed it for copied scripture. The custom of awning bells began on a fog day when two buyers searched for each other's stalls from morning to noon. Within living memory the red leaves of Thu Diệp Thôn came onto its stalls as bookmarks for scripture, and scholars from three sects now climb the stair to buy them.
levels: A second side stair of stalls branches off halfway up, and an inn with a double grey roof stands at the foot.
A covered market hall straddles the stair's midpoint, and a stone gate arch marks the market's lower entrance.

46.name: Tùng Hạ Thị
46.look: In a wide clearing under old pines, a market stands in a perfect ring: round stall-houses with low grey cone roofs set shoulder to shoulder around an open circle. A single gate in the ring opens onto the road through the pine sea.
46.lore: Tùng Hạ Thị began as a ring of tents pitched by pilgrims who came to hear the pine waves of the new palace, and it kept the ring when the tents became houses. It sells to caravans on the road through the pine sea and to travellers bound for the palace. The loose cultivator Lâm Dã Hạc was born here to a woodcutter's family, and the market still points out the roof where a crane landed on the day of his birth.
46.history: In 205 pilgrims who came to hear the pine waves of the newly founded Tùng Đào Cung stayed on, and Tùng Hạ Thị began as a ring of tents beneath the pines. As the palace grew, the pilgrims' ring became a market for the road through the pine sea, and the tents were rebuilt as round houses on the same circle. Caravans made it a resting place, and woodcutters' families settled behind the ring. In 1145 Lâm Dã Hạc was born here to a woodcutter's family, and a crane landed on the roof the day he was born. In 1190 wolves from the deep pines followed the caravans to Tùng Hạ Thị, and Tùng Đào doubled the road watch, posting guards at the ring's gate.
levels: A second, outer ring of stall-houses is begun and a caravan yard is fenced beside the gate.
A round two-storey market hall rises in the centre of the ring, and a timber palisade with a roofed gate encloses both rings.

47.name: Đào Sa Thị
47.look: Where the river spreads its sand into the sea, a market sprawls across the flats on stilts. Rows of wooden washing cradles stand in the shallows, rocked by washers in wide straw hats, and at low tide the whole flat glitters with fine gold. Along the landing lie the charred ribs of burned ferries, left where they sank.
47.lore: Around 800 gold-washers learned that after a thousand washings the river sand gives up its gold, and Đào Sa Thị grew beside Lãng Đào Môn. It is a market of scales, sieves and quick hands under Tùng Đào's peace, where anyone who keeps their head down can find work at a cradle. The washers still tell how Triệu Huyết Y hid among them for two years after the hunt that killed her master, and lately some swear they have seen her again.
47.history: Before 800 the sand flats at the river mouth held little but gulls and driftwood. Around 800 gold-washers learned that after a thousand washings the river sand gives up its gold, and Đào Sa Thị grew beside the new ferry sect Lãng Đào Môn, which made its landing here. For three centuries the market lived on gold dust and ferry traffic under Tùng Đào Cung's peace. In 1090 Thiên Xu, Tùng Đào and Băng Tâm killed the demonic-path (ma đạo) master Mặc Huyết Sinh, and his last disciple Triệu Huyết Y escaped; in 1092 she hid for two years among the gold-washers here. A generation ago the Ferry War broke out, and in 1173 Lạc Hà raiders burned Lãng Đào's boats at the Đào Sa landing. For years afterward the washers fished nails from the river along with their gold. The burned ribs still lie at the landing, and the market washes on.
levels: A raised boardwalk links the stalls to a rebuilt landing, with a red-doored assay house at its head.
A market square on piles behind a timber palisade, a small customs pagoda flying Tùng Đào's colours, and washing cradles out to the far sandbars.

48.name: Tống Khách Thị
48.look: A forest market strung along the road on a gentle rise, its stalls tucked under dark fir eaves. At the eastern end stands a small eight-sided farewell pavilion over a stone table, where a single cup is always set out full.
48.lore: Travellers leaving the frost coast are seen off here at dawn, and the market lives on what they buy for the road: furs, dried fish and warm wine. Since a traveller seen off in 900 never returned, the market pours a farewell cup for him at the pavilion every year. The wandering sword sage Tư Không Hạc Niên, bound to no sect, has lived here since his duel of 1130 and teaches no one, however many come to ask.
48.history: Tống Khách Thị grew where the frost coast's road climbs inland, the last place travellers on Băng Tâm's roads took a cup before the long way south. Its name comes from the Băng Tâm poem: at dawn I see my guest off. In 900 a traveller was seen off from the market at dawn and never returned; the record keeps no name for him, and the market has poured a farewell cup for him every year since. The eight-sided pavilion at the eastern end was built, the stallholders say, to keep that cup out of the snow. In 1130, after his three-day duel with Thang Vô Tạ of Phất Y Cốc on Cùng Mục Phong ended with no winner, the wandering sword sage Tư Không Hạc Niên settled here. He teaches no one, though young swordsmen come up the road every year to ask. The market has grown used to him, and he to the market.
levels: A walled inn yard joins the market, and the stalls double along the road under longer eaves.
The market gains a gate and a covered street, and a second, larger pavilion rises beside the old one, which is kept exactly as it was.

49.name: Tương Phùng Thị
49.look: A market built half on the water at the quay below Bình Thủy Môn: boats lashed side by side into a floating raft of stalls that rises and falls with the tide. Planks run between them, and faded green awnings drift like duckweed on the strait.
49.lore: The market grew beside Bình Thủy Môn in 525 and has never had a fixed shape; boats join and leave, and no stall sits in the same place two days running. It is said that anyone looking for a lost friend need only wait long enough at Tương Phùng Thị, and the strait ferries leave from its outer boats.
levels: A stone quay with warehouses anchors the raft, and the boats spread into two lashed arms.
A covered market hall stands on piles over the water, and the raft rings it in a wide floating crescent.

50.name: Vật Hoa Thị
50.look: A busy open market on the dry steppe below Thiên Bảo Trai, rows of awnings around a central square. In the square stands a great bronze steelyard on a stone frame, taller than a house, where any trader may have goods weighed in public.
50.lore: The market of the land's riches grew beside Thiên Bảo Trai in 500 and sells what the Trai refines and what the bay digs, grows and catches. Its public scale is the market's law: a deal weighed there cannot be undone. The famous alchemist Lạc Đan Thanh has kept a pill stall here since 1110 and charges whatever he likes.
50.history: In 500 a market for the land's riches grew beside Thiên Bảo Trai and was called Vật Hoa Thị. It sold the Trai's refinings and the red gold of Xích Kim, and drew traders from all round Thu Thủy Loan. In 1004, a year after Kim Cốc burned, Kim Cốc's merchants came begging here, and Thiên Bảo Trai hired the ones who could still count. The traders say the great scale was set up in the square after the crash, to keep the market honest. In 1105 Lạc Đan Thanh bought the Đào Nguyên Đồ, the only map of the way into the fisherman's lost valley, here for a pill no one else could make. In 1110 he set up his pill stall in Vật Hoa Thị, and he has charged whatever he likes ever since. Who sold him the painting is not recorded.
levels: A covered arcade rings the square and a caravan yard is walled in beside the road.
A stone exchange hall with a high double roof faces the scale, and the market's walls take in a second square.

51.name: Hạc Đinh Thị
51.look: Where the river spreads into shallows below Lạc Hà's seat, the market (phường thị) sits on a scatter of sandbar islets joined by plank causeways, its stalls under reed awnings. White cranes stand in the shallows between the islets and do not move for the crowds.
51.lore: Hạc Đinh Thị, the Market of the Crane Shoal, has traded since 320 in the sect's pills, river fish and the talismans of Nam Phố Đường. Cranes are never driven off; a stall a crane chooses to stand beside is thought lucky for the season. A talisman contest is held on the largest islet each autumn, and the market still talks of 1190, when the fourteen-year-old Tô Mộ Vân beat the scribes of Nam Phố Đường.
levels: More islets are joined; a timber market hall on piles stands at the centre of the causeways, and a ferry landing serves the sect road.
The causeways become a raised stone walk on low arches across the whole shoal, with a two-roof market tower at its heart; the cranes still stand below.

52.name: Thiên Quyền Thị
52.look: At the foot of the Pivot's mountain, a square market of grey stone halls opens around a tall timber gantry from which hangs a giant bronze steelyard, its beam as long as a boat. Every large sale in the market is weighed on it in public view.
52.lore: Thiên Quyền Thị, the Market of the Heavenly Balance, opened beside Thiên Xu Tông in 200 as a market of weight and measure, and its scales are the fairest on the continent. The sect's standard weights are kept here in a locked hall and brought out each spring to test every scale in the market; a trader whose scale fails is barred until the next spring's test.
levels: A second gantry and a covered arcade of money-changers' stalls ring the square, and a stone weights hall with bronze doors stands on its north side.
The market is walled and gated in stone, with a drum tower over the gantries and a long caravan yard on the road toward Thạch Kiều Thành.

53.name: Thiều Âm Thị
53.look: At the foot of Phượng Minh's ridges, a market of bamboo-roofed stalls lines a river among bamboo groves, and every lane is hung with curtains of bamboo flutes and pipes drying on strings, clicking and whistling in the wind. A raised music stage stands over the water.
53.lore: Thiều Âm Thị, the Market of the Shao Music, was opened by Phượng Minh's founder in 485 when he cleared the ridges for the new palace. It sells instruments, strings and lacquered drums, and its players are hired for rites all over the south. In 1195 a musician here played a tune no one taught him and every bird on the ridge fell silent; Phượng Minh's elders paid his passage far away, and players since are asked, politely, to name the teacher of any tune they perform.
levels: A covered market hall of bamboo and a second stage on the far bank join the lanes, with a footbridge between them.
The market is walled with a red gate tower, a drum tower and an instrument-makers' guild hall, and a stone landing takes the river boats.

54.name: Hạnh Hoa Thị
54.look: A market town on the river below the southern road to Thính Vũ Lâu, built of deep, narrow lanes between tall grey-tile houses. From every eave hang woven baskets of apricot blossom (hạnh hoa), so after rain the lanes are roofed in pink and white. Apricot trees crowd the river bank behind the stalls.
54.lore: The market grew up in 700 below Thính Vũ's southern road, and after a night of spring rain its lanes sell flowers, as the old poem of the small tower promises. It is also known for the healer Giả Hồi Xuân, born here in 1020, who cures what the alchemists of three sects would not touch. On mornings after rain the sick wait in the flower lanes alongside the buyers.
levels: A covered flower hall at the market gate and a stone quay on the river.
A second walled quarter of healers and herb sellers; the apricot grove is walled as a market garden.

55.name: Quy Điểu Trấn
55.look: A walled lakeside town of grey roofs whose shore is lined with rows of tall birch poles, each crowned with a straw nest-basket. In autumn every pole and roof ridge is crowded with returning birds; in winter the market tents stand out on the ice beyond the harbour wall.
55.lore: Quy Điểu Trấn began as a traders' camp named for the birds that return to the lake each autumn in great flocks, and townsfolk still raise a new nest pole for every child born. Lake pearls made it rich, and each winter its market moves out onto the ice, where pearl buyers walk from stall to stall over the frozen water. It is a Tùng Đào town, and much of what Hàm Nguyệt Trang's pearl beds yield passes over its scales.
levels: The wall runs further along the shore and the nest poles stand in double rows; a stone pearl market hall rises by the harbour.
A second harbour basin is cut, and a tall grey-roofed bird-watching tower stands over the shore where the winter ice market is held.

56.name: Mục Ca Thành
56.look: A walled city of low grey roofs sits on open coastal grassland, hunched against the wind. Around its walls a ring of round dry-stone sheepfolds lies across the grass like beads on a string, and at dusk the herders' songs carry from fold to fold.
56.lore: Thúy Vi founded the city on its cape where herders sing to their flocks, and the songs are still how flocks are counted, called home and sold. Each herding family owns a fold in the ring and a tune no one else may sing at it. The city lives on wool, hides and the sea, and buys its grain, so a poor harvest anywhere on the cape hits it hard.
56.history: Long before any sect claimed the cape, herders drove their flocks along this grassy shore and sang to them. Thúy Vi Tông took Tuyết Hỏa Giác in the Age of the North Star Compact, and in 700 founded Mục Ca Thành on the cape where the herders sang. The city grew as the cape's wool and hide market, and its folds were added one by one around the walls as families settled. Its grain came from the cape villages and through the harbour of Yên Ba. In 1196 a poor harvest drove grain prices in the city so high that the herders went to sing their songs for coin in Yên Ba's streets. The songs came home with them changed, and old herders complain that the young now sing for strangers.
levels: A second ring of folds is built and a long covered wool hall rises inside the walls.
A tall drum-and-song tower stands at the city's centre, and the harbour gains a stone mole for the wool ships.

57.name: Bạch Sa Trấn
57.look: A small walled town of whitewashed walls and grey roofs sits on a beach of dazzling white sand. Along the shore stand long rows of whitewashed net-drying frames, so many that from the sea the town seems fenced in white lattice.
57.lore: The Thẩm family, fishers of the white sands, built the first houses here, and the clan hall is still the town's court. Since a Thẩm daughter married into a merchant house of Yên Ba, the town trades as much as it fishes. A peach petal netted in midwinter is kept in a sealed jar at the clan hall; the elders say the hidden valley's stream has opened again, and strangers have begun asking which way the currents run.
57.history: In 380 the Thẩm family, fishers of the white sands, built the first houses of Bạch Sa on this beach. For centuries it was a fishing village, and once Thúy Vi Tông took the cape it owed its catch to that sect. When Thúy Vi founded the port of Yên Ba Thành a generation later, Bạch Sa's fish went to its markets. In 1040 a daughter of the Thẩm clan married into a merchant house of Yên Ba, and the white sands became a trading town. In 1120 a fisher of Bạch Sa netted a peach petal in midwinter, far from any peach tree, and the elders said the hidden valley's stream had opened again. Since then cultivators come through asking about tides and streams, and the Thẩm clan answers them politely and tells them nothing.
levels: A merchants' quarter of two-storey warehouses grows inside an extended wall and the pier is rebuilt in stone.
A tall double-roofed clan hall of the Thẩm stands at the town's heart, and a small harbour wall curves around the rows of net frames.

58.name: Bách Diệp Trấn
58.look: A walled town of grey roofs at a river mouth stands inside a vast grid of ancient cypresses planted in straight rows. From any approach the dark columns of the trees march out in lines, and the town sits at the centre of the pattern.
58.lore: Không Sơn Viện's students planted the cypress groves around Bách Diệp as a lesson in patience, and the trees have long outlived the academy. No townsman may cut a cypress, and a dead one is replaced by a seedling grown from its own cones. The town trades cypress incense and resin along the coast.
58.history: In the Age of First Gates the river mouth here was a fishing landing below the hills of Không Sơn Viện. In 240 the academy's students planted the cypress groves around Bách Diệp as a lesson in patience, setting each seedling on a measured line. The town grew up in the middle of the grid, its streets laid along the rows the students had drawn. When Không Sơn's last master gave the hills to Thúy Vi Tông, the town passed with them, and the new sect kept the old rule that no cypress may be cut. Over the centuries the groves grew taller than any roof, and the town learned to live by their resin and incense. Townsfolk say the trees are the academy's last lesson, and the only one anyone ever finished.
levels: The grid is extended along the river and an incense workshop quarter is added inside a longer wall.
A tall cypress-wood hall of the incense guild rises at the town's heart, and a stone quay lines the river mouth.

59.name: Tiều Ca Trấn
59.look: A walled timber town of grey roofs sits on the coast below steep forested ridges. A long wooden log flume runs from the ridge tops straight down to the harbour, and logs rattle along it into the water.
59.lore: Woodcutters singing on the ridges below Không Sơn Viện were once asked to sing more quietly, and the town they founded is still called Tiều Ca. Its woodcutters sing to this day, but only below the old academy's boundary stones, out of habit rather than fear. Its timber goes by sea to the cape and to Yên Ba.
59.history: Woodcutters worked these ridges in the Wild Age, long before any sect stood above them. When Không Sơn Viện was founded on the mountain, its students found the woodcutters' songs too loud for their quiet. In 190 the woodcutters singing on the ridges below the academy were asked to sing more quietly, and the town they founded on the coast is still called Tiều Ca. They set boundary stones on the slope, and above those stones the woodcutters fall silent to this day. The log flume was built to bring timber down without the shouting of teams and oxen, and it became the town's pride. After the hills passed to Thúy Vi the timber trade grew, and Tiều Ca's logs now go by sea to the cape and to Yên Ba.
levels: A second flume comes down a neighbouring ridge and a sawmill house stands over the log pond.
A stone harbour wall shelters the timber ships, and a tall woodcutters' guild hall rises inside the walls.

60.name: Lộc Minh Trấn
60.look: A walled town of grey roofs lies on a low river mouth at the forest's edge, every beam end of its timber houses carved. At the end of its ferry pier stands a life-sized stag carved from pine, head raised as if calling across the water.
60.lore: A deer called at the forest's edge every dawn for a year, and the Lâm family settled where it called and named the place Lộc Minh. The Lâm clan's woodcarvers are known across the pine sea, and they made the beams of a new hall in Tùng Gian Thành from a single fallen pine. The town is held by Lãng Đào Môn, the ferrymen's sect (môn phái) that carries the river trade, and its pier is one of their landings.
levels: A carvers' quarter of open workshops spreads along the river bank and the ferry pier is doubled.
A tall carved timber hall of the Lâm clan rises over the town, and a stone ferry landing replaces the old pier with the stag moved to its end.

61.name: Cổ Độ Thành
61.look: A walled city stands among bamboo groves on the bank of the southern river, where a broad stone ferry stair runs down into the water. At the top of the stair, set upright on a stone plinth, stands a single huge rusted iron link from a sunken chain, taller than a man.
61.lore: Cổ Độ Thành stands at the old ferry on Tùng Đào's southern river, and its ferrymen still cross it as they did before the city had walls. In the War of the Pivot they carried the iron chain for Thiết Tỏa Quan link by link, and now they drag those links back out of the river and sell them to smiths. The great link at the ferry stair is said to be the first one raised, and no one has ever sold it.
61.history: Long before it had walls, a ferry crossed the southern river here, and the old ferry gave the city its name. In 320 Tùng Đào Cung founded Cổ Độ Thành at the crossing. In 506, during the War of the Pivot, the ferrymen of Cổ Độ carried the iron chain for Thiết Tỏa Quan link by link up the river road. Two years later Thiên Xu broke the fort, and the thousand-fathom chain sank to the river bed. For centuries the river kept it, until in 990 the people of Cổ Độ began dragging its links from the river, and smiths paid well for the old war iron. Smithies have grown up around that trade, and the clang of iron by the ferry stair is now as old a sound as the boatmen's calls.
levels: A smiths' quarter with tall chimneys grows outside the river gate, and a second ferry stair is built downstream.
A tall drum tower of the ferrymen rises over the stair, and the walls take in the smiths' quarter and a stone river quay.

62.name: Hà Bạn Trấn
62.look: A low riverside town whose fishing lanes all end at the water. At its upstream corner a great timber waterwheel turns beside a mill house, grinding roots from Thải Chi Cốc into powder, and its creak carries to the road. Herb sacks stand stacked on the short jetties, waiting for boats.
62.lore: Hà Bạn Trấn was a fishing hamlet until 290, when the river's new course ran past its door and it grew into a town on the new bank. It now answers to Thải Chi Cốc, grinding and shipping the valley's herbs downriver. The townsfolk have a saying for every stroke of luck: the river came to us, so we do not chase it.
levels: A second waterwheel and a stone mill house, with a covered herb wharf along the bank.
The wall runs along the river with a water gate, and a row of mills turns in a cut channel beside the town.

63.name: Lâm Hạ Trấn
63.look: The town sits so deep in the shade of old beeches that its roofs are green with moss even in summer. Between the houses stand round timber granaries raised on squat stone staddles shaped like mushrooms, so that no rat can climb them. At noon the lanes are cool and dim, and smell of grain dust.
63.lore: In 600 Tùng Đào Cung set its northern granaries in the shade of Lâm Hạ Trấn, so the grain would keep, and the town has lived as a storehouse ever since. Its people are granary-keepers, coopers and rat-catchers, proud that their grain does not spoil. Felling a shade tree inside the town is the one crime the elders never pardon.
levels: More round granaries on staddle stones and a timber fence around the storehouse quarter.
A stone granary hall with a tall vented roof under the oldest beeches, and a full town wall with a grain gate on the river.

64.name: Bích Khê Trấn
64.look: A small walled town on a brook so green it looks dyed. Below the walls the stream runs over shallow stone weirs where jade-pickers kneel, sorting pebbles into baskets by colour. Polishing wheels hum in the workshops along the main street.
64.lore: A jade-green brook below the ridges gave Bích Khê Trấn its name around 300, and its trade in river jade. Pickers comb the brook bed after every flood, and the carvers in town turn the pebbles into seals and hairpins for Thiên Xu's officials. When a match is made, the bride's family gives an uncut pebble from the brook as its promise.
levels: A carvers' street with a covered market, and a stone footbridge across the green brook.
A larger wall, a jade hall with a green-glazed roof, and weirs stepping the brook far upstream.

65.name: Thanh Bách Thành
65.look: A walled city of grey roofs and dark, narrow cypresses on the northern road, a cypress standing over every courtyard. Outside its north wall lies a small round crater pond, glassy black at the rim, where a star fell in 980. Ore carts and officials' carriages pass through its gates all day.
65.lore: Thiên Xu Tông founded Thanh Bách Thành on its northern road in 520, and the city is named for its green cypresses. In 980 a star fell near the city; the fragment was sold to Thối Tinh Môn for three years of the city's taxes, and the crater filled with rain. Townsfolk toss a coin into the pond for luck, though the clerks say the city has paid that star enough already.
65.history: Thiên Xu Tông founded Thanh Bách Thành on its northern road in 520, in the first years of the North Star Compact, to guard the road between the heart and Khai Dương Thành. Cypress seedlings were planted in every courtyard, and the city took their name. It grew as a waystation for ore carts, officials and the Pivot's patrols in Dao Quang Lĩnh. In the Phá Quân rebellion of the Age of Vein Wars its gates stayed shut to the rebels, and it quartered Thiên Xu's troops. In 980 a star fell near the city; the fragment was sold to Thối Tinh Môn for three years of the city's taxes. The crater pond outside the north wall is all the city kept of it, and the old cypresses still stand over the courtyards.
levels: A second market quarter inside the walls and a shrine pavilion on the crater pond's rim.
An outer wall enclosing the crater pond, and a tall tax hall with stacked roofs among the oldest cypresses.

66.name: Hòe Âm Trấn
66.look: A small harbour town where a river reaches the sea, and from its back gate an avenue of ancient locust trees climbs toward the mountains, their crowns meeting overhead in a green tunnel. Fishing boats and the hermitage's supply carts share one narrow quay. In early summer the locust blossom drops on the road like pale snow.
66.lore: Locust trees planted by the Tiêu family shaded the road into the mountains, and around 520 their village took the name Hòe Âm; it now answers to Lê Hoa Am. In 930 a hunter of the town found a sealed cave on the mountain with a sword's cold light behind the seal; he ran, and never found it again. Every hunter since has looked for that cave, and tavern talk names more dead swordsmen behind its seal than the mountain could hold.
66.history: In the first years of the North Star Compact the Tiêu family planted locust trees along the road from the river mouth into the mountains, to shade the carts that climbed to the ice. Around 520 the cluster of houses at the foot of their avenue took the name Hòe Âm, for the locusts' shade. The village fished, hunted the lower slopes and carried supplies up the mountain road, and grew into a small harbour town. After the hermitage of Lê Hoa Am was founded on the heights, the town came to answer to it and to carry its stores. In 930 a hunter of Hòe Âm found a sealed cave on the mountain with a sword's cold light behind the seal; he ran, and never found it again. Since then every hunter of the town has looked for that cave, and none has found it. Half a century ago the Tiêu clan sent a son to the hermitage's gate and saw him turned away, and he too took up the hunter's bow. The locusts still shade the road, older now than any house beneath them.
levels: A stone quay with a hunters' market, and the locust avenue extended further up the mountain road.
A larger wall with a harbour gate, a Tiêu family hall with a two-tier roof, and a waystation for Lê Hoa Am's pilgrims at the avenue's end.

67.name: Hồi Lan Thành
67.look: A harbour city on the desert coast, built behind a long curved breakwater that hooks out into the sea and turns the waves back on themselves. Sand-coloured walls enclose low warehouses under pale grey roofs. Ships from the south crowd the still water inside the hook.
67.lore: Băng Tâm Các founded Hồi Lan Thành on the desert coast in 760, after the Desert Road War, so that trade with the south need not trust the desert alone. Its harbour filled with southern ships by 770, once the caravan road was safe. In 1160 a merchant of the city brought the first southern rice through the desert since the war, and Băng Tâm taxed it at half; the rice merchants still toast him at every new year.
67.history: The Desert Road War ended a generation before the city's founding with the border where it had been, and Băng Tâm Các looked for a road south that Phượng Minh's fire could not cut. In 760 it founded Hồi Lan Thành on the desert coast and raised the breakwater that turns the waves and gives the city its name. By 770 the harbour was full of ships from the south, now that the caravan road was safe. The city grew on salt, wool and southern goods, and on the trade that had once passed Cô Thành. In 1160 a merchant of Hồi Lan Thành brought the first southern rice through the desert since the Desert Road War, and Băng Tâm taxed it at half. The sea road and the rice road have both run through the city since.
levels: A rice market quarter and warehouses along the inner breakwater.
A second hooked breakwater forming a full harbour ring, with a watch pagoda at its tip and a walled merchant quarter outside the old wall.

68.name: Mộc Lan Thành
68.look: A walled harbour city on the flat frost coast, its grey roofs low against the sea wind. A double row of old magnolia trees runs the length of the harbour wall, and in spring their white blossoms line the quay like snow that will not melt. Inland, the white cone of Sương Diễm Sơn stands over the city.
68.lore: Băng Tâm Các's younger port on the frost coast trades furs, timber and live beasts from Vô Tung Lâm; hunters sell their catches on the magnolia quay, and buyers come from as far as Thiên Bảo Trai. The city remembers the week in the Age of the North Star Compact when Sương Diễm Sơn breathed fire and everyone slept on the beach; on that night each year, families still lay their bedding out on the sand.
68.history: Băng Tâm Các founded Mộc Lan Thành on the frost coast in 620, more than a century after taking Hàn Sương Châu from Hàn Giang Môn. Its builders planted magnolias along the new harbour wall, a southern tree coaxed to bloom in the cold, and the city took its name from them. Within a century of the founding, Sương Diễm Sơn breathed fire under the frost for a week, and the people of Mộc Lan Thành slept on the beach until it sank. The city grew as the coast's market for the furs and timber of Vô Tung Lâm, a forest only the coast's woodcutters and hunters dare. In 1180 hunters brought a white bear out of Vô Tung Lâm alive and sold it here to a buyer from Thiên Bảo Trai. The tale of that bear's long road south is still told in the harbour taverns. Today the city lives by the sea and the forest at once.
levels: A fur market hall with a high grey roof rises behind the quay, and the magnolia rows run on along a new sea wall.
The walls take in the beach quarter, a stone breakwater shelters the harbour, and a three-roofed gate tower faces the volcano inland.

69.name: Kê Minh Trấn
69.look: A small walled port town on the grassy frost coast, low grey roofs around a single harbour. Above its gate stands a tall pole topped by a bronze rooster, green with age, that turns with the wind.
69.lore: The cocks of Kê Minh crow even in the dark of winter, when the sun barely rises, and the town has kept the cock as its emblem since the Age of Seven Seats (Thất Tọa Kỷ). Its fishers set out at the first crow, not the first light, and a household whose cock falls silent fetches a new one before nightfall.
69.history: Kê Minh grew on the grassy frost coast as a fishing harbour in the days of Hàn Giang Môn. By 360 its cocks were known to crow even in the dark of winter, when the sun barely clears the sea, and the town took the cock as its emblem. Its fishers learned to set out at the first crow rather than the first light, and its boats were the first on the water all along the coast. When Hàn Giang Môn fell and the frost coast passed to Băng Tâm Các at the end of the Age of Seven Seats, the town changed its flag but not its emblem. The bronze rooster above the gate was cast, the townsfolk say, to go on crowing if every bird in the town ever fell silent. They boast that no bad news has ever reached Kê Minh before the first crow.
levels: The harbour wall is lengthened into a stone pier and a fish market roof rises by the gate.
A second ring of wall takes in the poultry yards and net sheds, and a covered gatehouse lifts the rooster pole higher still.

70.name: Xích Ngạn Trấn
70.look: A small walled town atop red cliffs on the island's east coast, its grey roofs bright against the rust-red rock. A long stair cut into the cliff face zigzags down to a cove where the boats are drawn up.
70.lore: The first mainland traders named the red cliffs Xích Ngạn in 330, and the town that grew on top kept the name. Its people grind the red rock into a pigment for the island's sails, and a Xích Ngạn boat is known far out at sea by its rust-coloured canvas.
levels: A pigment mill and drying yard sit inside the walls, and a second stair is cut to a new landing.
The town fills the clifftop, a stone pier runs out from the cove, and a tall grey-tile hall overlooks the sea from the cliff edge.

71.name: Hải Yến Trấn
71.look: A fishing town of low grey roofs on the flat island shore. Every house wears deep double eaves, and under them the sea swallows' nests cluster so thickly that the eaves look whitewashed; at dusk the air above the town is a whirl of birds.
71.lore: Since the Age of the North Star Compact the people of Hải Yến have sold swallows' nests to alchemists (đan sư), who prize them for pills that clear the breath. Families own eaves the way others own fields, and a daughter's dowry is counted in nests. Harvesters take only the nests the birds have left.
levels: Tall nest houses with many tiers of eaves rise inside the walls, and the harbour gains a stone quay.
A ring of nest towers stands along the walls, and a nest market hall with a high grey roof faces the harbour.

72.name: Triều Âm Thành
72.look: A walled city on the island's western shore at a river mouth, grey roofs stepping up from the water. Along its sea front runs a stone breakwater bored with round holes that moan and sing as the tide pushes through.
72.lore: Lạc Hà Tông founded the city in 540 as its western foothold on Cô Vụ Đảo. Its people tell time by the breakwater's note, low at the ebb and high at the flood, and its watchmen call the tide instead of the hour. Musicians from the mainland come to tune to it, and the children call the sound the island breathing.
72.history: A generation before the city, Cô Vụ Đảo became Lạc Hà Tông's land under the Strait Oath. In 540 Lạc Hà founded Triều Âm Thành on the island's western shore, where a river meets the sea, as a harbour of its own beside the old Cô Phàm ports. Its builders bored the breakwater so the tide would pass through rather than break it, found that it sang, and named the city for the sound. When the Cô Phàm fleet was lost in the Age of the North Star Compact, Triều Âm's harbour took much of the island's sea trade. In the great storm of the Age of Vein Wars, while the fishing fleet sheltered at Nguyệt Loan Thôn, the breakwater is said to have shrieked all night and held. Lạc Hà's ships to and from the island still call here first.
levels: The breakwater is lengthened along the river mouth and a customs hall rises at the harbour gate.
A second harbour basin is walled in, and a tall bell-less listening tower stands on the breakwater's end, open to the sea wind.

73.name: Thanh Điền Trấn
73.look: A small walled market town in a sea of bright green fields that run to the horizon. Outside its gate stretches a long row of hitching rails where the farmers' horses wait, since the fields are too far to walk.
73.lore: The fields around Thanh Điền stretch so far that its farmers ride to work, and children learn to sit a horse before they can walk far. The town answers to Mục Vân Trang, whose head Khấu Mục Vân was born here in 940 on the same night as a spirit foal; the town still holds a horse fair on that night.
levels: A walled horse yard joins the town and the hitching rails double along the road.
A granary row and a fair ground with a viewing stand rise beside the walls.

74.name: Thảo Đường Thành
74.look: A walled city on the flat coastal plain, its grey roofs low among farms. Outside the walls lies a chequerboard of grass-banked ponds, each a square of sky, with fish and ducks raised in every one.
74.lore: Lạc Hà Tông founded the city in 680 among the farms of the western plain, and it lives by them: rice, fish ponds, ducks and hemp. Its name comes from the ponds the first farmers dug; each family owns a square, and the banks between are common ground. Its market day is the slowest and friendliest on the plain.
74.history: Farmers worked this stretch of the western plain long before the city, under Lạc Hà Tông's rule since the Age of Seven Seats. They dug grass-banked ponds for fish and ducks and to catch the plain's floods before they reached the fields. In 680 Lạc Hà founded Thảo Đường Thành among the farms, to gather their harvest and guard them. Through the wars of the Compact age its fields and ponds kept the western plain fed. During the War of Broken Halberds Lạc Hà built its western watch at Lô Cảng Thôn to guard the coast boats along this shore. Today the sect's stewards come here to count harvests, not swords.
levels: A new granary ward is walled in and more ponds are dug in rows along the road.
A tall grain hall with a double roof rises at the city's heart, and canals link the pond grid to the sea.

75.name: Ngư Lương Trấn
75.look: A small walled town where a plain river spills into the sea. Across the river mouth runs a great zigzag weir of stone and bamboo, the largest on the plain, its traps glinting with fish.
75.lore: Lạc Hà's rule brought fishing weirs to the plain's rivers in 430, and the town grew around the largest. The weir is rebuilt piece by piece every year, the family that tends a stretch of it keeps that stretch's fish, and quarrels over the weir go to the town's oldest fisher.
levels: A fish market roof and smoking sheds rise on the bank by the weir.
A second weir is built upstream and the walls take in both banks, joined by a footbridge along the old weir.

76.name: Liễu Ngạn Trấn
76.look: A small walled town on a river through flat grassland, set behind a high earthen levee. On the levee stands a tall stone flood-pillar cut with the marks of every great flood, the highest painted red; willows line the bank on either side.
76.lore: In 410 the townsfolk planted willows on the bank at Liễu Ngạn to hold the river where it floods, and the town has fought the river ever since. When the water climbs past the red mark on the pillar, the drum is beaten and every household sends someone to the levee.
levels: The levee is faced with stone and a drum house is built beside the flood-pillar.
A stone river gate and a sluice tower guard the town, and the levee runs on past the walls on both sides.

77.name: Hòa Phong Trấn
77.look: A small port town on the open bay coast, its grey roofs low and airy. On every roof stands a tall woven wind-scoop turned toward the sea, so the whole town seems to lean into the breeze.
77.lore: In 900, the year of the southern plague, a gentle sea breeze kept Hòa Phong Trấn free of fever, and the town has built wind-scoops on its roofs ever since to keep the sea air moving through every room. Sick travellers are brought here to recover, and its healers swear by the breeze before any pill.
levels: A house of healing with a long open veranda rises facing the sea.
The town grows a seaside terrace of guesthouses for the sick, each with its own tall wind-scoop, and a stone quay for the boats that bring them.

78.name: Ngũ Cốc Thành
78.look: A walled port city on the bay coast, its quay lined with granaries. Along the waterfront stands a row of tall round grain towers, each roofed differently for its grain, with wooden chutes running down to the ships.
78.lore: Ngũ Cốc Thành grew rich on the trade Kim Cốc lost when Kim Cốc Viên burned. It ships the grain of the bay and the western plain, and many of its merchants are Kim Cốc families who rebuilt their fortunes in grain. Each grain tower has its own guild, and their rivalry runs the city.
78.history: Before this city, much of the bay's trade went through Kim Cốc Thành, the merchant city around Kim Cốc Viên. A few years before this city was founded, Kim Cốc Viên collapsed in a market crash and a great fire, and Kim Cốc Thành burned. Its merchants were begging in Vật Hoa Thị the next year, and its trade looked for a new harbour. In 1010 Ngũ Cốc Thành was founded on the bay coast and grew rich on the trade Kim Cốc lost. Its builders raised the grain towers on the quay first and the walls after, so the trade would never wait. Under Lạc Hà Tông it is now the bay's grain port, and its guilds, remembering Kim Cốc's fire, keep their granaries in stone.
levels: A guild hall for the grain towers rises behind the quay, and a breakwater shelters the ships.
A second row of grain towers is built on a new pier, and the walls take in the barge canal from the plain.

79.name: Phong Lâm Trấn
79.look: A walled harbour town among red maples where a river meets the sea, its grey-tile roofs half hidden in leaves. At its centre stands the old Tạ clan hall, its deep eaves lined end to end with the mud nests of swallows, so that in spring the hall seems to breathe birds.
79.lore: Phong Lâm Trấn, Maple Wood Town, grew among the maples Lạc Hà's founder planted around the first hall, and is now kept by Nam Phố Đường. The Tạ family, once great in another land, arrived in 470 with nothing but their name, and the swallows of their old hall followed them; no one in town will knock down a swallow's nest. In 1000 the Tạ and their old rivals the Vương exchanged letters for the first time in four hundred years, and the letter is read aloud in the clan hall every New Year.
79.history: In 295 Lạc Hà Tông's founder planted maples around the first hall, and Phong Lâm Trấn grew among them as a landing where the river meets the sea. Townsfolk still point to a moss-grown stone plinth under the oldest maples and call it the first hall. Through the Age of First Gates and the Age of Seven Seats the town shipped timber and fish to the sect upriver. In 470 the Tạ family came with nothing but their name, and the swallows of their old hall followed them to nest under the eaves of the new one. The Tạ never regained their old greatness, but they became the town's clerks and harbour reckoners. Some four centuries later the new Nam Phố Đường took the town into its keeping, and its scribes began to buy paper and pine soot on the quay. In 1000 the Tạ and the Vương, old rival clans now far apart, exchanged letters for the first time in four hundred years.
levels: The wall reaches the waterline, a stone quay takes larger boats, and a second clan hall rises opposite the Tạ hall.
A curved harbour mole runs out under the maples, a two-storey gate tower stands on the sea wall, and the Tạ hall gains an upper storey whose new eaves the swallows fill within a spring.

80.name: Tang Ma Thành
80.look: A walled city on a river among endless rows of mulberry and blue-flowering hemp. Its river channels are crossed not by stone but by a lattice of swaying hemp-rope bridges slung between timber towers, which hum when the wind blows. Rope walks run along the outer wall, where long strands are twisted under open sheds.
80.lore: Tang Ma Thành, Mulberry and Hemp City, is Lạc Hà Tông's silk and rope city on the Ngư Ca plain. Its hemp ropes are so strong that Lãng Đào's ferrymen will buy no other, and its rope-makers swear no Tang Ma rope has ever parted under load. The talisman mistress Châu Phi Vân was born here and drew her first talisman in mulberry juice at four; children of the city still paint charms on their doors in purple juice each summer.
80.history: Lạc Hà Tông founded Tang Ma Thành in 330 among the mulberry and hemp fields of Ngư Ca Xuyên, the same year it took the bay of Thu Thủy Loan. Silk from its mulberry groves and rope from its hemp fed the sect's treasury through the Age of Seven Seats and the long Compact. The city lay far behind the front both when Lạc Hà lost the War of the Pivot and when it lost on Chiết Kích Nguyên, and its looms never stopped. In 930 Châu Phi Vân was born here, and at four she drew her first talisman in mulberry juice. By 1100 its hemp ropes were so prized that Lãng Đào's ferrymen would buy no other. In 1174, in the Ferry War, Tùng Đào raiders cut every rope bridge on the Ngư Ca border, and Tang Ma wove new ones in a month.
levels: Weaving halls and silk-dyeing yards spill outside the wall, and a stone gatehouse rises over the main rope bridge.
A second wall rings the rope walks and dyeworks, a tall drum tower stands at the centre, and the lattice of rope bridges spreads over every channel, hung with silk pennants.

81.name: Thạch Kiều Thành
81.look: The first city of the heart sits astride a river in rolling steppe, a walled grid of grey roofs crossing the water on one great stone bridge. The bridge wears its age plainly: its old central arches are dark, almost black, while the wide new deck and outer arches added in 1050 are pale grey. Bell towers stand at both ends.
81.lore: Thạch Kiều Thành grew from the stone bridge where mortal traders from four coasts first met, and is the city where the North Star Compact was set in 510. Its people call the bridge the oldest thing in the heart, and the old stones taken out when it was widened are kept in the Pivot's hall. On the day the Compact was signed every bell in the city rang without being struck, and on that day each year the bells are left silent, so as not to answer. Both the head of Thiên Xu Tông, Doãn Ngọc Hành, and his disciple Doãn Hi Hòa were born here.
81.history: In 50 mortal traders began to meet at a stone bridge here, where the roads from four coasts cross. Under Thiên Xu Tông's protection the crossing grew into Thạch Kiều Thành in 150, the first city of the heart. In 270 Kỳ Tùng Ẩn and Chung Hoài Cực met here and drank for three days, and the Pine and the Pivot kept the peace for two centuries. In 510 Chung Hoài Cực set the North Star Compact before the seven sects in the city and stamped it with the Bắc Thần Ấn, and every bell in Thạch Kiều rang without being struck. On the night the founder died in 760, Doãn Ngọc Hành was born here under the fifth star of the Dipper. In 1050 the stone bridge was widened for the first time, and its old stones were carried to the Pivot's hall. In 1130 Doãn Hi Hòa was born here at sunrise, and Doãn Ngọc Hành took her as his disciple when she was five.
levels: A second wall takes in the caravan yards on both banks, and a tall drum tower rises at the bridge's north end.
The city spreads across both banks in a double grid, with a three-roof Hall of the Compact beside the bridge, bell towers on every gate, and stone embankments lined with river barges.

82.name: Song Kiều Trấn
82.look: A walled town on the river road where two humpbacked stone bridges cross the river side by side, one for carts going in and one for carts going out, with a small toll house on a pier between them. In the square behind stands a row of open ore scales under a long tiled roof.
82.lore: Song Kiều Trấn, Twin Bridges Town, has weighed the miners' ore on open scales in its square since 235, when Thiên Xu's assayers first did it in public view; no miner of Ngọc Hành has rebelled since. The Ôn clan built the twin bridges in 900 and keeps the tolls, and an Ôn sits in the toll house every day of the year. Locals cross by one bridge and come home by the other; using the wrong one is said to bring a bad bargain.
levels: A second wall takes in an ore yard beside the bridges, and an Ôn clan hall with a two-storey gate faces the toll pier.
The town spreads across both banks inside one wall, with a drum tower over the square and a stone assay hall raised over the open scales.

83.name: Mạch Điền Trấn
83.look: A walled town in flat wheat country where a river meets the gulf, dominated by one tall granary raised on a ring of mushroom-shaped staddle stones, its steep thatched roof the highest thing on the plain. Wheat barges tie up at a timber quay below.
83.lore: Mạch Điền Trấn, Wheat Fields Town, grew around its granary after 530, when its wheat fields were set to feed Phượng Minh's palace. The staddle stones keep out rats and high tides alike, and townsfolk boast that their granary never lost a sack in the hungry years.
levels: A second granary on staddle stones and a stone harbour wall join the town, and the town wall is extended to the quay.
A row of great granaries stands along the harbour, with a granary-master's hall and a drum tower over the gate.

84.name: Thanh Khê Thành
84.look: Phượng Minh's port on the gulf sits where a clear brook runs into the sea, a walled grid of grey roofs around a wide harbour. All along the harbour wall hangs an unbroken row of red lanterns, lit every night, so from far out at sea the city shows as a glowing line on the water.
84.lore: Thanh Khê Thành, Clear Brook City, was founded by Phượng Minh Cung in 560 as its port on the gulf. In the Cinnabar Vein War, in 1157, its harbour sheltered Phượng Minh's wounded and the city's lanterns burned all year; the custom stayed, and each family keeps one lantern on the harbour wall lit from dusk to dawn, for those who came home and those who did not. Its brook water is so clear that sailors fill their casks here before any long voyage.
84.history: Phượng Minh Cung founded Thanh Khê Thành in 560 as its port on the gulf, where a clear brook runs into the sea. In its first two centuries it shipped the palace's rice and wheat along the coast and drew in the trade of the south. When Thôn Hải Môn's pirates burned the pearl harbour Châu Lệ Cảng two centuries after the founding, Thanh Khê armed its boats and watched its harbour mouth by night. Soon after, Phượng Minh's fleet sailed in the Pirate Purge under the Pivot's writ, and the Purge ended at Thôn Hải Môn itself. When Thính Vũ Lâu attacked Đan Sơn Mạch and the war dragged on, the harbour became the palace's place of healing. In 1157 it sheltered Phượng Minh's wounded, and the city's lanterns burned all year; they are lit still.
levels: A second wall takes in shipyards along the brook, and a stone harbour arm doubles the anchorage under the lanterns.
A red gate tower stands at the harbour mouth, a three-roof harbour hall faces the gulf, and the lantern row runs round the whole enlarged harbour.

85.name: Hoàng Vân Thành
85.look: A broad walled city on the river where the rice plain lies flattest, crowned inside its walls by a ring of tall round granaries capped in yellow-glazed tile. At harvest a haze of rice chaff hangs over the roofs and turns gold in the low sun, which gives the city its name. Grain barges crowd the river quay below the granary gates.
85.lore: This is Phượng Minh Cung's granary city, and its keepers count grain the way other cities count gold. When the seven-year drought struck in 649 its granaries fed the whole south, and the Palace's power has rested on its rice ever since. In 1060 it opened its doors to Băng Tâm's desert in a famine year, and the old quarrel of the Desert Road was quietly let go. Every granary keeper swears an oath at the river never to sell the last basket.
85.history: Phượng Minh Cung founded Hoàng Vân Thành in 600 as the granary of the rice plain of Triêu Dương Nguyên. Its first round granaries were raised along the river, where the barges of Thủy Điền and the inland villages could reach them. In 649 a drought began that lasted seven years; the granaries were opened and fed the south until the rains came back. That drought made the Palace's rice its strength, and granary after granary was added in the years that followed. In the Desert Road War, Phượng Minh and Băng Tâm Các fought over the caravan road between the desert and this plain, and the city's grain carts rolled to the front instead of the markets. The truce the Pivot imposed brought the caravans back, but the bitterness lasted for centuries. In 1060, in a famine year in the desert, the granaries were opened to Băng Tâm's people, and the quarrel was quietly forgotten. Its keepers still tell that story to every new apprentice.
levels: A second ring of granaries rises outside the walls and a stone grain wharf runs along the river.
A walled granary district with a yellow-roofed counting hall at its heart; a canal basin is cut from the river for the barges.

86.name: Đạo Hương Trấn
86.look: A small walled town of grey-tile roofs in a sea of rice, the smell of ripening grain heavy on the river wind. Along the field road outside the east gate stands a long row of carved stone stakes, one for each generation of the Vương family, each beside the paddy that generation planted.
86.lore: The Vương family, rivals of the Tạ in another land, settled here in 520, and every generation since has planted one new field and set its stone, carved with the planter's name and the year's first rain. In the last days of 1199 the Vương sent a letter of betrothal to the Tạ of Phong Lâm. The town is still waiting for the reply, and its matchmakers are keeping very quiet.
levels: The Vương build an ancestral hall facing the row of stones, and the town walls are faced in brick.
A second walled quarter for rice merchants and a stone-paved field road; the row of generation stones now runs to the river.

87.name: Lục Dã Trấn
87.look: A walled town in open green meadows, ringed by a chequer of square herb beds in a dozen shades of green, each bordered by a low stone channel of spring water. In the morning the beds steam faintly and smell of mint and bitter root.
87.lore: Since 662 the meadows of Lục Dã have belonged to Lễ Tuyền Phái, which grows its healing herbs here. Mai Lễ Tuyền, the school's head, was born in the town in 850, and the townsfolk say her first cry made the spring flow sweeter. Mothers still bring newborns to the spring channel at the town gate for a first wash, hoping for the same luck.
levels: A drying pavilion for herbs and a walled seed garden of Lễ Tuyền Phái beside the town.
A brick-walled town with a healers' hall at the gate, and the herb chequer spread far across the meadows.

88.name: Bình Dã Trấn
88.look: A walled town in an open plain cleared from the forest, its grey roofs gathered around a huge paved yard of sun-baked brick. On dry days the yard is covered edge to edge with mats of drying tea, herbs, cloth and grain brought in from the wet country around.
88.lore: Bình Dã became a town in 410 on the one open plain in the south where it rarely rains. Forest folk carry their wet harvests here to dry, and the town lives on the fees. When rain does come, the yard-keepers beat a gong and the whole town runs out to roll up the mats.
levels: A second drying yard outside the walls and roofed sheds to store the mats.
A brick-walled town with a raised drying terrace on every rooftop and a merchants' hall facing the great yard.

89.name: Xuân Thảo Thành
89.look: A city on a river at the forest's edge, enclosed by thick earthen walls whose tops are capped with living turf, green even in the dry months. Inside, grey-tile roofs stand among young trees, and in the meadows outside the walls old blackened stumps lie grown over with grass.
89.lore: Thính Vũ Lâu founded Xuân Thảo Thành in 640 on the forest land the Pivot gave it after the Petal Shore fighting. Its people take their name from the old line that wildfire cannot burn out the grass, for the spring wind brings it back. Every spring the citizens recut and replant the turf on the walls together, and it is a festival day. The charred stumps in the meadows are left untouched.
89.history: The land of Xuân Thảo was once forest on the edge of Lạc Anh Phái's Petal Shore. When Lạc Anh split, Lạc Hà Tông and Thính Vũ Lâu both claimed the empty shore, and their disciples fought in the burning orchards. Fire swept the land, and Hồng Vũ Thành burned, its petals and ashes falling together like red rain. Then the Pivot's judgement gave the bay to Lạc Hà and the forest to Thính Vũ. Twenty years after the judgement, in 640, Thính Vũ founded Xuân Thảo Thành on ground the fighting had burned, where new grass had come up through the ash. The city grew as a market for the forest villages and a stop on the road from the Tower toward the coast. Its turf walls were never stormed, and through the Age of Vein Wars it has stayed one of the Tower's quietest cities.
levels: A second turf-capped wall ring and a stone bridge over the river with a market at its foot.
A walled forest-trade city with a timber hall on a grassy mound at its heart, its own roof turfed like the walls.

90.name: Lãng Hoa Thành
90.look: A walled port city on a dry, wind-bitten steppe coast at the mouth of a river. Its sea wall is pierced with rows of carved stone blowholes, and when the waves strike, white spray bursts from them in plumes like flowers along the whole waterfront. Behind the wall, grey roofs climb a low rise toward a watch hall.
90.lore: Thính Vũ Lâu founded the city in 800 on the sea-spray coast, once the Pirate Purge had made it safe at last. Its people are mostly fishers and salt-boilers who came down to the shore when the pirates were gone. On storm days children run along the wall racing the spray, and the one soaked by the biggest plume is called lucky for the year.
90.history: For centuries this coast lay nearly empty, open to the raiders of the southern gulf. Once Thôn Hải Môn was founded on its islet its sails came often, and the watchtowers of Vọng Hải learned to see them a day before they landed. Then the Pivot called the Pirate Purge, and it ended with Ô Kình Hải dead on his islet. Two decades later, in 800, while the War of Broken Halberds held the Tower's strength in the north, Thính Vũ Lâu founded Lãng Hoa Thành on the sea-spray coast, safe at last from pirates. Its builders cut the blowholes into the sea wall to break the force of the storm waves. With the Tower's eyes on the war, the young city grew up largely on its own. Since the Age of Vein Wars began it has been a fishing and salt port, far from the quarrels over veins.
levels: A second harbour mole with its own blowholes, and stone salt pans along the shore.
A walled upper town around the watch hall, and a long spray wall running the whole bay.

91.name: Vọng Hải Trấn
91.look: A walled town in coastal bamboo at a river mouth, below a line of low sea cliffs. Along the cliff tops stand tall watchtowers with stone footings and bamboo upper storeys, each with a signal frame looking out over the gulf.
91.lore: Vọng Hải belongs to Xuyên Lâm Môn, whose people keep the watchtowers manned. In 780 the towers saw Thôn Hải's sails a day before they landed, and the warning is still told as the saving of the coast. The town keeps a watch on every tower though no pirate has come in centuries, and a watcher caught asleep must carry water to every house.
levels: A walled signal post joins the towers along the cliffs, and a fishing harbour is dug in the river mouth.
A brick-walled coastal town with a beacon hall and a covered stair from the harbour to the towers.

92.name: Phong Đăng Trấn
92.look: A walled harbour town in fertile river meadows by the sea, its fields heavy with grain. In its main gate hangs a huge wooden steelyard balance, its beam as long as a boat, where grain carts are weighed for the tax before they enter.
92.lore: The Lục family's harvests at Phong Đăng are so rich that since 600 Thính Vũ has collected its grain tax here first each year. The first cart weighed on the great steelyard is always the Lục family's, and the whole town turns out to watch the beam. The neighbouring villages grumble that the beam is honest only once a year.
levels: A walled granary yard for the tax grain and a stone quay for the boats.
A brick-walled town with the Lục family's manor on a rise and a second steelyard over the harbour gate.

93.name: Thạch Cơ Thành
93.look: A walled harbour city on a flat stretch of coast, built around a long stone jetty that juts far out into the gulf. Most of the jetty is grey, sea-worn stone, but its outer end has been rebuilt in bright red stone that stands out against the water.
93.lore: Thạch Cơ Thành rose in 776 around the stone jetty where Phượng Minh's and Lạc Hà's fleets gathered for the Pirate Purge under the Pivot's writ. In 1190 a storm cracked the jetty, and Phượng Minh rebuilt it with red stone from the ruins of Xích Thành. Old sailors grumble that the red end is unlucky; young ones say it is the strongest part.
93.history: Before the Purge this was a quiet stretch of shore within sight of the pirates' gulf. In 776 Đỗ Tinh Hà called the Pirate Purge, Phượng Minh's and Lạc Hà's fleets sailed under the Pivot's writ, and Thạch Cơ Thành rose around the stone jetty where they gathered. Five years later the Purge ended at Thôn Hải Môn with Ô Kình Hải dead, and the fleets came home here. The captives freed from Thôn Hải's hold were landed at the jetty and walked home to villages like Lô Châu. After the war the city stayed on as a port and a station for the Palace's ships in the gulf. In 1190 a storm cracked the jetty, and Phượng Minh rebuilt it with stone from the ruins of Xích Thành. Its red end is now the first thing incoming ships see.
levels: A second jetty beside the first and a walled shipyard on the shore.
A fortified harbour city with a stone lighthouse at the red end of the jetty and a sea wall around the anchorage.

94.name: Tang Điền Trấn
94.look: A walled coastal town on rust-red earth, surrounded by long rows of mulberry bushes. Among the rows stand low two-storey silkworm sheds with slatted wooden walls, and in season the whole town smells of boiling cocoons.
94.lore: Mulberry fields have been planted in the red soil of Tang Điền since 200, and they feed the silkworms of the south. The town now belongs to Phần Vũ Đường. Its silk women say the red soil puts fire in the thread, and some claim that Xích Thành's fire-silk began with their worms.
94.history: Mulberry was first planted in the red soil of Tang Điền in 200, in the Age of First Gates, and its silkworms soon fed the looms of the south. When Xích Thành Môn rose among the red cliffs a generation later, the town fell under its shadow, and its silk women still claim the sect's fire-silk banner began with their worms. Under the heir who burned villages, the town's elders say, it paid in silk to be spared. After Phượng Minh destroyed the gate under writ, Tang Điền passed with the rest of Đan Huyệt Châu to the Palace. The silk caravans that rest at Tang Âm carried its thread along the coast road. When Phần Vũ Đường was founded in the old vents, the town was given to the new hall, and its mulberry rows now feed the hall as well as the looms. The red earth and the slatted sheds are much as they were in the first planting.
levels: A reeling house by the shore and more silkworm sheds in the outer fields.
A brick-walled silk town with a dye works and a stone pier for the silk boats.

95.name: Tuyết Lộc Thôn
95.look: A handful of low log houses with grey tile and turf roofs sit on the snowy north shore of the lake, entered through a gate arch built entirely of shed reindeer antlers. Herds graze the lichen between the houses and the water's edge.
95.lore: Reindeer herders settled the lake's snowy north shore in 140, and their camp became Tuyết Lộc Thôn; each spring the herders add the year's finest shed antlers to the arch. A fisher of this village pulled from the lake the great pearl that started Hàm Nguyệt Trang's pearl farms, and the village answers to the manor. Since the Long Lake War, Băng Tâm fishers share the northern shore, and the herders trade them hides for salt.
levels: The antler arch is doubled in height, and a row of smokehouses and a fenced winter corral grow along the shore.
A small stone shrine to the lake's first pearl stands beside the arch, and a longer jetty serves the fishers of the northern shore.

96.name: Hàn Yên Thôn
96.look: A huddle of grey-roofed houses with tall stone chimneys sits on the lake shore, where on still winter mornings the smoke hangs frozen in pale columns. At the ice edge stands a lone post with a bronze bell, rung at every dusk.
96.lore: The village takes its name from a winter so cold that smoke froze above its chimneys. When a snow-leopard spirit beast took a child from here, Hàm Nguyệt Trang's disciples tracked it for forty days across the ice; since then the bell at the shore calls the children in before dark. Villagers leave a fish on the bell post's stone base on the night the hunt set out, for the disciples who went.
levels: A palisade faces the forest and a second bell post stands at the village's back toward the trees.
A small stone watch-house for the lake patrol rises beside the shore bell, its single grey roof the tallest in the village.

97.name: Noãn Ốc Thôn
97.look: Domed stone houses, thick-walled and half sunk into the ground, cluster on the lake shore like loaves of bread, each capped with a small grey tile roof. Between them a timber bath-house stands over a hot spring, its steam visible far across the ice.
97.lore: Tùng Đào's first steward of the north built warm stone houses for the lake villages, and the hamlet beside them is still called Noãn Ốc. Since a hot spring was found under the snow here in 1015, old cultivators come every winter to soak their bones, and villagers rent bath hours by the burning of an incense stick. Locals say the steward's houses stay warm because he mixed a little of his own qi into the mortar.
levels: New domed houses ring the bath-house and a covered walkway links them against the snow.
A two-storey guest lodge for visiting cultivators rises beside the spring, and the bath-house gains a second, stone-walled pool.

98.name: Mạch Lãng Thôn
98.look: A few grey-roofed farmhouses stand among wheat fields that ripple like waves over dark volcanic soil. Low walls of black lava stone divide the gold fields into long strips running down to the sea.
98.lore: Wheat first grew here in the warm ash of the cape, and the fields of Mạch Lãng Thôn are still the oldest on it. Farmers say the ash remembers the fire and keeps the seed warm through the frosts. At harvest they leave the last strip standing for the wind to thresh.
levels: The lava-stone walls extend up the slope over new strips and a stone threshing floor is laid by the houses.
A small granary barn with a double grey roof and a windmill on the slope serve the wider fields.

99.name: Phong Phàm Thôn
99.look: A village of grey roofs sits on a windy headland above its boat sheds. On the point stands a tall mast hung with long cloth streamers of many colours, which the sailors read before every launch.
99.lore: The sailors of Phong Phàm Thôn learned to read the cape's winds so well that their sails never go slack. Every family hangs its own streamer on the wind mast, and children learn the winds by watching how each one flies. Merchants of the coast hire Phong Phàm pilots whenever they can get them.
levels: A second mast stands on the far point and the boat sheds grow into a small yard with a stone slipway.
A pilots' hall with a lookout gallery rises beside the mast, and a short stone breakwater shelters the boats.

100.name: Hòa Thử Thôn
100.look: Low farmhouses sit among millet and grain fields on the coast. Beside them stand rows of small granary huts raised on mushroom-shaped stone stilts, keeping the grain clear of damp and rats.
100.lore: Grain from Hòa Thử Thôn fed Yên Ba Thành through the long winter of 860, and the city has not forgotten. The village keeps one granary hut empty in every row in memory of that winter, filled only when another bad year comes. Its millet wine is poured at harvest feasts all along the cape.
levels: The granary rows double and a stone road links the village to the coast road.
A large stone grain store with a double roof rises at the end of the rows, and a small pier ships grain to Yên Ba.

101.name: Ẩn Loan Thôn
101.look: A few houses cling above a narrow cove hidden between cliffs, out of sight from the open sea. A steep stair cut into the rock leads down from the village to the mouth of a sea cave at the water's edge.
101.lore: One winter a pirate crew hid in the cove below the village, and the villagers fed them and said nothing. When Thôn Hải fell the pirates vanished in a single night, leaving a chest of salt and a child; some say the child's line still lives here. The villagers are polite to strangers and tell them very little.
levels: A rope hoist is rigged beside the stair and a few new houses climb along the cliff top.
A small stone harbour wall is built across the cove's mouth, and a grey-roofed watch-house stands over the cave stair.

102.name: Ô Đề Thôn
102.look: A small fishing village of grey roofs lies on the shore under a long ridge. On the ridge top a single huge bare oak stands black against the sky, its branches crowded with roosting crows.
102.lore: Crows gathered on the ridge in such numbers that the village beneath was named Ô Đề. Villagers feed them at the new year and believe the crows warn of storms by leaving the oak. Fishers look up at the ridge before they set out.
102.history: Fishers beached their boats under this ridge in the Age of First Gates, without a village to speak of. In 410 crows gathered on the ridge in such numbers that the village growing beneath was named Ô Đề. The great oak on the crest was already old then, and the crows have roosted in it ever since. Fishers learned that the birds leave the oak before a storm, and began to watch the ridge before setting out. The custom of feeding the crows at the new year followed, and no villager will harm one. The village passed with the hills to Thúy Vi Tông, and its boats now sell their catch to the sect's towns along the coast.
levels: A few more houses climb the slope toward the ridge and a small fish-smoking shed lines the shore.
A small shrine to the crows stands at the foot of the oak, and a stone pier serves the boats.

103.name: Lâm Tuyền Thôn
103.look: A coastal village of grey roofs lies under wooded slopes, with a long line of split bamboo pipes running down from the woods on wooden trestles. The pipes end in a row of stone troughs in the village square, always running.
103.lore: A spring in the woods above the village cured the coughing sickness of 760, and the village took its name from its woods and springs. The pipe line was built to bring the water down for the sick, and every family repairs its own length of it. Travellers still come to fill jars at the troughs.
103.history: Before it had its name, the village was a few fishers' houses on the shore below the wooded slopes. In 760 a coughing sickness spread along the coast, and a spring in the woods above the village cured those who drank from it. The village took its name from its woods and springs, and its families together built the long bamboo pipe line to carry the water down to the sick. Each family took one length of it to keep in repair, a duty passed from parent to child. Travellers and the sick of other villages came to fill jars at the troughs, and some of them stayed. The spring has never failed, and the villagers say that is because no one has ever sold its water.
levels: A small roofed spring-house is built at the top of the pipe line and a second line feeds a bath-house.
A healers' lodge with a double grey roof stands by the troughs, and the trestles are rebuilt in stone.

104.name: Thu Diệp Thôn
104.look: A small village of grey roofs by the shore stands in front of a grove of maples that burns crimson every autumn. Wooden frames of pressed leaves dry in rows along the house walls.
104.lore: Red leaves from Thu Diệp Thôn are sold in Lam Yên Thị as bookmarks for scripture, and scholars from three sects come to buy them. Each leaf is pressed between boards for a season. The villagers say a leaf picked by a cultivator turns brown, so only mortals may gather them.
104.history: For most of its life the village was a quiet fishing place on the shore, known only for the red maples behind it. Its people pressed the leaves for their own pleasure and for the little shrines of the coast. In 1140 red leaves from Thu Diệp Thôn began to be sold in Lam Yên Thị as bookmarks for scripture, and scholars came from three sects to buy them. The trade made the village busier than it had ever been, and drying frames went up along every wall. The rule that only mortals may pick the leaves grew with the trade, and the villagers keep it strictly. The grove is now tended as carefully as any herb terrace in the hills.
levels: The maple grove is extended up the slope and a long drying shed for pressed leaves is built.
A small hall for sorting and wrapping the leaves stands by the road, its double grey roof facing the grove.

105.name: Bạch Hoa Thôn
105.look: A small coastal village of grey roofs stands in a bright grove of white birches. Among the pale trunks the black stumps of old burned trees still stand, so the grove is pied black and white.
105.lore: White birches grew where a forest fire had burned, and the new village was named Bạch Hoa. Villagers strip birch bark for writing sheets and boxes, and will not pull up the old stumps, saying they hold the ground for the birches. Charcoal from those stumps is never burned in a house.
levels: A bark workshop with long drying racks is built at the grove's edge and the jetty is lengthened.
A small double-roofed shrine stands among the oldest stumps, and a stone pier serves boats carrying bark goods.

106.name: Thanh Tùng Thôn
106.look: A river village of grey roofs sits beside a grove of tall pines planted in neat rows, each with a small flat stone at its foot. The rows run from the riverbank to the forest edge like ranks of soldiers.
106.lore: When a beast tide overran Hổ Khiếu Trấn, its survivors moved to Thanh Tùng Thôn and planted a green pine for each of their dead. The pines are tall now, and each spring families sweep the stones beneath their own trees. No one cuts or taps them.
levels: A low stone wall is built around the memorial grove and a few new houses line the river path.
A small ancestral hall with a double grey roof stands at the head of the pine rows.

107.name: Tùng Phong Thôn
107.look: A small river village of grey roofs lies in the pines. Between two great pines at its edge long strings are stretched, and they hum and moan whenever the wind blows, a sound that carries over the whole hamlet.
