107.lore: Vạn Hác Viện's zither students practise in Tùng Phong hamlet, and the villagers have learned to sleep through anything. A student once strung the wind strings between the two pines, and the village keeps them tuned in return for the students' quiet hours. Children here can name a note before they can name the stars.
levels: A small open practice pavilion for visiting students is built near the strings.
A second pair of pines is strung across the river, and a guesthouse with a double grey roof stands by the ford.

108.name: Tuyết Ốc Thôn
108.look: In winter the village almost vanishes: low turf-roofed houses sunk half into the ground, chimneys smoking through the drifts. Each house is marked by a tall red-painted door-pole so neighbours can find each other under the snow. In summer the poles stand oddly tall over a cluster of grassy mounds by the upper river.
108.lore: Winters on the upper river are so deep that the houses of Tuyết Ốc have been built half under the snow since at least 340. Families dig tunnels from door to door and visit underground all winter. A new bride paints her husband's door-pole fresh red on her first spring in the village.
levels: A longhouse dug into the riverbank for winter gatherings, with snow-tunnels from every door.
A small timber stockade and a raised storehouse above the snowline, and door-poles crowned with carved finials.

109.name: Hàn Mai Thôn
109.look: A handful of grey-tile houses sits around a small snowy square, and in the middle of the square grows one gnarled winter plum behind a low bamboo fence. In the cold months its red blossoms are the only colour for days of travel. Villagers bow to it on their way down to the river.
109.lore: In 420 a winter plum bloomed through the snow above a buried child, and the diggers found her alive; the village was named Hàn Mai. The tree in the square is said to have grown from a cutting of that plum. Every child born in winter is carried to the tree before it is given a name.
levels: A small shrine roof beside the plum and a few new houses facing the square.
A walled courtyard around the plum with a gate arch, and a second, younger plum planted at the village edge.

110.name: Bạch Lang Thôn
110.look: The village circles a hollow at its heart, ringed with white-limed boulders: the old den of the white wolf king. Children run between the houses with wolf-tooth charms clicking at their necks. A path from the hollow leads down to the river, where women beat laundry on flat stones.
110.lore: Thôi Khinh Hồng of Tùng Đào Cung slew the white wolf king of Cửu Khúc Xuyên, and in 456 the village built on its den was named Bạch Lang. Its children wear wolf-tooth charms. Each spring the boulders around the den are limed white again, and the village says that the year they are left grey, the wolves will come back.
levels: A timber fence around the village and a small shrine at the lip of the den.
A stone wall with a gate carved with a wolf's head, and a hunters' lodge beside the den.

111.name: Ba Quang Thôn
111.look: A fishing village on the shore of a chain of small mountain lakes stepping down a grassy slope, its boats drawn up on the gravel. At midday the lakes throw so much light that the village seems to stand in a blaze. Flat reed rafts lie on the beach, ready for the evening nets.
111.lore: Light glints so brightly on the mountain lakes at Ba Quang that travellers have taken the village for a fire since at least 600, and more than one has run up with a bucket. Its people net lake fish and ferry Cửu Cao Phái's riders across the water. The elders squint their whole lives, and a squint is thought handsome here.
levels: A timber boat landing and a drying rack for nets along the lowest lake.
A small walled hamlet with a lakeside shrine and a crane perch for Cửu Cao's riders.

112.name: Hạc Quy Thôn
112.look: A quiet marsh-edge village of reed-thatched and grey-tile houses on a slow river. In the meadow beyond, the villagers keep a crescent-shaped landing pool dug in the turf and edged with flat grey stepping stones, where the cranes come down each year. They clear its weed by hand all summer.
112.lore: Cranes return to the marshes here on the same day every year, and since 700 the village where they land has been called Hạc Quy; Cửu Cao Phái rides the first of them. Ung Hạc Minh was born here in 1010, the year the cranes stayed a month longer. On landing day the whole village stands silent around the crescent pool until the last bird folds its wings.
levels: A reed-roofed watching shelter beside the crescent pool and a few new houses along the river.
A timber fence, a small shrine to the cranes, and a rest hall for Cửu Cao's riders.

113.name: Lộc Uyển Thôn
113.look: A hillside village of log houses above a high meadow where deer gather each spring. At the meadow's edge stands a black stone stele carrying Thiên Xu's ban on hunting, and shed antlers are heaped around its foot. A rail fence keeps the village goats off the deer's grass.
113.lore: Deer have gathered each spring in the high meadow of Lộc Uyển since before 380, when Thiên Xu forbade hunting there. Children collect the antlers the stags shed and lay them at the stele as a gift to the Pivot. Poachers from outside are rare; the villagers report them before the deer have even scattered.
levels: A gamekeeper's lodge beside the stele and a fenced herb garden.
A small walled hamlet with a gate house of the Pivot's wardens and a covered antler hall.

114.name: Đỗ Quyên Thôn
114.look: A fishing village sits on a grey shore under steep slopes that turn blood-red with azaleas each spring. Its low houses are roofed with dark stone slabs against the wind, and its boats lie hauled up on black volcanic shingle. In bloom the slope looks like a fire about to come down on the roofs.
114.lore: Azaleas bloom red on the slopes above Đỗ Quyên Thôn each spring, and since at least 640 the villagers have said they are the dead of the eruption. No one picks them. On the first day of bloom the village leaves rice cakes at the foot of the slope and does not fish.
114.history: Fishers lived on this shore below the ice mountains while Hồ Thiên Phái still stood on the ice nearby, trading fish for the school's furs and salt. When Chúc Long Sơn erupted in the Age of Seven Seats and buried the school, ash fell on the village and the sea ran warm and grey for a season. The survivors stayed, and their dead were buried on the slope above the houses. Băng Tâm Các claimed the empty ice two generations later, and the village came under its rule. In time red azaleas covered the slope where the graves lay. By 640 the villagers said that the azaleas blooming red above Đỗ Quyên Thôn each spring were the eruption's dead, and the custom of leaving rice cakes at the foot of the slope had begun. No one in the village picks them, and when the mountain rumbled again in the last winter the azaleas were the first thing the fishers looked at in spring.
levels: A small timber jetty and a shrine at the foot of the azalea slope.
A low stone sea wall, a boat shed, and a terraced path up through the azaleas to a lookout.

115.name: Hoàng Oanh Thôn
115.look: In a sheltered coastal valley, a ring of grey-tile houses stands among bare willows hung with woven straw bird shelters. All winter the shelters flash yellow with orioles, and their song carries down to the boats. Snow lies on the ridges all around.
115.lore: Orioles winter in the valley of Hoàng Oanh Thôn, the only birdsong in the ice mountains, and the village has woven shelters for them since at least 850. Nuns from the hermitage up the mountain are said to come down in winter only to listen. A child who throws a stone at an oriole must sleep one night with the goats.
115.history: The valley was a fishing cove long before it had a name, sheltered from the north wind by the ridges around it. Late in the Age of Seven Seats it came under Băng Tâm Các with the rest of the ice mountains. At some time no one recorded, orioles began to winter among its willows, the only birdsong anywhere in the ice mountains. By 850 the birds were known across Băng Tâm's land, and the village had taken the name Hoàng Oanh for them. The villagers began weaving straw shelters for the birds and hanging them in the willows each autumn. Nuns from Lê Hoa Am are said to walk down the mountain in winter only to hear them. The orioles have never failed to come, and the village takes their arrival as the true start of its year.
levels: A timber boat landing and more willows planted along the stream.
A small walled hamlet with a listening pavilion among the willows and a stone jetty.

116.name: Ngư Đàm Thôn
116.look: Behind a bitter salt shore where nothing swims, a small oasis holds a grid of square fish ponds edged with mud brick and shaded by date palms. Low flat-roofed houses of the same brick line the dikes between the ponds. Children with wooden clappers chase the herons off the shallows.
116.lore: Since around 500, fish ponds dug in the oasis have given Ngư Đàm Thôn its name and Băng Tâm's desert its only fish; the sea beside it is too salt and barren to net. Carp travel from here to the seat in water jars. A fish dish at a Băng Tâm feast means it came from Ngư Đàm, and the village is proud of it.
levels: More ponds dug toward the dunes and a covered jar store by the landing.
A mud-brick wall around the oasis, a water tower, and a small shrine on the central dike.

117.name: Liên Đường Thôn
117.look: In the middle of the open steppe, a hollow of spring-fed ponds blooms pink and white with lotus all summer. A few mud-brick houses with reed roofs stand on the banks, and a wooden viewing pier reaches out over the leaves. Caravans halt on the rise above just to look.
117.lore: Lotus ponds have bloomed at Liên Đường since around 560, and caravans stop just to look. The village now answers to Dạ Quang Môn, whose riders water their horses here and leave the flowers alone. Lotus root and seed are its living, and a lotus seed is pressed into the hand of every traveller who asks the way.
levels: A caravan rest yard on the rise and a second viewing pier.
A low earth wall around the ponds, a lotus pavilion on an island in the largest pond, and a horse trough fed by the spring.

118.name: Mã Minh Thôn
118.look: Round corrals of piled dry stone ring a cluster of felt tents and mud houses on the steppe behind the range. The neigh of horses carries far over the grass. To the west a low hump of sand covers the old wells where the village once stood.
118.lore: Nomad herders drove their horses across the steppe behind the range as early as 100, and their camping ground became Mã Minh Thôn. In 1050 a sandstorm buried its wells, and the village moved a short way east, horses and all. Its herders sell remounts to Băng Tâm's caravans and to anyone else who can pay.
levels: New stone-lined wells and a long horse barn with a thatched roof.
A walled horse market, a herders' hall, and corrals spread out across the plain.

119.name: Tiều Lộ Thôn
119.look: A woodcutters' village where the forest comes down to the shore, its log houses under grey-tile roofs around a small timber jetty. At the forest's edge a fan of red-painted marker posts leads off among the trees, each one the start of a different path into Vô Tung Lâm.
119.lore: The woodcutters' paths into Vô Tung Lâm vanish under the snow every night, and only the people of Tiều Lộ Thôn can find them again; outsiders who need the forest hire a Tiều Lộ guide or go without. The village answers to Trạc Anh Đài, and it is said the poles of the terrace's drying lines are cut by Tiều Lộ hands.
119.history: Woodcutters settled this shore where Vô Tung Lâm comes down to the sea, cutting timber for the boats of the frost coast. By 540 their paths into the forest were known to vanish under the snow every night, and only the people of Tiều Lộ Thôn could find them again. They marked the start of each path with a painted post and kept the rest of the way in their heads, passed from parent to child. Hunters and timber buyers from the coast's towns learned to hire a Tiều Lộ guide or stay out of the trees. When the fishers and sea hunters of the coast founded Trạc Anh Đài, the village came under the terrace's hand, and it is said Tiều Lộ's woodcutters cut the poles for the terrace's drying lines. The elders boast that the village has never lost a guide in the forest, though it has lost many who went in without one.
levels: A sawpit and a log slide down to the jetty, and more houses climb along the posts toward the trees.
A palisade circles the village, a covered timber yard faces the water, and the red posts gain carved caps for each family's path.

120.name: Lâm Ẩn Thôn
120.look: A coastal village so deep in old firs that from the sea only its chimney smoke shows above the canopy. A single long plank jetty runs out of the trees into a quiet inlet.
120.lore: In the Age of the North Star Compact (Bắc Thần Kỷ) a hermit sheltered here and taught the village children to read tracks in the snow, and every child of Lâm Ẩn still learns tracks before letters. Hunters from Mộc Lan Thành come to hire them, and it is said no beast passes near the village without being named by its footprints.
120.history: Lâm Ẩn Thôn grew in a stand of old firs on the frost coast, so deep in the trees that passing boats saw only its smoke. Its people lived by fishing the inlet and hunting the forest edge. In 780 the village sheltered a hermit who taught its children to read tracks in the snow; the record keeps no name for him. He stayed until the children could tell a fox from a marten by a single print, and then, the villagers say, he walked into the forest and left no track at all. Every child of Lâm Ẩn has learned tracks before letters ever since. Hunters from Mộc Lan Thành come to hire them, and Băng Tâm's patrols ask a Lâm Ẩn tracker first when something goes missing in the woods.
levels: A tracking lodge is built under the firs and a second jetty reaches the inlet.
The village grows a hidden ring of houses under the canopy, a smokehouse row along the shore, and a small hall where the children learn the tracks.

121.name: Lô Hoa Thôn
121.look: A marsh village on the grassy coast, its stilt houses standing in a sea of reeds. In summer the reeds flower white and the whole marsh looks snowed over, with only grey roofs and winding boat channels showing through.
121.lore: The people of Lô Hoa cut reeds for thatch, mats and net floats, and sell the reed-flower down the coast to Liên Giang and Mộc Lan for stuffing winter quilts. Children are told the summer snow is the frost coast's reminder that winter is never far away.
121.history: Reed-cutters built their stilt houses in this coastal marsh, where the reeds grow tall enough to hide a boat and the spring thaw floods the ground. From the first they cut reeds for thatch, mats and the floats of nets. In 640 the reed flowers covered the marsh like snow in summer, and the sight drew travellers from along the coast. The village learned to sell the soft reed-flower for stuffing winter quilts, and the white summers made its name. Its reeds and down now go by boat to the ports of Liên Giang and Mộc Lan. Each summer, when the marsh first turns white, the children run the plank walks shouting that the snow has come early.
levels: A reed-drying yard on stilts and a boat shed are added, and the plank walks reach a new row of houses.
A raised earth bank with a small grey-tile hall rises in the marsh, and the channels are lined with posts for the reed boats.

122.name: Bối Sa Thôn
122.look: A fishing village on a gleaming white beach on the island's grassy coast. On the sand above the tide line stands a small mound-shrine built entirely of white shells, with the village's drying mats spread around it.
122.lore: Since the Age of First Gates (Khai Môn Kỷ) the islanders have gathered shells on Bối Sa's beach to trade as coins on the mainland, long before any sect held the island. Old shell money is still taken in the village for small things, and every child adds a shell to the shrine on its first birthday.
levels: A shell-sorting shed and a boat slip are added, and the shrine is given a low stone ring.
The village grows a short stone quay and a small hall for the shell traders, and the shrine mound rises higher every year.

123.name: Lãng Thạch Thôn
123.look: A small village behind a sea stack on the island coast. The stack, Wave Rock, stands split in two from crown to waterline, and through the gap shows the dark mouth of a sea cave.
123.lore: Wave Rock split in a storm in 960 and opened a sea cave full of old charts drawn by the lost sailors of Cô Phàm Các. The village answers to Bình Thủy Môn, and its fishers still row visitors into the cave; rumour says not every chart was carried out.
levels: A landing stage is built at the cave mouth and a chart-copiers' hut rises in the village.
The village gains a small walled yard and a stone jetty reaching toward the split rock.

124.name: Dương Liễu Thôn
124.look: A village on the island's dunes, its grey roofs sheltered behind long rows of wind-bent willows planted along the sand ridges. Their roots bind the dunes, and from the sea the village looks hedged in green.
124.lore: Since 750 the villagers have planted willows on the dunes to hold the island's sand against the storms. Each household tends its own row, and a newborn's cord is buried at the foot of a new willow.
levels: New willow rows run along the outer dunes and a boat shed is built in their lee.
A wattle sea fence stretches behind the willows, and a small grey-tile hall stands on the highest dune.

125.name: Tình Sa Thôn
125.look: A village of low grey roofs on a broad, sunny sandbar at a river mouth. On the bar lies a long driftwood effigy of a whale, built by the villagers and weathered silver.
125.lore: In 1190 a whale stranded on Tình Sa's sunny sands lived three days while the islanders worked to give it back to the sea. The villagers built the driftwood whale to remember it, and mend it from new driftwood whenever a storm takes a piece.
levels: A fish-drying frame and a jetty into the river channel are added.
The village spreads along both banks of the river mouth, joined by a plank footbridge, and a small shrine roof shelters the whale's head.

126.name: Nguyệt Loan Thôn
126.look: A fishing village around a perfect crescent cove, its arms of rock nearly closing at the mouth. Inside rides a crowded fleet of island boats, their masts thick as reeds.
126.lore: In the great storm of 870 the moon-shaped cove sheltered the island's fishing fleet, and boats from every harbour on Cô Vụ Đảo still run for Nguyệt Loan when the sky turns. Captains who ride out a storm here hang a carved wooden moon on the village boat shed in thanks.
levels: A storm wall is built along the cove's curve and a long boat shed rises at its head.
Mooring piers ring the cove, and a small grey-tile storm shrine stands on the tip of one rocky arm.

127.name: Điền Viên Thôn
127.look: A village of gardens and fields on the plain coast, its grey roofs half hidden by orchard walls. In nearly every garden wall is a round moon gate, and through them show the small studies of retired scholars.
127.lore: Since 890 the gardens and fields of Điền Viên have fed the scholars of Nhạn Thanh Thành, who retire here to farm. The village answers to Mục Vân Trang, and its old scholars write letters for the herders and are paid in vegetables.
levels: A small library pavilion and a shared orchard are added.
A walled scholars' garden with a pond pavilion forms the heart of the village, and new moon gates open onto the fields.

128.name: Yến Quy Thôn
128.look: A small farm village on the plain coast, its grey roofs gathered around one old farmstead. The old farm's roof ridge is lined end to end with little clay swallows, and the real birds perch among them.
128.lore: Swallows returned to the same farm every spring for a hundred years, and by 300 the village was named Yến Quy, Swallows' Return. The farm still stands; each family adds a clay swallow to its ridge, and a year when the real birds are late is a year to plant carefully.
levels: A new barn and a threshing floor are built beside the old farm.
The village grows a small walled yard and a shrine hall, its ridge also lined with clay swallows.

129.name: Chu Tân Thôn
129.look: A ferry village on the low, wet shore, below the level of the sea at high tide. Two tall carved ferry posts stand at the old ford, joined by a heavy rope across a narrow tidal creek, with a flat barge crawling along it.
129.lore: A ford on the plain's widest river became Chu Tân Thôn in 520; the river has since wandered from the village, but the old ford's posts still stand, and at high tide the villagers haul travellers across the creek on the rope ferry. The village answers to Mục Vân Trang, whose herds cross here every spring, and the ferrymen know each horse by name.
levels: A ferry inn and a holding pen for herds are built by the landing.
A second rope and barge are added, and a small walled waystation stands on the far bank.

130.name: Lô Cảng Thôn
130.look: A village of reed-thatched boat sheds around a sheltered reed harbour on the plain coast. Out of the reeds rises a tall timber watchtower flying Lạc Hà's sunset-red banner, the sect's western watch.
130.lore: The reed harbour at Lô Cảng shelters the coast boats from the open sea, and in 800 Lạc Hà Tông built its western watch here. Watchmen and fishers share the village, and the tower lights a fire when strange sails are seen.
levels: A walled barracks yard joins the watchtower and a jetty runs through the reeds.
A stone signal platform tops the tower, and a second harbour pool is cut into the reeds.

131.name: Diêm Điền Thôn
131.look: A village at the edge of a vast glittering grid of salt pans on the flat west coast. Between the shallow white squares stand rows of shining salt cones, raked up by hand.
131.lore: Salt pans dug at Diêm Điền in 200 made the continent's first sea salt, before any great sect held the west. The salt-makers keep the first pan unused and fenced, and pour a handful of new salt into it every year.
levels: A salt store with a high grey roof rises and the pans spread along the shore.
A walled salt yard and a stone loading jetty serve the pans.

132.name: Khê Thanh Thôn
132.look: A village on a clear grassland brook, its grey roofs strung along the water. Over the brook stand a row of small covered rinsing sheds on stilts, where the water chatters loudly over the stones beneath them.
132.lore: The brook at Khê Thanh runs so clear that since 700 Thiên Bảo Trai has washed its finest refinings in it. The Trai's apprentices come down with covered baskets, the villagers are paid to keep the banks free of mud and cattle, and the brook's chatter is said to sing the flaws out of the metal.
levels: More rinsing sheds are built downstream and a small inspection hall for the Trai's stewards rises on the bank.
A walled storehouse for refinings and a stone footbridge join the village across the brook.

133.name: Khê Đầu Thôn
133.look: A small village at the head of a brook on the grassland, where the water rises from the ground. The spring pours from a stone spout carved as a carp's head into a round basin, and the brook starts from its overflow.
133.lore: Khê Đầu sits where the brook begins, upstream of Khê Thanh, and its water is the clearest of all; Thiên Bảo Trai washes its finest refinings at both villages. The villagers guard the spring like a shrine and let no one wash in the basin itself, only below it.
levels: A low wall and a small roof are built around the spring basin.
A spring hall with a grey-tile roof shelters the carp spout, and a stone channel leads the brook toward Khê Thanh.

134.name: Hải Môn Thôn
134.look: A fishing village on the bay coast beside a great natural rock arch, the Sea Gate. Twice a day the tide runs through the arch in a white rush, and the village boats wait on the inner side for the slack.
134.lore: Since 450 the village has been named for its Sea Gate, the rock arch the tide runs through twice a day. Fishers time everything by it, and a bride and groom row through the arch at slack water for luck.
levels: A boat shed and a stone landing are built inside the arch's shelter.
A small grey-tile shrine stands on the arch's landward foot, and a jetty reaches out to the slack-water channel.

135.name: Tân Khẩu Thôn
135.look: A village at the mouth of a harbour on the bay coast, its houses all facing the sea. On the landward side they join into one long blank wall with no windows, turned against the plain.
135.lore: Refugees from Vô Định Thành founded the village in 805 after the battle on the plain, and never speak of it; the blank wall says it for them. Their children are less careful: not long ago children of Tân Khẩu dared each other to touch the edge of the miasma (chướng khí) by Vô Định Thành, and one did not come back.
levels: The village lengthens along the shore and a small fish market roof is built at the harbour mouth.
A stone quay and a lantern post mark the harbour mouth, and the blank wall is raised and capped in grey tile.

136.name: Hoa Khê Thôn
136.look: A handful of grey-roofed cottages along a clear brook in open grassland, with wild plum and pear on its banks. Just below the last house a low fence of bamboo stakes crosses the brook, and in spring it catches a pink drift of petals and paper slips.
136.lore: Flower Brook Village has kept a custom since at least 560: every spring, when petals float down the brook, lovers write their names on slips and drop them in together. If the two slips catch on the bamboo fence side by side, the pair are thought bound for life; the village's old women sort the slips each evening and never tell what they find. The village pays its dues to Nam Phố Đường.
levels: A small shrine to the brook's spirit stands beside the petal fence, and a tea house for spring visitors opens on the bank.
A cluster of inns and paper shops lines both banks, and a covered walk follows the brook down to the petal fence.

137.name: Ngân Than Thôn
137.look: A low village on a gravel bend of the river, its shallows lined with long wooden sluice boxes where flecks of silver glint under the moving water. Heaps of washed grey gravel stand in rows behind the houses.
137.lore: Since 400 the people of Silver Shoal Village have panned the river shallows for silver, which Lạc Hà Tông takes for its coin. Panners work in pairs, one rocking the sluice and one singing the count, so the river here is never quiet. A sluice that turns up a large nugget is retired and hung over the door of the family that worked it.
levels: A weighing house with a sect clerk's office stands at the landing, and a small water wheel rocks the sluices.
A walled assay yard and a smelting kiln with a tall clay chimney stand behind the village, and a stone landing takes the silver barges.

138.name: Phương Thảo Thôn
138.look: A fishing village behind low dunes, where long swathes of golden-green sweet grass are laid out to dry in neat combed rows across the sea meadow. Open-sided weaving sheds face its small harbour.
138.lore: Phương Thảo Thôn, Fragrant Grass Village, cuts the sweet sea-meadow grass that has been woven into the mats of Lạc Hà Tông's meditation halls since 640. Its weavers say a good mat smells of the sea for a lifetime; a disciple who wears one through is sent here to cut the grass for its replacement.
levels: A fenced mat-drying yard and a jetty for the sect's grass barge join the village.
A walled weavers' quarter with a guild hall and a stone harbour arm shelters the grass boats, and the drying rows cover the whole meadow.

139.name: Thủy Khẩu Thôn
139.look: Where a slow brook mouths into the main river stands a small village of grey roofs beside a dead-straight channel, dug by hand and banked with long ridges of spoil planted with willows. A stone tablet stands where the channel opens onto the river.
139.lore: Thủy Khẩu, Water's Mouth Village, lives on the boat trade where the brook joins the river. In 720 the mouth silted up, and Lạc Hà's disciples dug it out by hand in one winter; the tablet records the cut, and every winter the villagers walk the willow banks and each lift one spadeful so the river will remember.
levels: A small lock of timber gates closes the channel, and a boatyard grows on the willow bank.
A walled river station with a toll house and granary guards the cut, and the channel is faced with dressed stone.

140.name: Mộc Hương Thôn
140.look: A woodcutters' village of steep grey roofs under groves of tall incense trees on a river bank. Low clay curing kilns stand in a row along the water, and their thin blue smoke hangs over the river and smells sweet a long way downstream.
140.lore: Since 600 the scented wood of Mộc Hương Thôn's groves has been burned in the hall of the Pivot. The villagers cut only fallen or dying trees and plant a sapling for every log; logs are cured slowly in the kilns, and a log meant for the Pivot is wrapped in yellow cloth before it leaves.
levels: A walled yard of curing kilns and a timber landing for the wood barges stand by the river.
A small walled town of carvers and incense-makers grows around the kilns, with a gate pavilion on the forest road.

141.name: Thụ Âm Thôn
141.look: A village sheltering whole under the canopy of one vast old tree, its roofs dappled and its lanes always cool. From the far edge of the shade, on clear days, villagers can see a grey haze lying low over the plain beyond.
141.lore: Thụ Âm Thôn, Tree Shade Village, lives under its great tree near the edge of the poisoned plain left by the battle of Chiết Kích Nguyên. In 900 a boy of the village followed his goat into the miasma and walked out three days later, grey-haired and calm; the village tells it as a warning, and goats here are tethered to the tree's roots every night. The tree is never pruned, and a branch that falls is burned on the plain side of the village to keep the haze away.
levels: A shrine is built into the roots of the great tree, and a walled goat fold and a waystation stand at the edge of the shade.
A small walled town spreads beyond the canopy, with a watch tower facing the miasma plain and a lodge for travellers bound for the battlefield.

142.name: Thủy Đối Thôn
142.look: A village on a fast stream where a row of waterwheels drives long wooden trip-hammers that rise and fall into stone mortars, thudding all day under open sheds. Flour dust whitens the roofs.
142.lore: Since 700 the water mills at Thủy Đối have ground the wheat of Thanh Mạch for all of Tinh Hán Thành. The hammers stop only on New Year's night, when the village stills the wheels and the silence wakes the babies.
levels: More wheels and a granary on stone piers line the stream, and a cart yard opens on the road to Tinh Hán.
A walled mill town with a sluice gate across the stream and a millers' guild hall grows around the hammer sheds.

143.name: Thanh Mạch Thôn
143.look: A farming village on a low rise above a river, its houses gathered around a round threshing floor of polished stone on the hilltop, with a heavy stone roller standing upright at its centre. Green wheat falls away on every side.
143.lore: Thanh Mạch Thôn, Green Wheat Village, grows the wheat the mills of Thủy Đối grind for Tinh Hán Thành. Its threshing floor is the village's meeting place, court and festival ground; the stone roller is laid down only for the harvest and set upright again when the last sheaf is in.
levels: A granary and a shrine to the field spirit stand beside the threshing floor, and irrigation channels run down to the river.
A small walled town with a market lane grows around the threshing floor, and a waterwheel lifts river water to terraced fields.

144.name: Châu Bạng Thôn
144.look: A fishing village on the inland sea whose house walls are set all over with oyster shells, so the whole village glitters white and pearl-grey in the sun. Diving boats are drawn up on a beach of broken shell.
144.lore: Pearl oysters in the shallows gave Châu Bạng Thôn its name in 400 and Tinh Hán Thành its pearl trade. Every diver sets the shell of their first pearl into the wall of the family house, so a house's walls tell how many divers it has raised.
levels: A walled pearl-sorting yard and a stone jetty for the Tinh Hán boats stand on the beach.
A small walled harbour town with a pearl guild hall grows behind the beach, with oyster beds fenced in the shallows.

145.name: Đào Khê Thôn
145.look: A small village beside a brook below the ridges, built at the edge of a wide terraced stone platform where wild peach trees grow straight out of the cracks between old paving slabs. Broken stone column bases stand in rows among the trees.
145.lore: Since 400, when wild peach trees grew over the empty palace grounds of the fallen Cửu Thiều Cung and gave the brook below its name, Đào Khê has lived beside the ruin. Villagers pick the peaches but will not cut a tree or lift a paving stone, and nobody sings in the orchard; the dead of the old palace lie in the hills nearby, and grief, the old people say, is still in the ground.
levels: A shrine to the dead of the old palace stands at the orchard's edge, and a peach-drying yard and a small inn join the village.
A walled village of peach farmers and wine makers spreads along the brook, with a gate pavilion facing the ruined platform, on which it never builds.

146.name: Hà Loan Thôn
146.look: A village on a wide river bend, every house raised high on timber stilts above the floodplain and joined by plank walks. Boats are tied under the houses, ready for autumn.
146.lore: The river bend at Hà Loan has flooded every autumn since at least 700, so its people build their houses on stilts. When the water comes the village simply moves into its boats, and the flood is a market season: traders row from house to house selling under the eaves.
levels: A raised granary and a shrine on a stone mound join the stilt houses, and an earth dike begins along the bend.
A long earthen dike rings the bend, and a small walled market on a raised platform stands among the stilt houses.

147.name: Bích Lãng Thôn
147.look: A fishing village lying just below the level of the gulf behind a seawall of great woven bamboo baskets packed with stones, stacked in a long curve. Bamboo groves crowd the houses, and jade-green waves break against the baskets.
147.lore: Bích Lãng Thôn, Jade Waves Village, fishes the gulf, and its boatmen have long said the jade-green waves carry the fishing boats home. The village lies below the sea and lives by its basket wall, re-woven every winter from Trúc Thực Viên's bamboo; the garden keeps the village, and the village gives the garden fish meal for its beasts.
levels: A second ring of baskets and a stone sluice gate guard the village, and a fish-drying yard opens on the wall.
The basket wall is faced with stone and topped by a walk, and a small walled harbour with a shrine to the waves stands at its end.

148.name: Thủy Điền Thôn
148.look: A handful of grey-tile houses on a low dyke between flooded paddies, beside the river. On the bank a great bamboo waterwheel, its rim strung with tube buckets, creaks round and lifts water into the oldest fields on the plain.
148.lore: Rice was first planted on this plain in 140, in the flooded fields of Thủy Điền, and its paddies are older than every sect but two. Farmers here measure age in harvests, not years. Each spring, before any other village plants, a child of Thủy Điền sets the first seedling, and the plain follows.
levels: A second waterwheel and a stone sluice; a barn for seed rice stands on the dyke.
A walled hamlet with a small shrine to the first rice and a row of wheels along the bank.

149.name: Âu Lộ Thôn
149.look: A low marsh shore of the eastern gulf, where a stand of dead trees is white with nesting gulls and herons and loud from dawn to dusk. The village houses sit back from the waterline on the landward edge of the marsh, and on their walls hang old diving baskets and weighted ropes, dry for centuries.
149.lore: Fishers say the birds were here before the sects and will be after. In 763, after Thôn Hải's pirates burned Châu Lệ Cảng, the harbour's pearl divers settled here on the inland side of the marsh, away from the open sea, and never dived again. Their descendants fish only from the shore and hang an empty diving basket above every new door.
levels: A boardwalk across the marsh to a small fishing jetty; the divers' quarter gains a shrine to the pearl harbour.
A walled fishing hamlet with drying racks along the shore; the heron trees are fenced and left untouched.

150.name: Ngân Hạnh Thôn
150.look: A forest village on a small river among the oak woods at the plain's edge, its grey roofs gathered under one colossal ginkgo (ngân hạnh) that dwarfs them. In autumn the tree turns gold in a single night, and by morning the roofs are carpeted yellow.
150.lore: The ginkgo is older than the village, which grew up around it. Every autumn the villagers sit up to see the night it turns, and no one has yet managed it. Its roasted nuts are sold on the road, and children are warned that greedy eaters get bad dreams.
levels: A roofed bench ring around the ginkgo's trunk and a stone bridge over the river.
A walled hamlet with a small temple at the ginkgo's foot and an inn for the road.

151.name: Lý Hoa Thôn
151.look: A fishing hamlet on a sandy beach, its boats drawn up below an orchard of white plum (lý hoa) that runs right down to the high-tide line. In early spring the orchard is so white that beach and blossom are hard to tell apart, and grey snow geese sit among the branches.
151.lore: Plum blossom here is so white that snow geese land among it by mistake, a tale told since 560. The villagers leave the geese alone, and say a goose that wakes in a plum tree brings a good catch.
levels: A stone landing for the boats and a pickling shed for plums.
A small walled harbour hamlet; the orchard is terraced up the dunes behind it.

152.name: Hoàng Ngưu Thôn
152.look: A cattle village on the open plain, its grey roofs gathered beside a great round corral of piled fieldstone. Yellow oxen graze in loose herds all around, and the grass near the corral is worn to bare earth.
152.lore: Yellow oxen ran wild on the plain left empty after Cửu Thiều fell, and in 400 the village that tamed them took their name. Its oxen pull ploughs and barges across much of the rice plain. On the first day of spring the herders paint one ox's horns red and walk it round the corral to bless the year.
levels: A second corral and a roofed ox market beside the road.
A walled hamlet with a tannery and a shrine to the ox at the corral gate.

153.name: Kiều Bạn Thôn
153.look: Where the forest road crosses a slow river, a roofed timber bridge with deep eaves carries the traffic, and under those eaves hang rows of worn straw sandals. A cluster of grey-tile houses and an inn crowd its northern end.
153.lore: The village grew up around the crossing in 680 and took its name from the bridge. Travellers leave their worn-out sandals hanging under the eaves and buy new ones at the far end, so that their tiredness stays on the bridge. Once a year the village burns the old sandals on the bank.
levels: A second inn and a stone pier strengthening the bridge's middle.
A walled hamlet at the bridgehead with a sandal-makers' row and a small shrine to travellers.

154.name: Bình Độ Thôn
154.look: A ferry landing on a wide, slow forest river, where a broad flat raft with a small thatched sleeping shelter on its deck is poled across from a village of grey-tile houses. The water here is glassy and barely moves.
154.lore: The ferry at Bình Độ has been famous since 460 for being so calm that sleeping passengers are carried over without waking. Ferrymen never raise their voices on the river, and the village forbids drums on the bank. Travellers who are carried over asleep are woken on the far side with a cup of tea.
levels: A second raft and a stone landing stair; a tea house on the bank.
A walled hamlet at the landing with a covered waiting hall, and ferry landings on both banks.

155.name: Hoa Điền Thôn
155.look: A river village set among sweeping fields of flowers in long strips of purple, yellow and white. Along the village edge runs a wall of stacked hollow-log beehives, humming loudly all summer.
155.lore: Since 540 the flower fields of Hoa Điền have fed the bees of the rain forest, and its honey is sold in Thu Trì Thành. Beekeepers tell their bees every piece of village news, births and deaths first, or the bees will leave.
levels: A second hive wall and a honey-boiling shed by the river.
A walled hamlet with a wax-chandlers' row and a jetty for the honey boats to Thu Trì.

156.name: Yên Kiều Thôn
156.look: A river village in low meadows, where a long, narrow bridge of grey stone slabs on many low piers runs out across a misty river and fades into fog before it reaches the other side. On rainy days its far end cannot be seen at all.
156.lore: The misty bridge at Yên Kiều vanishes in the rain, and since 760 travellers who cross it have said it is longer than it looks. The village now belongs to Hồng Đậu Trang, whose guests pass this way. Locals cross only in pairs, holding a rope between them, and count their steps aloud.
levels: A rope rail along the bridge and a small shrine at its near end.
A walled hamlet with an inn for Hồng Đậu Trang's guests; lamps of red glass on posts along the bridge.

157.name: Ương Ca Thôn
157.look: A hill village above a river, its grey-tile houses at the top of a stair of curving rice terraces. At the head of the terraces stands a round stone stage open to the sky, where the singers stand at planting.
157.lore: Farmers have sung as they plant the terraces here since 540, and the song is the oldest in the south. Since Thu Phần Các came, the villagers hear singing from the graves of Lôi Trạch every autumn, and they sing louder at planting to drown it. Nobody in Ương Ca sings the planting song in autumn.
levels: More terraces cut down to the river, and a roof of thatch over the singing stage.
A walled hill hamlet with a hall of the planting song beside the stage.

158.name: Song Khê Thôn
158.look: A village where two brooks, one clear and one tea-brown from the forest, run together in a Y below the houses. On the point of land where they meet stands a tiny roofed shrine with two bamboo dippers tied together by a red cord.
158.lore: Lovers who drink from both brooks are said never to part, a belief recorded since 1000. Couples come from as far as Thu Trì to drink with the joined dippers. The village matchmaker keeps the cord and swears she has never had to replace it.
levels: A pair of small stone bridges over both brooks and a wedding inn beside the shrine.
A walled hamlet with a lovers' pavilion over the confluence.

159.name: Thượng Độ Thôn
159.look: A ferry village on the upper river, where a ferry boat is hauled across on a rope strung between two tall carved stone posts. The post on the near bank is charred black to its top.
159.lore: In the Thunder Vein War of 1045, Phượng Minh's raiders reached the upper ferry at Thượng Độ before the Pivot's envoys stopped them. They burned the landing and scorched the stone post, which the villagers have never cleaned. The villagers say it is the nearest the Palace has come to the Tower's heart, and Thính Vũ's disciples stop here to look at it.
levels: A stone landing on both banks and a guard hut beside the charred post.
A walled hamlet with a small fort at the ferry, the charred post kept inside its gate.

160.name: Hà Châu Thôn
160.look: A river village of grey roofs on the bank, facing a raw new isle of grey mud and gravel that has risen in the middle of the river. Two rival boundary flags flap on the isle, one at either end.
160.lore: In 1199 an earthquake raised a river isle at Hà Châu out of the water, and Thính Vũ and Xuyên Lâm both claim it. Villagers row out each morning to see whose flag has been moved. Nothing grows on the isle yet, but everyone is sure something valuable will.
levels: A jetty out to the isle and the first willows planted on it.
A walled hamlet across both bank and isle, joined by a wooden bridge.

161.name: Cúc Viên Thôn
161.look: A small harbour village on a flat coast, its grey roofs half hidden by banked beds of yellow and bronze chrysanthemums that fill every slope and yard. In autumn the gardens grow so thick that the paths between them cannot be seen.
161.lore: In the War of the Vermilion Caves in 586, the villagers of Cúc Viên hid Phượng Minh's scouts among the chrysanthemums. The Palace has not forgotten, and its people still buy the village's flowers for the autumn rites. Every household keeps one bed planted thick enough to hide a grown person, just in case.
161.history: The chrysanthemum gardens of Cúc Viên were already old when Xích Thành Môn held the coast of Đan Huyệt Châu. When the gate's heir turned to burning villages, Cúc Viên lived in fear of the red banners like every village on the coast. In the War of the Vermilion Caves, in 586, the villagers hid Phượng Minh's scouts among the chrysanthemums while the gate's patrols searched the shore. The scouts' reports are said to have helped the Palace bring the war to its end a few years later. When the coast passed to Phượng Minh, the Palace remembered the village and began to buy its flowers for the autumn rites. Through the pirate years the gardens were trampled more than once, but the beds always grew back. Every household still keeps one bed planted thick enough to hide a grown person.
levels: A flower market under a roof by the landing and terraced beds up the dunes.
A walled hamlet with a small shrine to the hidden scouts amid the gardens.

162.name: Tang Âm Thôn
162.look: A harbour village on the coast road whose heart is a single vast old mulberry tree, its crown spread wide over a dusty caravan yard. Carts and pack animals stand in its shade, and the village houses face inward toward it.
162.lore: Since 600 the mulberry shade at Tang Âm has been the resting place of the silk caravans. Carters say the tree's shade is cooler than any roof, and that tying an animal to the trunk brings bad luck. The village lives on caravan inns and fodder.
162.history: The great mulberry at Tang Âm is older than the village, and herders sheltered under it long before any road ran along the coast. In 600, in the Age of the North Star Compact, the silk caravans of the south began to rest in its shade, and the village grew up around the yard to serve them. Its inns took in carters hauling thread from the red-soil fields of Tang Điền and goods bound for the port cities. In the pirate years the caravans ran fewer and under guard, and the villagers built their houses facing inward toward the tree. After the Pirate Purge the road filled again. The rule against tying an animal to the trunk is said to come from a carter whose mule tore down a limb, and whose luck went with it. Carters still touch the bark for luck before they leave.
levels: A long caravan inn with stables along the yard.
A walled caravan stop with a roofed gate on the coast road, the tree still at its centre.

163.name: Hồ Tâm Thôn
163.look: Behind the coastal dunes lies a round lake cut off from the sea, and the village sits on a small island in its middle, joined to the shore by a stone causeway. In the shallows beside the island stands a tall stone pillar notched with water marks, by which the villagers read the lake's strange tide. Their sea boats are dragged over the dunes to the beach.
163.lore: The lake at Hồ Tâm rises and falls with the tide though it touches no sea, and since 900 Phượng Minh's scholars have not been able to say why. The villagers do not mind; they set their fish traps by the pillar. Children are told the lake breathes with the sea through the gills of a sleeping creature.
163.history: The lake behind the dunes has fed fishers since before the sects came to the coast, and the island village is older than anyone can remember. Under Xích Thành Môn, and then under Phượng Minh Cung, it paid its dues in dried fish. In 900 Phượng Minh's scholars came to study the lake that rises and falls with the tide though it touches no sea, and they could not say why. They raised the notched stone pillar in the shallows to measure it, and their successors still come to read it. The villagers soon learned to set their fish traps by its marks. No explanation has ever been agreed on. The children's tale of a sleeping creature breathing with the sea is told more often than any scholar's.
levels: A wider causeway and a boat slipway over the dunes.
A walled island hamlet with a scholars' tide hall built around the pillar.

164.name: Lô Châu Thôn
164.look: A river village on a low island of reed marsh, its houses raised on stilts with walls of bundled reeds lashed tight under grey-tile roofs. Paths of reed mats float between them, and the marsh around is cut into neat bays where reed is harvested.
164.lore: In 765 Thôn Hải's raiders carried off the whole village of Lô Châu; only the reed cutters hidden in the marsh escaped. In 782, after the Purge, captives freed from Thôn Hải's hold came home and rebuilt it reed by reed. Every family still keeps a reed bundle from that rebuilding hanging above the door, and the reed cutters are given the first seat at every feast.
164.history: Reed cutters lived on the marsh island of Lô Châu from the early ages, selling reed for thatch and mats up and down the river. In 765 Thôn Hải's raiders came up the river and carried off the whole village; only the reed cutters hidden in the marsh escaped. For years those few kept the island alive alone, cutting reed with no one to sell it to. When the Pirate Purge broke the pirates' hold, the captives held there were freed. In 782 they came home to Lô Châu and rebuilt it reed by reed. Every family hung a bundle from that rebuilding over its door, and the reed cutters were given the first seat at every feast. The custom has held ever since.
levels: A reed-weavers' shed and a timber jetty on the river.
A walled island hamlet on raised earth, its stilted houses joined by roofed boardwalks.

165.name: Bích Ngọc Khoáng
165.look: A stepped quarry face is cut into a forested hill, its terraces banded with bright green stone. A cart ramp zigzags down the cut to the road at its foot.
165.lore: Green jade was found in these hills when they belonged to Không Sơn Viện, but the academy forbade mining it, so the mountain stayed quiet. When the hills became Thúy Vi's, the mine was opened at last in 505. Today Hồng Lô Cốc works it under Thúy Vi, and its jade goes into pill bottles and furnace fittings.
165.history: The green hills of Thanh Loan Lĩnh kept their jade unseen through the Wild Age. In 300 green jade was found in the hills, but Không Sơn Viện forbade mining it, so the mountain stayed quiet. For two centuries the find was known and left alone, and the academy's students walked past the green outcrops on the way to their lessons. When the hills passed to Thúy Vi Tông, the new sect wanted stone for its furnaces and pill vessels. In 505 the green jade mine of Bích Ngọc Khoáng was opened at last. In time its working passed to Hồng Lô Cốc, the alchemists' valley sworn to Thúy Vi, which cuts the jade into pill bottles and furnace fittings.

166.name: Vân Mẫu Khoáng
166.look: On a bare mountain slope a fan of glittering silver mica tailings spills down from a dark mine mouth, shining like a cloud resting on the rock. Above it thin seams in the cliff catch the light.
166.lore: The monks of Vân Khởi Quán opened this mine and say its stone is cloud made solid; they set it in the abbey's windows and lamps. When the mica ran thin, the abbot Tống Tọa Vân said that clouds, too, pass. The monks still dig a little each year, more for the lesson than for the stone.
166.history: The mica of this slope glittered unseen above the clouds until the monks of Vân Khởi Quán came up the mountain. In 560 they opened the mica mine and said the stone was cloud made solid. They set its thin sheets in the abbey's windows and lamps, so the halls glow pale at night. For five centuries the mine was dug by hand, a little at a time, as a practice as much as a trade. In 1080 the mica of Vân Mẫu Khoáng ran thin, and the abbot Tống Tọa Vân said that clouds, too, pass. The monks still dig a little each year, more for the lesson than for the stone.

167.name: Thạch Lục Khoáng
167.look: On a high slope of the pine sea, small mine mouths open between the exposed roots of giant old pines. Heaps of green malachite spoil lie below them, bright against the brown needles.
167.lore: Malachite was found under the roots of the oldest pines, and Tùng Đào let it be dug only where no tree must be cut. Miners tunnel between the roots and shore them with stone, never timber. Today Vạn Hác Viện holds the workings, and its malachite becomes green pigment for painters and inlay for zithers.

168.name: Băng Lăng Khoáng
168.look: A mine mouth high on a bare grey mountainside, a timber headframe and spoil heaps under snow. Over the adit hangs a curtain of icicles thick as a man, which the miners walk through and never break.
168.lore: Băng Tâm Các opened the mine in 580 for the cold metal in its rock; the shafts are hung with ice that never melts, even beside the miners' lamps. Miners wrap their boots in felt and speak softly underground, believing a shout can bring the ice down on them.
168.history: Băng Tâm Các took the frost land at the end of the Age of Seven Seats and searched its mountains for cold metal for its swords. In 580 it opened Băng Lăng Khoáng, a shaft hung with ice that never melts. The miners found that the ice grew back wherever it was broken, and learned to walk through the curtain of icicles at the mouth without touching it. Its cold metal went down the mountain to the Pavilion's sword smiths. The miners took to wrapping their boots in felt and speaking softly underground, believing a shout can bring the ice down. No one has ever seen the ice melt, even beside the lamps, and the mine is still worked today.

169.name: Xích Kim Khoáng
169.look: An open-cut mine in the dry badlands, its terraces cut into rock banded with streaks of red gold. At sunset the whole pit glows the colour of Lạc Hà's evening sky.
169.lore: Red gold was found here in 360, and Thiên Bảo Trai bought the mine before Lạc Hà's stewards heard of it; the Trai holds it still. Its gold goes to the treasure market and the refining furnaces, and miners say the seam runs redder the deeper it goes.

170.name: Thần Sa Khoáng
170.look: In the red badlands, a hillside is cut into stepped terraces of bright vermilion spoil, with a shallow washing pool on each step where the cinnabar is rinsed. A low stone furnace house squats at the foot.
170.lore: Cinnabar was found in these red badlands in 300, and Thiên Xu's alchemists opened Thần Sa Khoáng to supply the alchemists' first stone. Miners wear cloth over their mouths and rinse their hands in a stone trough before eating; the old ones say the red gets into your dreams.

171.name: Lưu Hoàng Khoáng
171.look: Flat pans of yellow sulphur crust spread across a grey badland floor, broken by steaming fissures, with low stone sheds where the crust is scraped and bagged. The ground around them is stained in rings of yellow, white and rust.
171.lore: Since 420 Thiên Xu has mined the sulphur crusts at Lưu Hoàng for fire powders, and the badlands smell of eggs for twenty li. Workers come in shifts and never sleep on site, and a gong is struck at the sheds whenever the fissures breathe harder than usual.

172.name: Vẫn Tinh Khoáng
172.look: On the high plain, a shallow round crater lined with dark, rust-streaked rock holds a timber headframe and winch over the deepest shaft at its centre. Small stone cairns mark the crater rim.
172.lore: At the end of the Wild Age stones fell from the sky on Thiên Tuyền Nguyên for nine days, and the iron at Vẫn Tinh is said to be from one of them. By 160 that star iron was being dug here, and Củng Tinh Quán keeps the mine still. The abbey's star-readers come each year to sight the crater rim against the stars.

173.name: Thiên Ngoại Khoáng
173.look: A sheer mountain face streaked rust-red, with a vertical line of square adits cut one above another and iron chains hanging from each down to the ore yard below. A sorting shed with a dark roof stands at the bottom by a stream.
173.lore: Thối Tinh Môn claimed the Mine of the Iron from Beyond the Sky in 335 and says its ore fell with the stars. Some star-readers quietly doubt it, but no smith who has worked the ore will hear a word against it.

174.name: Huyền Thiết Khoáng
174.look: Deep in the mountain a single great shaft opens under a massive stone winch house, and the ramp down to the road is worn into ruts a hand deep by carts that each carry one black ingot.
174.lore: Black iron was found deep under the mountain at Huyền Thiết in 280; it is so heavy that a cart carries only one ingot. Thiên Xu works it for armour and array anchors, and the oxen here are bred for the ramp and are the strongest in Ngọc Hành Sơn.

175.name: Can Tương Khoáng
175.look: High on a steep slope, two adits open side by side in the grey rock, one a little larger than the other, with a small stone shrine between them blackened by forge smoke. A narrow path zigzags down toward Phất Y Cốc.
175.lore: Named for Can Tương, the swordsmith of legend, this is where Phất Y Cốc digs the ore for its swords. The miners call the two adits the husband and the wife, after the legend of the paired swords, and ore from both is mixed in every blade; a sword of one ore alone, they say, will not keep its edge.

176.name: Bạch Ngân Khoáng
176.look: Below a hillside stained red with cinnabar, a fan of pale silver-grey spoil spills from the adit mouths, so the slope looks dipped in two colours. A walled smelting yard with a squat chimney sits at the foot.
176.lore: Silver was found below the cinnabar slopes at Bạch Ngân in 450, and Thiên Xu's coin is struck from it. The mine lies close to Phượng Minh's border; in the Cinnabar Vein War its miners slept in the adits while the fighting at Đan Sơn Mạch lit the ridge above.

177.name: Kinh Điện Khoáng
177.look: A mine on a bare ridge of Kinh Trập Sơn, where open-air forges stand on the rock beside the pit mouths, each with a tall iron rod raised above it to catch the lightning. The rock around them is streaked with burn marks.
177.lore: Lightning strikes the ore of Kinh Điện so often that since 220 Khải Lôi's smiths forged in the storm. Thính Vũ's smiths keep the old forges and still wait for storms to work. Miners wear wooden shoes and never carry iron tools in the rain.

178.name: Tử Kim Khoáng
178.look: A mine on a steep mountain slope, its tunnel mouths set in cliffs streaked purple and gold. Below them long fans of purple-tinted spoil spill down the hillside.
178.lore: Purple-gold ore, the colour of storm light, has been dug at Tử Kim since 300. The metal takes an edge well and is prized by Thính Vũ's sword smiths. Miners say a seam glows faintly before a storm, and they leave the tunnels when it does.

179.name: Vũ Hoa Khoáng
179.look: The highest mine in the thunder mountains, a stony upland where the stream beds have been dammed into long wooden sluices. In them lie heaps of smooth pebbles of every colour, red, agate-banded, green and white, gleaming wet in the rain.
179.lore: Rain-flower pebbles, said to be flowers that fell as rain while a master preached, were found here in 500, and Thính Vũ keeps the mine. It is held to be the richest mine ground in the Tower's mountains. Pickers sort the pebbles in the rain, when the colours show truest.

180.name: Đan Thạch Khoáng
180.look: A quarry cut into a red mountain, its face stepped in tall terraces of raw vermilion rock. Rough-cut red blocks lie in rows on the quarry floor, waiting to be dragged down the road.
180.lore: Red stone from Đan Thạch was cut for Xích Thành's walls from 280. Phượng Minh still quarries it for its own builders. Quarrymen say the stone holds the day's heat long after sunset, and sleep against the blocks in winter.
180.history: The red mountain of Đan Thạch was known for its colour long before anyone cut it. In 280 Xích Thành Môn began to quarry it for its walls, and the halls of the red cliff-gate rose out of its blocks. Through the gate's long rule the quarry fed its builders, and the terraces of the face grew deeper with each generation. Under the heir who burned villages the quarrymen worked for war. When Phượng Minh destroyed the gate under writ, the quarry passed to the Palace with the rest of the coast. Phượng Minh's builders have cut it ever since, and its red stone stands in walls across Đan Huyệt Châu. Quarrymen still sleep against the warm blocks in winter.

181.name: Phụ Tinh Phong
181.look: A glacier peak stands beside taller neighbours, white ice over dark rock. Its broad shoulder holds a flat terrace cut into the ice, still bristling with rows of rusted iron stakes where weapon racks once stood. At night a single faint star hangs just above its summit.
181.lore: From 760 the disciples of Phá Quân Môn drilled here at night under the faint companion star beside the Dipper, as if to prove the small star could break armies too. Since the rebellion was crushed no one drills here; the stakes remain and the wind sings over them. Thiên Xu's patrols come up now and then only to look, and go down again.
181.history: Thiên Xu's protection reached Dao Quang Lĩnh in the Age of First Gates, and this glacier peak, too cold to farm or mine, was left to the wind. Late in the Age of the North Star Compact, Phá Quân Môn was founded in the mountains below it as a vassal of the Pivot. In 760, the year Chung Hoài Cực died, Phá Quân's disciples began to drill at night on Phụ Tinh Phong under the faint companion star, cutting a terrace into the shoulder and setting iron racks for their weapons. Whether the drills were meant for the Pivot's enemies or the Pivot itself, no one asked until a century later, when Hạ Lang Tinh led Phá Quân Môn against its lord. Within a few years Thiên Xu destroyed Phá Quân Môn, and the night drills ended. The racks rotted down to their iron stakes, which still stand in rows on the terrace. No sect holds the peak today.

182.name: Trích Tinh Phong
182.look: The roof of the heartland: a dark rock peak rising clear of the clouds, its summit ending in a thin stone needle. Strips of white cloth tied around the needle stream in the wind, and below it a pilgrims' road of a thousand rock-cut steps runs up the spine of the ridge. On clear nights the stars seem to rest on the needle's tip.
182.lore: Thiên Xu's first watchmen climbed Trích Tinh Phong in 260 and reported that one could pluck the stars by hand, and the peak has carried that name since. By 1100 the pilgrims' road up it had been cut into the rock in a thousand steps. Pilgrims tie a white strip at the needle and make a wish on a star; it is bad luck to say which one.
182.history: In 260, in the Age of First Gates, Thiên Xu's first watchmen climbed Trích Tinh Phong and came down saying one could pluck the stars by hand. The Pivot, founded under the stars of the Northern Dipper, kept the summit as a place to watch them. Two centuries later its patrols found the Star Marrow vein, Tinh Tủy Mạch, high near the peak, and posted a guard that has never been withdrawn. Through the Age of the North Star Compact pilgrims climbed to the needle by goat paths and tied their white cloths at the top. By 1100 the pilgrims' road had been cut into the rock in a thousand steps. Since Băng Tâm's claim to the vein was rejected by the Pivot, pilgrims climb under the eyes of a doubled guard and circling cranes.

183.name: Hồi Lộ Phong
183.look: A steep ice peak is wrapped in a switchback stair carved into its flank, the steps doubling back so often that the stair looks like white thread wound around a spindle. Wind-scoured snow fills the turns. From below, climbers on it seem to vanish and reappear at random.
183.lore: Hồ Thiên's disciples carved a stair of ice up Hồi Lộ Phong around 300; it bends so often that companions lose each other in plain sight. The school is long gone, but the cold has kept the stair. Băng Tâm's disciples climb it roped together, and quote the old line: the mountain turns, the road bends, and you are gone.
183.history: Hồ Thiên Phái was founded on the ice below Chúc Long Sơn in 210, and this peak above its ice fields became the school's training ground. Around 300 its disciples carved a stair of ice up Hồi Lộ Phong, bending so often that companions lost each other in plain sight. When Chúc Long Sơn erupted in 425 and buried the school, the stair stood high above the ash and lava. When Băng Tâm Các claimed the empty ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn in the Age of Seven Seats, it found the stair still whole. Its disciples have climbed it roped together ever since, and have still lost one now and then. No sect holds the peak itself.

184.name: Lăng Tuyệt Phong
184.look: The highest summit on the continent: a white glacier pyramid standing clear above a sea of cloud, every other peak below it. A small cairn of pale stones sits on the very top. From its foot the summit looks close enough to touch, and is not.
184.lore: Băng Tâm's climbers reached the top of Lăng Tuyệt Phong in 480 and saw all the mountains small, and left the cairn that still stands there. Since then a disciple who means to enter a long seclusion often climbs it first. The cold at the summit is said to test the ice heart more cruelly than any master.
184.history: No climb of the continent's highest peak is remembered from the Wild Age or the Age of First Gates; even Hồ Thiên's disciples, who carved the stair on Hồi Lộ Phong, left no record of its top. Tần Ngưng Sương founded Băng Tâm Các in the Age of Seven Seats, and within a generation the sect had claimed the empty ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn. In 480 the sect's climbers reached the summit of Lăng Tuyệt Phong and saw all the mountains small. They left a cairn of pale stones at the top. In the centuries since, Băng Tâm's disciples have climbed it as a rite before long seclusion, and the sect has never set a building on it. No one claims the peak; the cold holds it.

185.name: Thanh Ải Phong
185.look: The highest peak of Ngọc Hành Sơn rises above bare grey ridges, its upper slopes wrapped in a band of soft blue haze that never burns off, so the summit is never seen. Climbers say the haze looks thick from below and is gone when walked into.
185.lore: Thanh Ải Phong, the Peak of the Blue Haze, is held by no sect; its name comes from the old line about blue haze that, walked into, is gone. Those who climb into the haze come down saying they found nothing but bare rock and their own footprints. In 1180 the haze lifted for a day for the first time in memory and a temple was seen on the summit; by evening it was gone, and the paths up the peak have never been busier.
185.history: Since the Wild Age the summit of Thanh Ải Phong has hidden in its blue haze, and the miners of the ranges below never could say what stands at the top. When Thiên Xu Tông took Ngọc Hành Sơn's ore mountains under its protection in the Age of First Gates, the peak was left unclaimed, for there seemed to be nothing on it to claim. Generations of hermits and treasure-seekers climbed into the haze and found only bare rock and their own footprints. The Pivot's surveyors left the summit blank on their mine maps and formation charts alike. In 1180 the haze lifted for a day for the first time in memory, and a temple was seen on the summit; by evening it was gone. Since then cultivators from across the heart have camped below the haze line, waiting for it to lift again.

186.name: Cùng Mục Phong
186.look: A narrow summit of pale granite stands above the ranges, so high that on clear days the plains and the shine of the inland sea seem to lie at its feet. Its flat top rock is criss-crossed with long, deep sword cuts that look as fresh as if they were made yesterday.
186.lore: Cùng Mục Phong, the Peak of the Farthest Sight, takes its name from the poem about climbing one storey more to see a thousand li further. In 1130 Tư Không Hạc Niên dueled Thang Vô Tạ of Phất Y Cốc here for three days; neither won, and Tư Không Hạc Niên left without a sect. Thang Vô Tạ will not speak of it, so Phất Y Cốc's disciples climb the peak to read the duel in the cuts; the summit winds are fierce, and not all of them come down.
186.history: In the Age of First Gates the peak was a lookout for the miners of Ngọc Hành Sơn, who watched from its spurs for beasts coming off the high valleys. Its name came from the old poem, and climbers took up the custom of adding one stone to the summit cairn to see a little further. After Phất Y Cốc was founded in the valleys below, its swordsmen used the summit for their trials, though no sect ever claimed it. In 1130 Tư Không Hạc Niên dueled Thang Vô Tạ of Phất Y Cốc on the peak for three days; neither won, and Tư Không Hạc Niên left without a sect. In 1131 Thang Vô Tạ would not speak of the duel, and Phất Y Cốc's disciples began to climb the peak to see the sword marks. The cuts have not weathered since, and climbers say the sword intent left in them still stings a careless hand.

187.name: Liệt Khuyết Phong
187.look: The highest summit of Kinh Trập Sơn, a sheer grey peak split from crown to shoulder by a deep vertical rift, as if cut by one stroke. The rock along the rift is fused black and glassy, and storm clouds gather on it more often than on any other summit.
187.lore: The peak takes its name from an old poet's line of lightning and thunder under which the ridges crumble. Khải Lôi's disciples once climbed it in storms to invite the lightning; Thính Vũ's disciples now drill on it in thunderstorms. The villagers below count the lightning and the disciples both, and lay a bowl of rice on the trail for each one who does not come down.
187.history: In the Age of First Gates, Khải Lôi Môn taught that a cultivator must invite the lightning, and this peak became its proving ground. By 440 the Gate's disciples were climbing it in storms, and only a third of them came down. The fused black rock along the rift is said to mark where the strongest strikes have landed. After Khải Lôi fell, the peak lay unused, and the mountain folk said its storms were waiting. Thính Vũ Lâu, whose arts lean toward Thunder, took up the old practice in its own way. By 1166, as the Tower rebuilt its strength after Đan Sơn Mạch, its disciples were drilling on Liệt Khuyết Phong in thunderstorms. The villagers below count the lightning and the disciples both.

188.name: Chúc Long Sơn
188.look: A black cone rises out of the ice fields, its flanks streaked with old lava under a skin of snow. In its crater a dull red glow shows through a lid of ice, like the half-open eye of something asleep. Steam drifts from cracks around the rim and freezes into feathers of rime.
188.lore: Ice hunters have said since the Age of First Gates that the Torch Dragon sleeps under Chúc Long Sơn and lights the mountain when it dreams. In 425 the mountain erupted under the ice and buried Hồ Thiên Phái with its founder Khúc Hồ Già. In 1199 it rumbled for the first time since that eruption, and the nuns of Lê Hoa Am prayed all winter.
188.history: In 120 ice hunters already told that the Torch Dragon slept under Chúc Long Sơn and lit the mountain when it dreamed. In 210 Khúc Hồ Già founded Hồ Thiên Phái on the ice below the fire mountain, where snow flies in the eighth month. In 425 Chúc Long Sơn erupted under the ice and buried the school with its founder, and Ngọc Hồ Sơn lay empty for forty-five years. Băng Tâm Các claimed the ice after those empty years and built nothing near the cone. For centuries the mountain slept, and only the red glow in its crater showed it was alive. In 1199 it rumbled under the ice for the first time since the eruption, and the nuns of Lê Hoa Am prayed all winter.

189.name: Sương Diễm Sơn
189.look: A broad snow-capped volcanic cone rising alone out of the forest. Down one flank runs a crimson fissure that never freezes, glowing through the snow and trailing a thin plume of steam.
189.lore: No sect holds the mountain; the fire under its frost draws cultivators of both fire and water to its slopes, each sure the other side's qi is the danger. The people of Mộc Lan Thành watch its steam the way sailors watch the sky.
189.history: Sương Diễm Sơn smoked under its snow long before any sect came to the north-east, and the fishers of Hàn Giang Môn called it the mountain of frost and flame. It stood outside every border when Băng Tâm Các took the frost coast in 498, and the Pavilion has never claimed it. In the Age of the North Star Compact Băng Tâm founded Mộc Lan Thành on the coast below it. In 700 the mountain breathed fire under the frost for a week, and the people of Mộc Lan Thành slept on the beach until the fire sank. Ash fell on the snow that winter, and the forest at its foot grew thick and dark in the years after. The crimson fissure on its flank has never closed since. Wandering cultivators climb to it to temper fire and water arts together, though few stay long.

190.name: Hạo Nguyệt Hồ
190.look: The long lake runs pale silver between dark forest shores, the largest water on the continent, its far end lost in haze. On one shore a thin stone causeway leaves a small fishers' shrine and runs straight out into the lake, stopping in open water.
190.lore: Fishers say a man once walked across this water into the moon, and they built a shrine where he set out; the causeway was laid later, stone by stone, by those who wanted to follow as far as they dared. The lake's pearls feed Hàm Nguyệt Trang and the shore towns, and once brought two great sects to war. Its water is cold and deep with qi, and the lake villages say the master who left the world here never quite took his home with him.
190.history: In the Wild Age fishers on the long lake saw a man walk over the water into the moon, and in 45 they built a shrine on the shore where he had set out. In 470 a fisher of Tuyết Lộc pulled a pearl the size of a fist from the lake; Hàm Nguyệt Trang bought it and began to farm pearls, and the pearl trade later made the shore towns rich. In 748 Hạo Nguyệt Hồ froze to its bed for one winter, and the spirit fish of Hàm Nguyệt Trang lived through it in the moon's reflection. Its pearls drew Tùng Đào Cung and Băng Tâm Các into the Long Lake War in 940. In 944 Đỗ Tinh Hà arbitrated: the lake stayed Tùng Đào's, and Băng Tâm won the right to fish its northern shore. In 1192 a white moon-fox was seen on the lake three nights running, and the villagers say a blessed land is waking somewhere in the north.

191.name: Phiến Băng Hồ
191.look: A small round lake set in a hollow of the forest. In winter it freezes as clear as glass, so the stones and weed of its bed show through the ice, and the dark specks of meditating disciples sit scattered across it like drops of ink.
191.lore: The lake lies near Băng Tâm Các, and its name comes from a line of the Pavilion's poem: one piece of ice heart. Since the winter of 1065, when it froze clear as glass and disciples who meditated on it saw their own hearts, Băng Tâm disciples walk out onto it each winter to sit. Its qi runs to wood and fire, strangely warm for a frozen lake, and the elders say that is why it shows a heart and not a face.
191.history: The lake has no recorded name from before Băng Tâm Các came to the cold north-east in the Age of Seven Seats. The Pavilion named it Phiến Băng Hồ after a line of its poem, one piece of ice heart. For centuries it froze white and cloudy like any forest lake. In 1065 it froze as clear as glass, and Băng Tâm disciples who meditated on it saw their own hearts. Since that winter disciples have gone out onto the ice every year; some come back calmer, and some come back and leave the sect. No one holds the lake, but no one fishes it. Elders of the Pavilion hold that the clear ice comes only in winters when the Pavilion's own heart is steady.

192.name: Tinh Lạc Hồ
192.look: High on the plain beside Củng Tinh Quán lies a dark, perfectly round lake so still it reads as black glass, rimmed by a single ring of pale stones. At night the whole Northern Dipper lies in it, star for star.
192.lore: Tinh Lạc Hồ, the Lake Where the Stars Fall, is a high lake that holds the Dipper at night as clearly as the sky. The star-readers of Củng Tinh Quán read it alongside their armillary, and they forbid boats, fishing and even skipping stones, lest a ripple spoil a reading. Herders believe a wish whispered at the water's edge on a windless night is heard by the stars themselves.
192.history: At the end of the Wild Age stones fell from the sky on Thiên Tuyền Nguyên for nine days, and the herders of the high plain came to believe the round lake was where the first of them had struck. When Củng Tinh Quán was founded nearby in the Age of First Gates, its star-readers studied the lake from the shore. In 155 they found that Tinh Lạc Hồ holds the Dipper at night as clearly as the sky. They set a ring of pale stones around the water to mark where readers may stand, and banned boats and fishing. When the abbey's armillary was finished a generation later, the abbey began to read sky and lake together, trusting a sign only when both agreed. No sect holds the lake itself, but no one has broken the abbey's ban in living memory.

193.name: Triêu Hà Hồ
193.look: A wide shallow lake in the open grassland, so still at dawn that the first clouds lie doubled on it. Each morning a mist rises off the water and turns rose, then gold, with the sunrise. In the eastern shallows lies a low, flat platform of weathered stone, half awash, where musicians once played to the sun.
193.lore: The plain folk say the east's dawn clouds answer Lạc Hà's sunset clouds in the west. In 200 the musicians of Vân Môn played to the morning sun over the lake, and the dawn clouds took the colour of their music. Hoa Triêu Dương, now head of Phượng Minh Cung, was born on its shore at dawn in 950 as the clouds turned red. Lễ Tuyền Phái keeps its sweet spring on the shore.
193.history: In the Age of First Gates the musicians of Vân Môn Thành, Cửu Thiều Cung's city on the plain, came to this lake to play to the rising sun. By 200 it was said that the dawn clouds took the colour of their music, and the players built a low stone platform in the shallows to stand on. After the War of the Nine Shao the musicians were gone, and for nearly two centuries only herders saw the dawns here. When Phượng Minh Cung took the plain, its people came back to the shore. In the Age of the North Star Compact healers founded Lễ Tuyền Phái beside the lake, at the sweet spring. In 950 Hoa Triêu Dương was born at dawn on the shore as the clouds turned red; a century and a half later she became head of Phượng Minh Cung. Since then pilgrims of the Palace come at dawn to watch the clouds, and some bring flutes.

194.name: Tàn Hà Hồ
194.look: A grey lake at the foot of the Tower's cone, its surface crowded with withered lotus: tall brown stalks, curled dry leaves and empty seedpods that are never cut and never cleared. Even in summer the lake looks like the end of autumn.
194.lore: Phó Tiêu Tương kept the withered lotus on the lake below her tower to listen to the rain on it, and the lake took the name Tàn Hà Hồ. Disciples of Thính Vũ sit on its shore in storms, learning to hear each drop on the dry leaves apart. No one may cut a stalk, and any lotus that blooms is left to wither.
