194.history: Phó Tiêu Tương founded Thính Vũ Lâu above this lake, and in 382, two years after the founding, she kept the withered lotus standing on the lake below her tower so that she could listen to the rain on it, and the lake was named Tàn Hà Hồ. From then on the Tower's sword disciples were sent to its shore to listen to the rain before they were taught the sword. When the founder died five centuries later the lotus was left as she had kept it. After the Night Rain Edict the lake shore became the place where new masters were first received, by night. In 1158, after the Tower's defeat at Đan Sơn Mạch, Mạnh Dạ Vũ did not leave the Tower for a year, and in all that year the rain on Tàn Hà Hồ never stopped. Disciples still call a long rain a head's mourning.

195.name: Phù Chử Đảo
195.look: A low wooded isle off the plain coast, its trees dark against the water. Around it floats a thick, shifting raft of wild ducks, so dense the water looks feathered.
195.lore: The isle takes its name from the old line about crane shoals and wild-duck isles. Since the Age of Seven Seats boats have had to wait for the ducks to move before they can land, and fishers say anyone who forces a way through will have no luck all season. No sect holds it, and only egg-gatherers go ashore in spring.
195.history: The isle had no name in any record before the fishers of the western plain began to row out to it. When Lạc Hà Tông took the grassland of Trường Thiên Nguyên early in the Age of Seven Seats, the isle was left outside its rule, too small to claim. By 470 wild ducks crowded Phù Chử so thickly that boats had to wait for them to move. Egg-gatherers from the coast villages row out every spring and take care to leave most nests. Hunters who shot into the flocks, the coast says, found the ducks gone the next year, and no one hunts there now. No sect has claimed the isle in any age.

196.name: Tịch Chiếu Đảo
196.look: The westernmost island, a low grassy hump in the open sea. On its western cliff stands a single long stone bench facing the sunset, and behind it the grass is dotted with small cairns of grey stones.
196.lore: Tịch Chiếu is the last land to see the sunset of Lạc Hà, and since the Age of the North Star Compact the sect's elders have gone there to die. They sit on the bench at evening; the cairns mark those who did not come back. The boats that bring them out do not wait.
196.history: Tịch Chiếu Đảo lies west of all other land, the last to see the sun go down over Lạc Hà Tông's western lands. No settlement has ever stood on it. Lạc Hà, founded late in the Age of First Gates in the western lands where the sun goes down, named it for the evening glow. By 600 the sect's elders had begun to go there to die, sailing out at the end of their lives to watch the last sunset. Each leaves a small cairn of grey stones on the grass. The island is held by no one, and fishers give it a wide berth out of respect. Elders who feel their time near still ask for a boat to Tịch Chiếu.

197.name: Tương Phi Đảo
197.look: A small steep island off the coast, covered from shore to crown in dense bamboo whose canes are flecked with purple-brown spots, like old tear stains. There is no landing and no roof; the bamboo comes right down to the rocks.
197.lore: The spotted bamboo on Tương Phi Đảo, the Isle of the Xiang Consorts, is said to be stained by the tears of two consorts mourning their lord, as in the old legend. Phượng Minh forbids cutting it, and boatmen passing at dusk fall silent out of respect. Flutes of the spotted bamboo made before the ban are said to play sadder than any other.
197.history: The island stood in the gulf long before any sect came south, and the coast people cut its spotted bamboo for flutes and brushes. In the Age of Seven Seats the legend took hold that the spots were the tears of two consorts mourning their lord, and pilgrims began to sail out to see them. In 500 Phượng Minh Cung, newly risen on the ridges, forbade cutting the bamboo. The island has never been settled or claimed, and Phượng Minh keeps its ban by custom rather than by holding the land. The instrument makers of Thiều Âm Thị treasure the old flutes made before the ban and will not sell them lightly. Boatmen of the gulf like to say that the ribs of Thính Vũ Lâu's famous umbrella were cut here long ago, though no one in the Tower has ever said so.

198.name: Dục Nhật Đảo
198.look: A forested island in the far south-eastern sea, its eastern shore facing open ocean where the sun rises straight out of the water. On that shore stands a great ring of sea-worn rock, an arch open to the sunrise, by which the gate of Phù Tang Cảnh opens. A single thatched hut sits under the trees above it.
198.lore: The first fishers of the gulf believed the sun bathed here every night before it rose. On this island Mạc Quy Khư entered the gate of Phù Tang Cảnh, the Realm of the Sunrise Mulberry, at its first recorded opening, and the Thiên Nguyên calendar (Thiên Nguyên lịch) counts its years from that day. Since 700 he has lived here by the gate, the oldest living person, and has never left. Pilgrims come by boat to ask him about the world before the sects, and he answers one question a year.
198.history: In the year 0 of the Thiên Nguyên calendar, Mạc Quy Khư entered the gate of Phù Tang Cảnh on Dục Nhật Đảo at its first recorded opening, and the calendar counts its years from that day. In 5 the first fishers of the gulf saw the sun rise out of the sea here, and believed it bathed at the island every night. Through the Wild Age and the ages of the sects, cultivators sailed here when the realm opened and went home again, and no sect ever held the island. Mạc Quy Khư's name grew with every age, until he was the oldest living cultivator in the world. In 700 he came to live on Dục Nhật Đảo by the gate of Phù Tang Cảnh, and he has never left it since. By 1100 pilgrims were coming by boat to ask the hermit about the world before the sects, and he answers one question a year. The island is still unclaimed, and the fishers of the gulf still bow to its sunrise.

199.name: Đồ Nam Đảo
199.look: A low grassy island in the southern sea, its crown pressed into a vast shallow hollow, as if something enormous had lain there. The grass in the hollow grows in long swirled streaks like the print of feathers, and seabirds wheel over it in their thousands.
199.lore: The great Bằng is said to rest on Đồ Nam Đảo before its flight to the south, as the old book tells of the bird that rises beyond the clouds and sets out southward. Fishers say the hollow is its bed, and that the wind there always blows toward the south. No one lives on the island; sailors land only to leave fish in the hollow for a fair wind.
199.history: Fishers of the southern gulf knew the island from the earliest ages, a bare grassy hump with no spring and no harbour. By 350, in the Age of Seven Seats, the tale was told that the great Bằng rested on Đồ Nam Đảo before its flight to the south, and the hollow on its crown was called its bed. Sailors began to leave fish in the hollow for a fair wind southward, a custom that has never stopped. In the pirate years of the Age of the North Star Compact, Thôn Hải's ships are said to have anchored off the island but never landed, holding it unlucky. After the Purge the fishers came back to its waters. No sect has ever claimed it, and no one has ever dug the hollow.

200.name: Phản Cảnh Lâm
200.look: From outside it is a dark sea of old spruce and larch rising gently to a low crown. At its heart a hollow ringed by giant trees holds a patch of amber evening light that lingers long after the rest of the forest has gone grey.
200.lore: Lost travellers have walked out of Phản Cảnh Lâm by the light at its heart, which stays until dawn, and the forest is named for that returning light. Woodcutters tie a strip of bark to the last tree they pass, so the next lost walker can follow the light out. The forest belongs to no sect; Tùng Đào's patrols skirt its edge, and hunters leave the inner hollow alone.
200.history: In the Wild Age and the Age of First Gates the northern forest was only a hunting ground for the lake villages, unnamed and unmapped. Late in the Age of First Gates its region passed under Tùng Đào Cung, but the palace never fenced or settled the deep heart of the wood. By 530 travellers knew that the evening light lingered in the heart of the forest so long that the lost could walk by it until dawn, and the forest took the name Phản Cảnh Lâm. The custom of tying bark strips to the trees grew from those walks, and the strips now mark several faint ways out. In 870 hunters found footprints in the snow leading into the forest and never out, and no one followed them. Since then the heart has been left alone, and the lake villages tell children that the light is someone waiting.

201.name: Vô Tung Lâm
201.look: A dark, rolling forest of spruce and fir under deep snow, its crowns bowed white. Through it runs a frozen stream like a white ribbon, and not one track crosses it or the snow on either bank.
201.lore: The Forest Without Tracks takes its name from the poem: on ten thousand paths, no human trace. Snow fills every path by morning and only the woodcutters of Tiều Lộ Thôn can find the ways again; white bears, snow foxes and stranger beasts live deep inside. Hunters who go in alone notch the trees behind them, and still come back mostly by luck.
201.history: No sect has ever claimed the forest, and no road crosses it. In the Age of Seven Seats the fishers of Hàn Giang Môn cut wood at its edge but never went deep. Early in the Age of the North Star Compact the woodcutters' paths into it were known to vanish under the snow every night, and only the people of Tiều Lộ Thôn could find them again. After Băng Tâm Các founded Mộc Lan Thành on the coast, the forest's timber and furs fed the city's market. Late in the same age a hermit sheltering at Lâm Ẩn Thôn, on the coast at the forest's edge, taught the village children to read its beasts' tracks in the snow. In the last generation of the Age of Vein Wars hunters brought a white bear out of Vô Tung Lâm alive and sold it in Mộc Lan Thành to a buyer from Thiên Bảo Trai, and the forest's beasts have had a price on the coast ever since. Still, no map shows its heart.

202.name: Đả Diệp Lâm
202.look: A grove of tall green bamboo on low hills, so dense that rain on the leaves roars like surf. In its heart is a clearing filled with cut bamboo stumps of different heights, standing in rows like a field of posts.
202.lore: The forest gives its line to Xuyên Lâm Môn nearby: pay no heed to the rain piercing the forest and beating the leaves. The school's young disciples train their footwork on the stumps in downpours, learning to keep their footing as the rain hammers the grove. Woodcutters who come for poles must leave the clearing alone.
202.history: The bamboo of Đả Diệp Lâm was old long before any sect came to Kinh Trập Sơn, and in Khải Lôi's day it was a wild grove that the Gate's people crossed on their way to the sea. After the Gate fell the grove passed into Thính Vũ Lâu's land, and woodcutters from the villages took its poles for houses and ferries. When Xuyên Lâm Môn was founded nearby in the Age of the North Star Compact, its staff fighters took the forest's line for their own and began to train in it. The clearing of stumps was cut in the school's early years, and every generation of disciples has recut it. In the year after the Night Rain Edict, while their head walked the forest road in protest against the Night Rain Edict, the disciples are said to have trained here through the whole rain in silence. A guide of Xuyên Lâm is still not trusted to lead travellers until they have crossed the stumps in a storm without falling.

203.name: Viên Đề Hạp
203.look: A narrow gorge cuts through the high mountains, its walls hung with vines and its river loud below. A timber plank road pinned to the cliff face runs the length of one wall, and gibbons swing above it, crying on both banks without end. Mist fills the gorge floor at dawn.
203.lore: The gibbons of Viên Đề Hạp cry on both banks without end, and since at least 600 caravan drivers have stopped their ears with wax to cross. Old drivers say the cries are worst for the homesick. No sect holds the gorge, and the plank road is mended by whoever needs it.
203.history: The river cut this gorge through the high mountains of Cô Yên Mạc long before any record was kept. Mortal caravaneers pinned the first planks to its walls to shorten the road between the desert and the lands beyond, though no one remembers when. By 600 caravans used it often, and the gibbons crying on both banks without end had taught the drivers to stop their ears with wax. In the Desert Road War, more than a century later, the plank road is said to have served as a back way for messengers, and both sides burned stretches of it. The planks were renewed after the Pivot's truce. No sect has ever claimed the gorge, and the gibbons have outlasted every war.

204.name: Vạn Trùng Hạp
204.look: A deep, twisting gorge where the river races white between ranks of steep ridges folded one behind another like stacked screens. A narrow plank road on timber beams socketed into the cliff runs along one wall above the rapids.
204.lore: Vạn Trùng Hạp, the Gorge of Ten Thousand Mountains, takes its name from the poem of the light boat that has passed ten thousand mountains. Boats in the gorge pass ten thousand mountains in a day, and the river is the fastest road to the sea. Travellers going upstream take the plank road; boatmen going down never look back, since a pilot who turns his head is said to lose the river.
204.history: The river cut Vạn Trùng Hạp through Ngọc Hành Sơn long before any cultivator came to the heart. When Thiên Xu took the ore mountains and founded its port Tinh Hán Thành on the inland sea in the Age of First Gates, the gorge became the quickest way to bring ore down toward the coast. Ore boats ran the rapids, and the wrecks of the reckless still lie in the deep pools. By 620 it was said that boats in the gorge passed ten thousand mountains in a day, and that the river was the fastest road to the sea. A plank road was socketed into the cliff for those going upstream, and it has been rebuilt beam by beam ever since. No sect holds the gorge, and its pilots answer to no one but the river.

205.name: Tinh Tủy Mạch
205.look: High on a black rock face near Trích Tinh Phong, seams of silver-white star marrow thread through the stone and glitter like frost even at noon. A low stone breastwork and a guards' fire pit sit on a ledge in front of the face. Cranes wheel over it in slow rings.
205.lore: Thiên Xu found the Star Marrow vein (linh mạch) high near Trích Tinh Phong in 470 and posted a guard that has never been withdrawn. Its qi (linh khí) runs to Metal and Earth, heavy and cold as iron. In 1188 Băng Tâm Các claimed it before the Pivot and was refused; since then the guard has been doubled, and Cửu Cao's cranes circle it day and night.
205.history: At the end of the Wild Age stones fell from the sky on Thiên Tuyền Nguyên, and the star iron in them drew the first cultivators to the heart; some say the marrow in this mountain is kin to that iron, though no one has proved it. In 470 Thiên Xu found the Star Marrow vein high near Trích Tinh Phong and posted a guard that has never been withdrawn. Through the long Compact the vein lay quiet near the border of Băng Tâm Các, never fought over. In 1188 Băng Tâm claimed Tinh Tủy Mạch before the Pivot; the claim was rejected, and Sở Ngọc Hồ withdrew in silence. In 1189 Thiên Xu doubled the guard, and Cửu Cao Phái's cranes began to circle the vein day and night. The silence from the desert seat has not yet been broken.

206.name: Thương Tùng Mạch
206.look: On a high summit above the pine sea stands a grove of pines with bark the colour of ash, older and paler than any around them. An old fence of stone posts and timber rails rings the grey grove, and the air inside is still even when the forest below is roaring.
206.lore: A wild spirit vein runs under the grey pines, close to the heart and the Pivot's border. Tùng Đào fenced it and still guards it, and its disciples cultivate there in turns. Foresters say the pines turned grey from drinking the vein's metal and earth qi.
206.history: Before it had a name, the grey grove on the summit was known to woodsmen only as a place where the wind fell silent. Tùng Đào Cung held the pine sea from its founding, but only in 470 did its disciples fence the grey pines over an old spirit vein near the heart and name it Thương Tùng Mạch. Under the North Star Compact, the vein could change hands only by a fall, a gift, an oath or a war licensed by the Pivot's writ, and it has stayed Tùng Đào's. In the Age of Vein Wars, when neighbours fight short wars over the wild veins near their borders, Tùng Đào set a standing watch on the grove, for it lies close to Thiên Xu's land. Its disciples cultivate there in turns, and the stillness under the grey pines is said to help a cultivator hear his own meridians.

207.name: Trường Hà Mạch
207.look: A high bare mountain on the border, its slope split by a long seam of amber-gold rock that winds down the face like a river. In the setting sun the seam glows as if the river ran with fire.
207.lore: Lạc Hà Tông found this spirit vein (linh mạch) on its new border with Thính Vũ Lâu in 620, the year the Petal Shore was divided, and named it for the line about the long river and the round setting sun. Its qi runs to earth and metal. Lạc Hà's disciples cultivate on its ledges with one eye on the far ridges, where Thính Vũ's land begins.
207.history: The mountain lay in no sect's reckoning until 620, when the Pivot's judgement divided the Petal Shore, the bay to Lạc Hà and the forest to Thính Vũ. That year Lạc Hà found the Long River vein on its new border with Thính Vũ and named it Trường Hà Mạch. On the eve of the War of Broken Halberds the founders of the two sects met on the Petal Shore and swore to end the Pivot's oversight, and through that war this border lay at the allies' backs, not their front. After the truce that ended it renewed the Compact, the two sects went back to watching each other. In the Age of Vein Wars, when neighbours fought short wars over the veins near their borders, Lạc Hà set a standing watch on the ridge; no war over this vein is recorded. Since Thính Vũ rebuilt its strength after Đan Sơn Mạch, the watch has been strengthened.

208.name: Kinh Lôi Mạch
208.look: High on a bare black ridge of Kinh Trập Sơn, seams of violet light run through the rock like veins under skin, brightening whenever thunder rolls. Nothing grows on the ridge, and the air above it smells of a struck flint.
208.lore: Kinh Lôi Mạch is a spirit vein (linh mạch) that carries Thunder from the storm peaks, the richest prize in the mountains and close to Thiên Xu's border. Lệ Tiêu Hồn, master of the Tower's soul vaults, has kept it since 1010. Phượng Minh Cung fought for it from 1040 to 1046 and lost; the south remembers.
208.history: The vein runs within reach of the storm peaks of Kinh Trập Sơn, and its qi has carried Thunder for as long as anyone has drawn on it. Khải Lôi Môn's cultivators knew the ridge in the Age of First Gates, and after the Gate fell it passed with the mountains to Thính Vũ Lâu. In 1010 Lệ Tiêu Hồn broke through in the Tower's soul vaults, and Mạnh Dạ Vũ made him keeper of Kinh Lôi Mạch. In 1040 Phượng Minh Cung went to war with Thính Vũ Lâu for the vein. In the war's last year the Palace's raiders reached the upper ferry at Thượng Độ before the Pivot's envoys stopped them. In 1046 the Pivot ended the Thunder Vein War: Thính Vũ kept the vein, and the south remembers. A century later the Tower struck at Phượng Minh's own vein, Đan Sơn Mạch, and lost.

209.name: Băng Phách Mạch
209.look: Below the ice mountains, a round cave mouth opens in a cliff, rimmed with ice so white it glows faintly blue, like the moon seen through mist. Inside, pillars of ice give off a cold light of their own. Frost feathers grow on the rocks for a long way around the entrance.
209.lore: Băng phách, the ice soul, is an old name for the moon, and Băng Tâm opened this spirit vein (linh mạch) below the ice mountains in 760. Its qi (linh khí) feeds the sect's ice cultivators and is fierce enough to freeze a careless breath in the throat. The storm peaks loom close, and beasts drawn to the vein's cold make the approach perilous.
209.history: Hồ Thiên Phái held these mountains from 210, but the deep cold under them was never tapped before the eruption of 425 emptied the land. Băng Tâm Các claimed the empty ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn in the Age of Seven Seats, and for nearly three centuries searched the ice mountains for a vein worthy of its arts. In 760, the year it also founded Hồi Lan Thành on the desert coast, the sect opened the Ice Soul vein, Băng Phách Mạch, below the ice mountains, and named it for the moon. Since then the vein has fed the sect's ice cultivators far from the desert seat. Its approach, close under the storm peaks, remains one of the most feared roads in Băng Tâm's lands.

210.name: Hỏa Ngọc Mạch
210.look: Far out in the western sea a black volcanic island rises in a steep cone, steam leaking from its flanks. Down the cone's sides run seams of fire jade that glow red-green through the rock at dusk, as if the mountain were cracked over a lamp.
210.lore: A spirit vein (linh mạch) of fire jade lies under the volcano, charted by Thúy Vi's surveyors and kept on a sealed chart. It sits at the edge of the cape's waters, where Lạc Hà's waters begin, and few ships come so far. Thúy Vi sends no settlers; those who go are alchemists and miners on short, guarded voyages.
210.history: In the Wild Age the island was only a smoking mark on the horizon for the cape's fishers. A few years before the find, Thúy Vi Tông took the cape of snow and fire and set its surveyors to chart the coast and the sea beyond. In 565 they found a pocket of fire jade under a volcano far out at sea, named it Hỏa Ngọc Mạch and kept the chart sealed. The vein became Thúy Vi's quiet treasure, worked in small voyages rather than settled. In the Age of Vein Wars it lies on the edge of Lạc Hà's waters, the kind of wild vein neighbours fight over, yet no war has been fought for it. The cape's sailors say the sealed chart is the reason: no one fights for what they cannot find.

211.name: Đan Sơn Mạch
211.look: A steep mountain flank of vermilion rock is split by a long seam that glows a deeper crimson at dusk, where the vein's qi runs close to the surface. Along the ridge above stand the scorched stone footings of watch platforms from the last war.
211.lore: Đan Sơn Mạch, the Vein of the Cinnabar Mountain, is Phượng Minh's spirit vein (linh mạch) near its border with the heart, named after the cinnabar mountain of the old classics where the phoenix is born. Thính Vũ Lâu attacked it in 1150 and was beaten in 1158 with Thiên Xu's help; Mạnh Dạ Vũ swore the Pivot would answer for it, and the palace has kept a guard on the ridge ever since. Alchemists of the south say cinnabar from the seam needs no grinding.
211.history: Cinnabar and silver had long been dug from the slopes around this mountain, and since the Age of Seven Seats Thiên Xu has struck coin from the silver at Bạch Ngân below it. In 900 Phượng Minh found the vein near its border with the heart and named it Đan Sơn Mạch, after the cinnabar mountain where the phoenix is born. The palace guarded it closely, for a vein so near another sect's border was exactly what the Age of Vein Wars was fought over. In 1150 Thính Vũ Lâu attacked Đan Sơn Mạch. In 1154 Doãn Ngọc Hành brought Thiên Xu Tông into the war on Phượng Minh's side, to enforce the Compact. In 1158 Thính Vũ Lâu was beaten at Đan Sơn Mạch and withdrew, and Mạnh Dạ Vũ swore the Pivot would answer for it. The watch platforms burned in the fighting still stand in ruin on the ridge, and the palace has not left the vein unguarded since.

212.name: Cao Cương Phong
212.look: A high bare ridge-top above the wutong hills ends in a flat crest of pale gold stone that takes the first light of dawn before anything else in the south. A single stone pillar stands on the crest, worn at its top into the shape of a perch.
212.lore: Cao Cương Phong, the Peak of the High Ridge, takes its name from the old ode in which the phoenix sings on that high ridge, and it is a sacred summit where the light gathers. Phượng Minh's disciples have climbed it at dawn since at least 600 and say the phoenix sang there. Pilgrims leave nothing on the crest, and what is left anyway is gone by the next dawn.
212.history: It is said that the court musicians of Cửu Thiều Cung named this crest after the ode of the phoenix singing on the high ridge, and played their dawn tunes toward it. After Cửu Thiều fell in the War of the Nine Shao the ridge went quiet for well over a century. When Phượng Minh Cung rose on the empty lands, its disciples took up the dawn climb. By 600 they said the phoenix had sung there, on that high ridge, and the climb became a rite of the palace. Light gathers on the crest at dawn more than anywhere else in the south, and cultivators of light come from far away to sit on it. No sect holds it; Phượng Minh says no one can hold a place the phoenix chose.

213.name: Không Sơn Viện
213.look: High on a ridge above the haze a cluster of old halls stands silent, their doors open, the roof of the great lecture hall sagging and its small pagoda missing its top tier. Beside the path a raw landslide scar runs down the slope, and in it a stone gate carved with lines of poetry stands half-buried, its opening blocked with newer stone.
213.lore: The Academy of the Empty Mountain was so quiet that, as its poem says, on the empty mountain no one is seen. Its last master gave it away and died here, and Thúy Vi has left it unlocked and unlooted ever since; no visitor takes so much as a brush. Travellers who sleep here tell of someone reading aloud in the next room.
213.history: In 180 Bùi Lộc Trại founded Không Sơn Viện in the hills of Thanh Loan Lĩnh, an academy so quiet that, as the poem says, on the empty mountain no one is seen. The woodcutters of Tiều Ca were asked to sing more quietly below it, and its students planted the cypress groves of Bách Diệp as a lesson in patience. When green jade was found in its hills the academy forbade mining it, and in the Age of Seven Seats fishers and ferrymen built Hàn Tân Thành under its protection. Bùi Lộc Trại died in 460, and Thôi Bất Kiến became master and took no disciple but one boy, Tống Tọa Vân. In 500, with no heir, Thôi Bất Kiến gave the hills, his whisk and his only student to Phùng Yên Hà, and the empty mountain became Thúy Vi's. He died in the empty academy in 520, and Phùng Yên Hà left it as it was, unlocked and unlooted. In 830 a landslide on the ridge uncovered a stone gate carved with Không Sơn's poem, and Thúy Vi sealed it again. In 1195 a traveller who spent a night in the empty halls swore he heard someone reading aloud in the next room.

214.name: Hồ Thiên Phái
214.look: On a flat, bleak tundra shore, a field of black frozen lava runs down to the water, and from it sticks the green-tiled tip of a single pagoda roof, curled eaves and all. No grass grows around it and no bird sings. The wind hums through gaps in the buried tiles.
214.lore: Khúc Hồ Già founded Hồ Thiên Phái on the ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn in 210, below the fire mountain, and in 230 forged the sword Phi Tuyết from ice that never melts. In 425 Chúc Long Sơn erupted and buried the school with its founder. Băng Tâm holds the shore and tells its disciples not to dig, but treasure hunters whisper that Phi Tuyết lies somewhere under the lava, still cold.
214.history: In 210 Khúc Hồ Già founded Hồ Thiên Phái on the ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn, below the fire mountain Chúc Long Sơn, where snow flies in the eighth month. In 230 Khúc Hồ Già forged the sword Phi Tuyết from ice that never melts. In the school's best years its disciples carved the winding ice stair of Hồi Lộ Phong. In 425 Chúc Long Sơn erupted under the ice and buried the school with its founder, and Ngọc Hồ Sơn lay empty. A year later steam still rose from the ice where Hồ Thiên had stood, and no bird sang there. Two generations later Băng Tâm Các claimed the empty ice and left the ruin as it lay. The villagers of Đỗ Quyên Thôn still say the red azaleas on their slopes are the eruption's dead.

215.name: Xích Thành Môn
215.look: On the coast of Đan Huyệt Châu, cliffs of deep red rock rise in rounded tiers like banks of rosy cloud above the sea. Into them are cut the broken terraces and gutted halls of the old gate, their fire-blackened walls open to the sky, with fresh pale quarry scars where stone has lately been taken away.
215.lore: Tôn Hà Khởi founded Xích Thành Môn here in 250, among red cliffs and vents where the rock rises like a rosy cloud. Its banner Xích Hà Kỳ was woven from fire-silk spun in the vents. Under his heir Chu Liệt Nhật the sect burned villages to feed its fire arts, and Phượng Minh destroyed it under the Compact's first writ. Herders do not graze here; they say the cliffs are still warm at night.
215.history: Tôn Hà Khởi founded Xích Thành Môn in 250 among the red cliffs and vents of Đan Huyệt Châu, and in 260 the sect wove its war banner, the Xích Hà Kỳ, from fire-silk spun in the vents. Within a generation its walls were cut from the red stone of Đan Thạch, and soon after it built Ngũ Thải Thành on the coast. Tôn Hà Khởi died in 560, and his heir Chu Liệt Nhật turned the sect to burning villages to feed its fire arts. After eleven villages had burned, Phượng Minh Cung asked the Pivot for a writ, and the first writ of the North Star Compact was granted. In 590 Phượng Minh destroyed Xích Thành Môn with Chu Liệt Nhật, and the Xích Hà Kỳ went to hang in the Palace's hall. Four centuries later the banner was lent to Phần Vũ Đường, which revived the fire arts in the vents inland. In the last years of the Age of Vein Wars, Phượng Minh took stone from these ruins to rebuild the cracked jetty of Thạch Cơ Thành.

216.name: Hàn Giang Môn
216.look: A broken sect seat on the frost coast: a stone gate arch fallen on its side and half buried in snow, behind it the stumps of halls stepping up a low bank. A fishing rod carved along the fallen lintel shows where the wind has swept the snow away.
216.lore: Here the Gate of the Cold River taught its fishers to cultivate alone in the snow beside holes cut in the river ice, sitting for days without moving. It fell to Băng Tâm Các in 498 with its last head Liễu Cô Chu. The coast's fishers still leave a fish on the fallen gate after a good catch, and no one, not even Băng Tâm's disciples, takes it.
216.history: Liễu Thoa Lạp founded Hàn Giang Môn on the frost coast in 300, a sect of fishers who cultivated alone in the snow on the cold river. By 330 its fishers were known for cutting holes in the river ice and sitting beside them in the snow for days without moving. A generation later the sect founded Liên Giang Thành where the cold rain joins the river. When Băng Tâm Các came to the cold north-east in the Age of Seven Seats, the two sects shared the ice uneasily. Half a century later Băng Tâm, under Tần Ngưng Sương, made war on Hàn Giang for the frost coast. In 498 Hàn Giang Môn fell with its last head Liễu Cô Chu, and Hàn Sương Châu passed to Băng Tâm Các. Its fishers stayed and fished the cold river under the Pavilion's flag, but the seat was never rebuilt, and the snow has had it since.

217.name: Thôn Hải Môn
217.look: A small forested islet in the southern gulf, ringed by rocks. At the waterline gapes the black mouth of a sea cave large enough to take a ship, its rim scorched and the stumps of a broken log boom still standing across it. Charred timbers of the old hold lie heaped inside the entrance.
217.lore: Ô Kình Hải gathered pirates on this islet in 640 and founded Thôn Hải Môn, the Gate That Swallows the Sea, and for over a century its ships raided the southern coasts. The Purge ended here in 781 when he died on his islet, and his sabre Kình Nha was lost in the burning hold. Treasure seekers still row out to dig in the ash, and some do not row back.
217.history: Ô Kình Hải gathered pirates on an islet of the southern gulf in 640 and founded Thôn Hải Môn; fishers say the pirate ships lay hidden in the great sea cave. A century and more later his pirates burned the pearl harbour of Châu Lệ Cảng, and soon after they carried off the whole village of Lô Châu. Then Đỗ Tinh Hà of Thiên Xu Tông called the Pirate Purge, and Phượng Minh's and Lạc Hà's fleets sailed under the Pivot's writ, while the watchers on the cliffs of Vọng Hải could see the pirates' sails a day before they landed. In 781 the Purge ended at Thôn Hải Môn: Ô Kình Hải died on his islet, and his sabre Kình Nha was lost in the burning hold. The captives held there were freed and went home to rebuild their villages. The islet has lain in Phượng Minh's land ever since, and no one has settled it.

218.name: Phá Quân Môn
218.look: On a high mountain shoulder, a gate arch split clean down the middle still stands, each half leaning away from the other, with seven iron star-studs running across its broken lintel. Behind it, scorched walls and the stump of a watchtower climb the slope. Grass grows in the old parade ground, and little else.
218.lore: Hạ Lang Tinh founded Phá Quân Môn in 720 as a vassal of Thiên Xu, naming it for the Army-Breaker, the Dipper's seventh star. In 870 Hạ Lang Tinh led it against its lord to win by war the land the Compact forbids, and in 874 Thiên Xu destroyed it; Đỗ Tinh Hà took Hạ Lang Tinh's spear. Miners of Dao Quang Lĩnh say the seventh stud on the gate glows on the night of the fall.
218.history: In 720 Hạ Lang Tinh founded Phá Quân Môn in the mountains of Dao Quang Lĩnh as a vassal of Thiên Xu, named for the Dipper's seventh star, the Army-Breaker. It held the high passes for the Pivot and trained hard; within two generations its disciples were drilling at night on nearby Phụ Tinh Phong. In 870 Hạ Lang Tinh led Phá Quân Môn against its lord, to win by war the land the North Star Compact forbids. Thiên Xu laid siege to the fort, and in 872 Cửu Cao's crane riders carried the Pivot's messages over it. In 874 Thiên Xu destroyed Phá Quân Môn; Đỗ Tinh Hà took Hạ Lang Tinh's spear, and Cửu Cao Phái received the rebels' holdings. The fort was never rebuilt, and Thiên Xu keeps the ruin as a warning to its vassals.

219.name: Kim Cốc Thành
219.look: The burned shell of a merchant city on the bay shore, its walls blackened and its streets choked with ash and weeds. At its heart stands the charred skeleton of a great garden pavilion, a few gold-glazed tiles still clinging to its broken ridge.
219.lore: Kim Cốc Viên, a garden of trade under Lạc Hà Tông, built this city around its gardens in 760 and lost it in a market crash and a great fire in 1003. The pearl Lục Châu was lost in the ashes, and scavengers still sift the old garden for it; they have found only melted coins and broken jade.
219.history: In 760 merchants of Thu Thủy Loan founded Kim Cốc Viên, a garden of trade under Lạc Hà Tông, and built Kim Cốc Thành around it. For more than two centuries its merchants dealt in everything the bay could sell, and its gardens were the wonder of the coast. In 1003 Kim Cốc Viên collapsed in a market crash and a great fire; Kim Cốc Thành burned, and the pearl Lục Châu was lost in the ashes. A year later its merchants were begging in Vật Hoa Thị, where Thiên Bảo Trai hired those who could still count. Within a decade its trade had gone to the new city of Ngũ Cốc Thành. Lạc Hà holds the ruin but has never rebuilt it, and its stewards call the ground unlucky for trade. Rumour holds that the pearl was never lost at all, only hidden.

220.name: Vân Môn Thành
220.look: Low grass-grown walls on the river, broken into a rough square, with the stumps of towers at the corners. In the middle stands the one thing still upright: a tall frame of two carved stone pillars and a crossbeam, where the stone chime Vân Môn Khánh hung in the city's hall.
220.lore: Cửu Thiều Cung built Vân Môn Thành in 130 and named it for the Vân Môn music, twin of the Thiều. When Cửu Thiều fell the city emptied within a year, and its people took the music with them to the four coasts. Herders who shelter in the ruin say the empty frame hums a low note in a strong wind, and they will not sleep under it.
220.history: In 130 Cửu Thiều Cung, the palace of court music on the ridges of Thê Ngô Lĩnh, built Vân Môn Thành on the rice plain it had taken under its protection ten years before. The stone chime Vân Môn Khánh was hung in the city's hall, and the city became the plain's centre of music and trade. Its musicians played to the dawn at Triêu Hà Hồ, and the rice of Thủy Điền filled its markets. At the end of the Age of First Gates, Thiên Xu Tông destroyed Cửu Thiều Cung in the War of the Nine Shao. In 341 Vân Môn Thành emptied within a year; its people scattered to the four coasts and took the music with them. Through the Age of Seven Seats its walls fell slowly while wild oxen grazed its streets. Phượng Minh Cung took the plain two centuries later but never resettled the city, and it lies in the Palace's land as a ruin. Whether the chime still lies under the rubble, no one on the plain will say for sure.

221.name: Lôi Trạch Thành
221.look: On a marshy river mouth by the sea, among old forest, stand the broken walls of a city whose stones are fused black and glassy, as if fired in a kiln. Over the old gate rises the shattered stump of a great drum tower, split down its middle. Reeds grow through the streets.
221.lore: Khải Lôi Môn built Lôi Trạch Thành in 170 at the river mouth below its mountains. At the end of the Age of Seven Seats the lightning of Hầu Xuân Lôi's own tribulation burned it, and the next year its people moved up the valley to Không Mông Thành. Its dead lie on the bamboo hills inland, where Thu Phần Các now keeps the graves, and in autumn ghosts are said to sing old poems there.
221.history: Khải Lôi Môn built Lôi Trạch Thành in 170, ten years after Lý Thiên Cổ founded the Gate, at the river mouth below its mountains. It was the Gate's market and harbour, and its great drum tower answered the thunder of the peaks. The city buried its dead on the bamboo hills inland, away from the marsh. Three centuries after its founding Hầu Xuân Lôi, head of the Gate, was struck down by his own tribulation, and its lightning burned Lôi Trạch Thành. In 481 the survivors moved up the valley to Không Mông Thành. Thính Vũ Lâu took the land but never rebuilt the city, and the marsh crept into its streets. Nearly five centuries later Lý Hận Bích founded Thu Phần Các among the city's graves and swore it to Thính Vũ Lâu, and since then the farmers of Ương Ca have heard singing from the graves each autumn.

222.name: Hồng Vũ Thành
222.look: Burned walls among wild peach trees on the Petal Shore, inland of the bay. In spring the peaches bloom through the roofless halls, and red petals drift down over the black stones like red rain.
222.lore: Lạc Anh Phái built this city on the Petal Shore in 260 and lost it in the war over the shore in 618, when petals and ashes fell together like red rain. Lạc Hà Tông holds the ruin. Every spring, when the peach trees bloom, ghost lights are seen moving through the ruins, and the people of the bay leave them alone.
222.history: In 240 Đào Tân Phân forged the twin swords Phi Hồng and Tàn Hồng from one peach branch hardened by a thousand springs, and decreed that whoever held both would lead the School of the Fallen Petals; the ground where this city would stand was the school's orchard. In 260 Lạc Anh Phái built Hồng Vũ Thành on the Petal Shore. When Đào Tân Phân died early in the Age of the North Star Compact without naming an heir, the two swords parted, and less than a century later the school split and its last head, Khương Vọng Nguyệt, vanished. Lạc Hà Tông and Thính Vũ Lâu both claimed the empty shore, and their disciples fought in the burning orchards. In 618 Hồng Vũ Thành burned in the fighting, and its petals and ashes fell together like red rain. The Pivot's judgement that followed gave the bay to Lạc Hà, and the ruin lies on its side of the line. On the eve of the War of Broken Halberds the founders of Lạc Hà and Thính Vũ met on the Petal Shore they had once fought over. Since 1180 ghost lights have been seen in the ruins every spring when the peach trees bloom.

223.name: Vô Định Thành
223.look: A burned city on the dry steppe at the edge of the poisoned plain, its walls broken and its streets empty; of the river that named it, only a dry stream bed under a broken footbridge is left. A grey-green bank of miasma lies against the ruins like fog that never lifts, and above it a charred bell tower still holds its bronze bell, green with verdigris.
223.lore: Lạc Hà Tông built the city in 600 on the river where three lands meet, and it burned in the battle of 803; the miasma took what was left. Its dead are still dreamed of in the river towns, and those who fled it founded Tân Khẩu Thôn. Children still dare each other to touch the edge of the miasma here, and in 1196 one did not come back. Some say the bell rings on the night of the battle with no one to pull it.
223.history: Lạc Hà Tông built Vô Định Thành in 600 on the river where three lands meet. For two centuries it traded across the borders that met at its gates. When the War of Broken Halberds broke out on the border plain where three sects' lands meet, Thiên Xu Tông under its war marshal Quý Trường Kích stood against Lạc Hà Tông and Thính Vũ Lâu. In 803 the war ended in one day at Chiết Kích Nguyên; Vô Định Thành burned in the battle on the plain, and the miasma took what was left. When the truce left the poisoned plain empty between the three sects' lands, refugees from the city founded Tân Khẩu Thôn at a harbour mouth on the coast. The river that named the city dwindled with it, and only a stream bed and a choked well remain. Its dead are still dreamed of in the river towns. In 1196 children of Tân Khẩu dared each other to touch the edge of the miasma by the ruin, and one did not come back.

224.name: Đông Lưu Thành
224.look: A long stone quay wall runs through an empty meadow, its rusted iron mooring rings hanging over grass where boats once tied up. Behind it stand the roofless stubs of warehouses, and a fresh scar of sand shows where a spring flood has opened up an old paved street. The living river runs past at a distance, along the edge of the bed.
224.lore: Mortal boatmen built Đông Lưu Thành on a great bend of the northern river in 90, long before any sect held this land. They gave the river spirit a pig every spring for safe passage, until the spirit stopped answering; ten years later the river left them, and the city was abandoned in 281. Old boatmen still say all things flow east, and do not finish the saying.
224.history: In 90, in the Wild Age when only hermits and beasts held the land, mortal boatmen built Đông Lưu Thành on a great bend of the northern river. From 100 they gave the river spirit a pig every spring for safe passage, and the city lived well on its boats. Late in the Age of First Gates, Tùng Đào Cung took the river basin, and the city fell under its protection. In 270 the river spirit stopped answering the boatmen's offerings. Ten years later the river left them, cutting a new course across the plain, and in 281 Đông Lưu Thành was abandoned; all things flow east. Some say the spirit itself stayed behind in a pool somewhere on the old course. For more than nine centuries the city lay under silt and grass, until a spring flood in 1198 uncovered its old street on the dry bed, and children found coins of a city no one remembers.

225.name: Hổ Khiếu Trấn
225.look: Deep in the pine sea, on a river bend, the walls of a small town have sunk under moss and young trees. Its timber watchtower lies toppled across the gate, scored with claw marks as long as a man is tall.
225.lore: Woodsmen founded Hổ Khiếu Trấn where the tigers are, and the tigers ended it. The beast tide that overran it left no one to rebuild, and Tùng Đào never resettled it; its survivors' children live at Thanh Tùng Thôn. Hunters say a tiger still dens in the old magistrate's hall.
225.history: In 380 woodsmen founded Hổ Khiếu Trấn deep in the pine sea, where the tigers are, and lived on timber and pelts. For centuries the town held its palisade against the forest. In 700 a tiger as large as a house was seen near the town; Tùng Đào sent three disciples, and two came back. In 734 a beast tide poured out of the deep pines and overran Hổ Khiếu Trấn, and the tigers' roar was the last thing its people heard. A year later the survivors moved to Thanh Tùng Thôn and planted a green pine for each of their dead. The town was never rebuilt, and the forest has taken back its streets.

226.name: Bích Không Cảng
226.look: The empty harbour below Đàm Ảnh Thành: long stone quays running out into blue water, lined with bare mooring posts and not one boat. At the root of the quays stands the roofless shell of a great sail loft, its rafters open to the sky.
226.lore: From here the sails of Cô Phàm Các vanished into the blue, and here the fleet failed to come home. Giang Bích Không made the Viễn Ảnh Châm for this harbour, a needle that always points to the last ship to leave port. The widows left a year after the loss and the quays have faced the empty sea since; fishers will not tie up here, and say the needle, wherever it is now, still points out past the harbour mouth.
226.history: Cô Phàm Các, founded on Cô Vụ Đảo by Giang Bích Không in the Age of Seven Seats, built the harbour of Bích Không Cảng below Đàm Ảnh Thành soon after. In 420 Giang Bích Không made the Viễn Ảnh Châm, a needle that always points to the last ship to leave port, and his sailors read the sea like a scripture. At the close of that age the Strait Oath bound the sect to Lạc Hà Tông, and Lạc Hà's cargoes sailed from these quays too. In the Age of the North Star Compact a storm sank the whole fleet with its head Mã Viễn Ảnh, and the Pavilion of the Lone Sail was lost at sea. In 706 the widows of Bích Không Cảng left the harbour, and the empty quays have faced the blue ever since. Lạc Hà holds the ruin and has never refitted it. What became of the needle is not recorded.

227.name: Cô Thành
227.look: On a white salt pan that was once a desert lake stands a square fortress, its walls glazed black and cracked by fire. One corner tower still rises to its full height; the rest have slumped. Salt crust creeps up the foot of the walls like frost.
227.lore: Băng Tâm Các raised Cô Thành in 520, a lone fortress on a desert lake to guard the caravan road; an old poem says the lone fortress looks far toward the jade gate. In the Desert Road War its garrison held out for two years against Phượng Minh's fire, drinking the lake down to salt, before it fell in 726. Caravans pass it in silence, and some leave a cup of water at the gate.
227.history: In 520 Băng Tâm Các raised Cô Thành, a lone fortress on a desert lake, to guard the caravan road between the desert and the rice plain. For two centuries it kept the road, until Băng Tâm Các and Phượng Minh Cung went to war over the caravan road. From 724 the garrison held out for two years against Phượng Minh's fire, drinking the desert lake down to salt. In 726 Phượng Minh's fire broke Cô Thành; the lone fortress fell and the lake turned to salt. Soon after, the Pivot imposed a truce on the Desert Road and the border stayed where it was; Băng Tâm kept the ruin and never rebuilt it. Much of the trade it once guarded later moved to the sea road through Hồi Lan Thành.

228.name: Châu Lệ Cảng
228.look: A curve of low coast where a beach of heaped white oyster shells glitters under rows of charred pier pilings standing in the shallows. Behind them the burned shells of warehouses and a broken harbour wall slope down into the sea.
228.lore: Phượng Minh Cung built the pearl harbour here in 600, and for over a century its divers brought up the pearls of the moonlit sea. In 762 Thôn Hải's pirates burned it; the divers fled, and the pearls in the sea are said to weep. Fishers passing on moonlit nights say the water over the old oyster beds glows faintly, and they do not stop.
228.history: Phượng Minh Cung built Châu Lệ Cảng on its eastern coast in 600, the same year it founded Hoàng Vân Thành, to bring in the pearls of the gulf. Its divers worked the oyster beds off the shell beach, and its pearls went to the Palace's hall and the markets of the coast. A generation later Ô Kình Hải founded Thôn Hải Môn on an islet of the southern gulf, and the pearl harbour lay within reach of his ships. In 762 Thôn Hải's pirates burned Châu Lệ Cảng. The divers fled, and the next year they settled inland at Âu Lộ and never dived again. The pirates were destroyed in the Pirate Purge two decades later, but no one came back to rebuild. The shell beach is all that is left, and the saying that the pearls weep has outlived the harbour.

229.name: Thiết Tỏa Quan
229.look: On a forested bluff above the river road stand the broken walls of a fort, its gate towers cracked and one fallen. At the bluff's edge a massive stone anchor-block still holds a great iron ring, snapped open, from which the chain once ran across the river.
229.lore: Thiết Tỏa Quan was the fort of Tùng Đào and Lạc Hà in the War of the Pivot, where they stretched an iron chain across the river road to the heart. Thiên Xu broke it, and the chain sank to the river bed, where the people of Cổ Độ now drag up its links. Tùng Đào holds the ruin but has never rebuilt it, and its elders bring disciples here to see what breaking the peace cost.
229.history: At the end of the Age of Seven Seats, Tùng Đào Cung and Lạc Hà Tông marched together on the heart of the continent, and Kỳ Tùng Ẩn broke the peace of the three days. In 503 the allies raised Thiết Tỏa Quan and stretched an iron chain across the river road to the heart. Through the years of the siege the ferrymen of Cổ Độ kept carrying the chain's iron up the river link by link. In 508 Thiên Xu Tông broke Thiết Tỏa Quan, and the thousand-fathom chain sank to the river bed. The war ended the next year with the allies beaten and no land taken, and soon after the North Star Compact was set at Thạch Kiều Thành. The fort was left as it fell. Nearly five centuries later the links of its chain began to be dragged from the river at Cổ Độ and sold to smiths.

230.name: Thu Phần Các
230.look: On a quiet bamboo hill inland from the ruins of Lôi Trạch, a pavilion of dark weathered wood with two small towers rises above slopes covered in old grave mounds. Between the bamboo, countless thin wooden slips, each brushed with a line of an old poem, hang on strings across the graves and clack softly in the wind.
230.lore: Thu Phần Các is a minor ma đạo sect of soul arts and grave wards, sworn to Thính Vũ Lâu by its founder and head Lý Hận Bích. It keeps the graves of Lôi Trạch Thành, where ghosts sing old poems in autumn. Its disciples copy down the poems the ghosts sing onto the wooden slips and hang them back over the graves. The villagers of Ương Ca stay away.
230.history: The bamboo hill was Lôi Trạch Thành's burial ground from the city's founding in the Age of First Gates, and its graves filled again when the tribulation lightning burned the city. After the survivors left for Không Mông Thành, the graves went untended for centuries and the bamboo grew over them. Mountain folk said that in autumn the dead sang old poems on the hill, and few went near. In 960 Lý Hận Bích founded Thu Phần Các among the graves, a sect of soul arts and grave wards, and swore it to Thính Vũ Lâu. By 962 the villagers of Ương Ca were hearing singing from the graves every autumn, and sang louder at planting to drown it. The pavilion keeps the hill silent in every other season, and its strings of poem slips grow longer with each autumn.
levels: A walled grave court with a ward-stone at each corner, and a second tower for the soul arts.
Terraced halls climb the whole hill, and the slip strings reach down to its foot.

231.name: Phục Hổ Cương
231.look: A long, low ridge on the Kinh Trập highland, shaped like a great cat crouched with its head on its paws. Its exposed rock is banded in yellow and dark grey stripes, and the grass on it is flattened into long paths.
231.lore: A tiger-kind beast holds this ridge, where the storms wake the hills. Herders say the ridge itself was a tiger that lay down to wait for the first spring thunder and never rose. When thunder rolls over the highland, the beasts on the ridge roar back, and the villages below bar their doors.

232.name: Vạn Xà Lâm
232.look: Deep jungle at the far end of Đan Huyệt Châu, where giant strangler figs have wrapped and swallowed older trees. Their grey roots coil over a black, still pool like nests of snakes, and real snakes lie sunning on them.
232.lore: The farthest beast lair from any town, the forest is home to snakes of every kind and the beasts that eat them. Alchemists' collectors come for venom and shed skins in the dry season, never in the wet. Locals say one snake in the forest is old enough to remember Xích Thành, and does not like fire.

233.name: Tuyết Lang Nguyên
233.look: Open tundra on a low rise, flat and white under a wide sky. Across it runs a low ridge of frost-split grey boulders, the dark mouths of wolf dens between them and trampled snow all around.
233.lore: Snow wolves run here in packs; no sect holds the plain and no road crosses it. Frost-coast hunters say the packs answer to an old grey she-wolf never seen in daylight, and they hunt only the plain's edges in winter and leave the ridge alone.

234.name: Bằng Sào Nhai
234.look: A sheer cliff of pale rock towers over the forest, and on a ledge near its top sits a nest the size of a farmhouse, woven from whole pine trunks bleached grey. Feathers longer than a man lie in the scree below. Nothing else nests within sight of it.
234.lore: A roc nests on these cliffs and hunts over the steppe and forest below. Herders drive their flocks under the trees when its shadow crosses, and Cửu Cao's riders fly their cranes wide of the cliff. Its fallen feathers are prized by fletchers and talisman (phù lục) makers.

235.name: Huyền Viên Lâm
235.look: A dense jungle below the wutong hills, where huge strangler figs rise above the canopy, their crowns knotted with the dark apes' woven sleeping platforms of branch and vine. Calls and crashing branches carry from inside, but nothing shows at the edge.
235.lore: Huyền Viên Lâm, the Dark Ape Forest, is held by no sect but by its dark apes, clever black-furred beasts that throw stones and remember faces. Herb gatherers go in only in the morning and leave fruit at the edge; those who do not, the villages say, find their way out blocked by fallen trees.
235.history: The jungle below Thê Ngô Lĩnh's wutong hills has belonged to the dark apes for as long as anyone has kept records. When Cửu Thiều Cung held the ridges, its musicians liked to say the apes sat silent at the jungle's edge to hear the palace's music. After the palace fell in the War of the Nine Shao the apes spread uphill into the empty lands for more than a century. Phượng Minh Cung, rising on those lands in the Age of Seven Seats, drove them back below the hills but never into the jungle itself. Since then the palace and the apes have kept an uneasy border: Phượng Minh's disciples hunt the edge for practice, and the apes take back what they can. No sect has tried to clear the forest, and the herb gatherers of the south prefer it that way.

236.name: Thương Ưng Đài
236.look: A high flat-topped stone table rises from the plateau, its cliff rim ringed with the stick nests of grey hawks and its top scoured to bare rock by the wind. The hawks circle it all day.
236.lore: Thương Ưng Đài, the Grey Hawk Terrace, is the hunting ground of the grey hawks on the high plateau near Chiết Kích Nguyên. Herders say the hawks will not fly over the poisoned plain, and that the day they do, the miasma is thinning. Young cultivators climb up to take hawk chicks for taming, and the hawks remember their faces.

237.name: Hắc Hùng Lĩnh
237.look: A forested highland ridge above the rain forest, its slopes broken by boulders. At the mouth of a dark cave stands a tilted slab of grey rock scored with deep parallel claw marks, the black bears' scratching stone.
237.lore: Black bears den in the caves of this ridge and come down to the forest's honey trees in autumn. Woodcutters of Tiêu Vũ Lâm measure their courage by how close they will walk to the scratching stone. Hunters say the freshest claw marks show how big the den's master has grown.

238.name: Thiết Bối Cốc
238.look: A broad highland valley whose rock walls have been gnawed and scraped, so bands of raw ore gleam like polished metal along the slopes. Big grey shapes move slowly among the boulders, their backs plated like iron.
238.lore: In Thiết Bối Cốc, Iron-Back Valley, beasts with iron-plated backs feed on the ore of Ngọc Hành Sơn, grinding the veins out of the rock. Smiths prize the plates they shed, and hunters come for them; the beasts are slow and seldom angry, but a herd on the move will flatten a camp.

239.name: Hàn Giao Chử
239.look: Out on a frozen tundra lake, a lone low islet of black rock is ringed by a coiling pressure ridge of ice that wraps around it like a serpent's body. In the thaw the ridge cracks and groans. Bones of deer and wolves lie bleached on the rock.
239.lore: Far north of Ngọc Hồ Sơn a cold flood-dragon (giao) coils around this islet, and hunters say its body is the ice ridge itself. Those who cross the frozen lake give the islet a wide berth. In hard winters its breath rises in a white column that can be seen from the shore.

240.name: Băng Tê Nguyên
240.look: A frozen tundra plateau is crossed by deep trenches worn in the snow by heavy beasts. Great grey boulders stand scattered over it, scored with long gouges and polished smooth where ice rhinoceroses rub their horns.
240.lore: Ice rhinoceroses cross this plain each season, cutting the same trenches year after year. Hunters judge a herd by the fresh gouges on the rubbing stones and steer well clear. Shed horn found here is prized by the alchemists of the hills.

241.name: Vụ Báo Lâm
241.look: A steaming jungle in the island's interior, its canopy drowned in white mist most mornings. Out of the mist rises a single black rock outcrop, where the leopards bask when the sun burns through.
241.lore: Mist leopards hunt here, grey-spotted and nearly invisible in the fog; islanders say you hear one only after it has passed you. No sect holds the jungle, and Bình Thủy's ferrymen warn travellers off the inland paths.

242.name: Hổ Khiếu Cương
242.look: A long bare ridge rises between the river's bends, its crest banded with dark and pale rock like a tiger's flank. The wind funnels through a notch in the crest with a low growl, and now and then a real roar answers it from the boulders below. No path crosses it.
242.lore: Herders of the lower basin say a roar on this ridge carries across all nine bends of the river, and they do not graze its slopes. A great tiger keeps its lair among the boulders, and hunters who go up for its pelt seldom come down the way they went. Tùng Đào's riders go around the ridge, not over it.

243.name: Thiên Chu Lâm
243.look: A low, steaming jungle by the bay, its canopy sagging under sheets of silver web strung from tree to tree. In the evening light the webs shine like sails across the whole wood.
243.lore: Poison spiders web this jungle so thickly that birds avoid it; no sect holds it and no road crosses it. Thiên Bảo Trai's refiners are said to buy spider silk, so a few desperate gatherers still go in with torches.

244.name: Hỏa Hồ Nguyên
244.look: A flat white tundra under a low sky, broken by scattered round patches of bare, thawed brown earth. Each patch marks a fire fox den, its snow melted away by the beast's heat, and trails of melted prints run between them.
244.lore: Fire foxes run on the snow of this plain, and their dens melt round holes in the white. The cape's hunters say a fox's warmth stays in its den long after it leaves, and travellers caught by a blizzard sleep in empty dens at their own risk. Fox pelts that never freeze are the prize of a brave hunter.

245.name: Tuyết Để Tuyền
245.look: A smooth snowfield lies high on the cape's mountains, white except for one blue ice cave at its foot. Steam pours from the cave mouth day and night, and the meltwater runs out warm and faintly green over the stones.
245.lore: Hot water rises under the snowfields here and carves a cave from below. Thúy Vi's alchemists climb up to bottle the water, saying it carries fire and frost together. The ice roof of the cave thins each summer, and more than one careless bather has brought it down on himself.

246.name: Noãn Ngọc Tuyền
246.look: High in the snowy mountains, a chain of steaming pools spills down a rocky slope. The stones around them are a pale jade green and warm to the touch, and snow never settles on them.
246.lore: Băng Tâm Các holds the spring, and its disciples come here to warm meridians numbed by long ice cultivation. Mountain folk say the stones are the bones of a fire beast sleeping under Hàn Sương Châu, the same that wakes in Sương Diễm Sơn; the Pavilion neither confirms nor denies it.

247.name: Hồ Tâm Thang
247.look: A small rocky islet sits in the middle of a cold mountain lake. Its hot springs have built a staircase of white and rust-orange mineral terraces down to the water, each step a steaming pool.
247.lore: Hot water at the lake's heart wells up on the islet and spills down its terraces into the cold lake. Thúy Vi disciples row out to soak and meditate there, one to a pool. Fishers say the lake never freezes within a stone's throw of the island.

248.name: Chu Sa Tuyền
248.look: In a jungle clearing, a single round hot spring boils up blood-red from the ground, steaming hard, and its overflow runs away through the trees in a bright vermilion stream. The jungle around is pale with rising steam.
248.lore: A red hot spring in the phoenix's cinnabar land, held by Phượng Minh Cung. Its water tastes of iron and stains skin pink for days. Fire cultivators come to soak after training in the vents, and herbalists scrape the red crust from the stream bed.

249.name: Ngọc Nhũ Tuyền
249.look: Among grey karst pillars, a stair of milky-green pools steps down a slope, each held in a pale lip of stone the warm water has laid down over the centuries. Steam drifts between the pillars on cool mornings.
249.lore: The Jade Milk Spring rises warm among the stone pillars of Ngư Ca Xuyên's karst, its water clouded like watered jade. Lạc Hà Tông holds it but keeps no hall here: the pillars are full of caves and the beasts that den in them, so the sect sends its disciples to bathe in groups, never alone.

250.name: Xích Viêm Khẩu
250.look: On a bare black cone high in Ngọc Hành Sơn, a wide red mouth glows and breathes heat, its lava cooling with a metallic sheen. A ring of carved grey warding pillars stands around the lower slope.
250.lore: Xích Viêm Khẩu, the Red Flame Mouth, is a vent of the volcano in Ngọc Hành Sơn, and the fire that comes out of it carries the mountain's metal. Thiên Xu holds it and lets no one camp inside the warding ring; its smiths and alchemists come only to draw fire for a single working and leave the same day. Miners below say the mountain grumbles before every vein war, though no one has made it prove it.
250.history: Xích Viêm Khẩu was burning before the first cultivators came to the heart, and the miners of Ngọc Hành Sơn called it the red mouth long before it had a written name. When Thiên Xu Tông took the ore mountains under its protection in the Age of First Gates, it took the vent with them. Its formation masters raised a ring of warding pillars on the lower slope to keep the vent's fire from the mines and the miners from the fire. Through the Age of Seven Seats the sect's smiths and alchemists drew fire here for workings that needed metal and flame together. After Chúc Long Sơn erupted under the ice and buried Hồ Thiên Phái in the Age of Seven Seats, the Pivot set permanent wardens at Xích Viêm, and the pillars have been kept in repair ever since. No eruption has been recorded here, and Thiên Xu means to keep it that way.

251.name: Niết Hỏa Khẩu
251.look: High in the wutong hills, a fire vent opens in a slope of black ash, ringed by burned wutong stumps that have sprouted fresh green shoots from their charred trunks. Heat shimmers over the mouth, and the ash around it is warm underfoot.
251.lore: Niết Hỏa Khẩu, the Nirvana Fire Vent, lies in the hills where, the saying goes, the phoenix is reborn in fire. Phượng Minh holds it, and its fire cultivators come to temper their arts in the heat; the wutong burned by each outburst always sprouts again, which the palace takes as the vent's blessing.
251.history: The vent has breathed fire in the wutong hills since before any sect came to Thê Ngô Lĩnh. Cửu Thiều Cung's people, it is said, called it the phoenix's nest and would not go near it. After that palace fell in the War of the Nine Shao the vent burned unwatched for well over a century. Phượng Minh Cung, a sect of fire and wood, took it into its lands when it was founded and made it a place of trial for its fire disciples. Each outburst burns the wutong around the mouth and each spring the stumps sprout again, so the ring of trees has never grown tall and never died. When the palace destroyed Xích Thành Môn in the Compact years it gained the vents of Đan Huyệt Châu as well, but its elders still call Niết Hỏa their first fire.

252.name: Hàn Diễm Khẩu
252.look: High on the ice mountains, a crack in the glacier breathes out pale blue flames that dance over the snow without melting it. The ice around the vent is glassy and scorched dark at the lip. Downwind, sulphur stains the snow yellow.
252.lore: Fire runs under the ice of Băng Tâm's land, and here it escapes as cold blue flame. Alchemists (luyện đan sư) prize its heat for furnaces that must not crack in the frost, but the ice around it is treacherous. Since Chúc Long Sơn rumbled, the nuns of Lê Hoa Am have watched this vent as closely as the mountain.

253.name: Chúc Dung Khẩu
253.look: On the east coast of Đan Huyệt Châu, a low volcanic cone of black rock opens in a wide crater whose lip is shaped like an open mouth. Inside, lava glows orange, and a thin tongue of it creeps down a notch in the rim, hissing where it meets wet rock.
253.lore: Named for the fire god Chúc Dung, the vent is the most dangerous place in the land of the vermilion caves, and Phượng Minh Cung keeps watch on it. Fire cultivators say its heat teaches what no vent inland can, if they live through the lesson. Fishers along the coast read its smoke for weather.

254.name: Lôi Ngô Lâm
254.look: In the lowland jungle under the storm peaks, a wood of tall wutong trees stands split and scarred by lightning, green crowns still living above trunks streaked with white burn scars and black splits. The air smells of rain and scorch, and the ground is littered with fused, glassy sand.
254.lore: Lôi Ngô Lâm, the Thunder-Struck Wutong Wood, lies under the storm peaks of Thê Ngô Lĩnh, and its trees are struck again and again yet keep growing. Phượng Minh holds it, and its instrument makers prize the struck wood for zither bodies, since a zither of thunder-struck wutong is said to answer the storm. Gatherers take only fallen wood, and never on a cloudy day.
254.history: Storms have broken on the peaks above this wood for as long as the south has records, and the tall wutong below take the lightning in their place. The court musicians of Cửu Thiều Cung, it is said, made their finest zithers from its struck wood. After Cửu Thiều fell in the War of the Nine Shao the wood went unvisited for more than a century. Phượng Minh Cung took it into its lands once it was founded, and its instrument makers came back to gather the fallen timber. When Phượng Minh went to war for the Kinh Lôi thunder vein and the Pivot left that vein with Thính Vũ, the palace's elders looked again to this wood as the south's own source of thunder. Since then the palace has guarded it more closely, and its struck timber goes only to Phượng Minh's own workshops.

255.name: Tẩy Kiếm Tuyền
255.look: A cold spring wells up in a rock basin on the mountainside, its stone rim cut with long grooves where blades have been laid.
255.lore: A Metal vein rises here with the water. Băng Tâm's sword cultivators wash a new sword in it before they first draw it in earnest.

256.name: Tha Hương Tuyền
256.look: A round warm pool in the grass behind the headland, rimmed with flat stones worn smooth by bathers and ringed by small wooden name boards.
256.lore: New disciples of Bình Thủy Môn bathe here on their first night and nail the name of their home village to a board beside the pool. It is said the water tastes faintly of whatever home the bather left.

257.name: Phong Văn Hồ
257.look: A small, shallow lake on the high plain just west of Tinh Lạc Hồ, its surface always wrinkled by the wind.
257.lore: Unlike its neighbour it holds no stars, for the wind never lets it lie still. Củng Tinh's novices are sent to watch it first, to learn what a broken reflection looks like.

258.name: Hạc Tê Lâm
258.look: Tall pines on a low rise above the marsh, their crowns flattened and white with droppings where cranes stand at dusk.
258.lore: Young cranes of Cửu Cao Phái roost here before they are trusted on the towers. The riders forbid felling any tree a crane has stood on.

259.name: Xích Sa Mạch
259.look: A patch of red sand in the desert that stays hot after sunset, shimmering faintly in the dark.
259.lore: A Fire vein lies under the red sand. Dạ Quang's riders temper their blood sabres here, and Băng Tâm lets them.

260.name: Trầm Bích Đàm
260.look: A round, still side lake behind a sand bar off the long lake, ringed by birches, so calm that the full moon lies in it like a jade disc dropped to the bottom.
260.lore: The sand bar closed this bay off from Hạo Nguyệt Hồ long ago, and Hàm Nguyệt Trang's novices practise here before they are let near the Moon Net. Its water is cold and deep, and pearl mussels grow slowly in it.

261.name: Cựu Châu Trấn
261.look: Low stone footings and the stumps of pier posts on a bare shore, half buried in sand and birch saplings, with heaps of old mussel shells grown over by moss.
261.lore: Pearl farmers built this town soon after the great pearl of 470 was found. When the lake froze to its bed in 748, the town's pearl beds died, and by the next year its people had moved to Hàm Nguyệt Trang's shore.

262.name: Lan Tân Trấn
262.look: On a wooded stretch of shore, house footings and a fallen harbour wall lie under creepers, with orchids rooted in the cracks of the old landing steps.
262.lore: Lan Tân was a small port that shipped orchids and resin from the forest until Thôn Hải's raiders burned it in 779. No one came back after the Pirate Purge, and Hồng Đậu Trang later carried off the dressed stone of its walls for its own terraces.

263.name: Tiêu Âm Mạch
263.look: Under a ring of old wild banana plants whose leaves the wind never tears, the ground breathes a faint green warmth and the rain falls softer.
263.lore: A spirit vein (linh mạch) of Wood (Mộc) qi in the jungle behind Hồng Đậu Trang, where the manor grows its charm-herbs. Visitors who sit too long in the shade wake with a headache and no memory of the hour.

264.name: Kê Quan Khoáng
264.look: Orange-red crusts of realgar coat a steaming volcanic crater wall, cut into ledges where miners chip the ore into baskets.
264.lore: Hồng Lô Cốc works the mine for realgar, the red cockscomb stone, which its alchemists use to drive poison from pills. Miners wear wet cloth over their faces, and a fresh hand who forgets it does not forget twice.

265.name: Tề Phi Mạch
265.look: A low rise of steppe below the seat where, at dusk, the sunset clouds and the wild ducks seem to fly together overhead.
265.lore: An Earth vein runs under the rise, named for the line in which the sunset clouds fly with the lone wild duck. Lạc Hà's inner disciples cultivate here at evening, and it is strongest in the hour of the glow.

266.name: Phá Chu Trấn
266.look: On the shore, rotted piers and the hulls of boats lie broken in the sand, among the stone footings of a small town.
266.lore: The boatmen's town where the families of the river fought over landings. In 786 a feud ended with half the town burned, and the survivors were among those who banded together as Lãng Đào Môn four years later.

267.name: Tẩy Sa Tuyền
267.look: A clear spring bubbles up through white sand in the woods behind the gate of hulls, its pool ringed with oar blades driven into the ground.
267.lore: A spirit vein of Water qi feeds the spring. Lãng Đào's disciples wash their oars in it before a voyage and plant an old oar beside it when they retire.

268.name: Hàn Ngọc Khoáng
268.look: A narrow adit cut into a glacier-polished wall far above the clouds, its mouth hung with prayer strips stiff with frost.
268.lore: The nuns of Lê Hoa Am cut cold jade (hàn ngọc) here, a stone that stays cold in the hand. Only nuns may enter, and they work in silence.

269.name: Cam Lộ Thang
269.look: A warm spring in the grass near the lake, edged with white stone and shaded by a small roofed pavilion.
269.lore: Lễ Tuyền Phái bathes its fever patients here before they drink the wine. The Pivot's envoys are given the pavilion while the jars are sealed.

270.name: Trì Vân Mạch
270.look: A low swell of pasture where the grass grows thick and silver-green and the spirit foals of Mục Vân graze in their first year.
270.lore: An Earth vein runs under the pasture, and the manor says a foal raised on it never tires. Khấu Mục Vân lets only his own riders cultivate here, at dawn, among the horses.

271.name: Cẩm Kê Nguyên
271.look: A grassy meadow by the hall where red and gold pheasants strut among the paper-drying lines.
271.lore: Spirit golden pheasants nest here, and their spurs can open a man's leg. The scribes of Nam Phố Đường buy their moulted tail feathers for fine brushes and leave the birds alone.

272.name: Thúy Bình Phong
272.look: A forested hill with a long flat face of trees stands behind the millet fields like a green screen.
272.lore: Wood qi gathers in the trees on its face, and Thúy Vi disciples sit there to cultivate. The farmers of Hòa Thử say it shelters their fields from the north wind.

273.name: Phương Phỉ Nhãn
273.look: A round hollow in the grassland stays green and flowering long after the grass around it has turned brown.
273.lore: A small wood vein rises in the hollow, and herbs grow there twice as fast as anywhere on the cape. Thúy Vi's gatherers pick it each spring and leave the roots.

274.name: Lão Tượng Lâm
274.look: Broad old oaks grow down to the shore below the crow ridge, their branches black with roosting birds at dusk.
274.lore: The crows of Ô Đề roost here when the great oak is full. Villagers cut oak for boats only where no crows sit.

275.name: Song Tỉnh Trấn
275.look: Empty stone houses stand around two well-heads in an overgrown square, a crack running across the ground between them.
275.lore: The town grew up around two sweet wells on the coast road. The earthquake of 1033 split the ground and turned both wells salt, and the town was empty within a year.

276.name: Thiền Minh Lâm
276.look: A sunny wooded slope above the pipe line, loud with cicadas all summer.
276.lore: The spring of Lâm Tuyền rises under these trees. Villagers say that if the cicadas fall silent at noon, someone is fouling the water.

277.name: Hồng Phong Đỉnh
277.look: A steep summit of limestone and maple turns crimson from crown to foot each autumn.
277.lore: Wood qi gathers in its maples, and the leaves from its top are the ones scholars pay most for. Only mortals of Thu Diệp may pick them.

278.name: Ngân Hồ Cương
278.look: A birch-crowned knoll riddled with fox earths, silver-grey fur caught on the brambles around every hole.
278.lore: Silver foxes den here, clever enough to rob the bark-strippers' lunches. Villagers say a fox that steals from you brings luck if you let it go.

279.name: Hỏa Tẫn Trấn
279.look: On the coast, charred posts and blackened stone hearths stand among young birches, the ground still dark with old ash.
279.lore: A timber town that burned with the forest in the great fire of 548. Its survivors moved inland, and the birches that grew over the burn gave Bạch Hoa its name.

280.name: Cổ Cái Lâm
280.look: Old pines with vast flat crowns that touch overhead, leaving the forest floor dim and soft with needles.
280.lore: These are the oldest pines near Thanh Tùng, and the villagers neither cut nor tap them. The survivors of Hổ Khiếu say their dead walk here.

281.name: Ban Hổ Lĩnh
281.look: A pine ridge above Tùng Phong, its bark clawed at head height and its paths marked with great striped hairs.
281.lore: Tigers hold the ridge, and when the wind turns toward the hamlet the wind strings hum a warning. Vạn Hác's students say a well-played zither keeps them away.

282.name: Thâm Tuyết Lâm
282.look: A fir forest where the snow lies deeper than a man is tall all winter, only the treetops showing above the drifts.
282.lore: The villagers of Tuyết Ốc tunnel into it for firewood. Hunters say bears and stranger beasts sleep under the snow here until the thaw.

283.name: Dã Mai Lâm
283.look: A wood of wild plum trees on the slope above the village, their red blossoms opening through the snow.
283.lore: The villagers of Hàn Mai say the plums grew from the seeds of their own tree. The swordsmen of Ngạo Tuyết Phái train among them in the blossom season.

284.name: Ngạo Tuyết Phái
284.look: A small school of grey-tiled halls among wild plums on a slope above the river, its practice yard ringed with plum trees.
284.lore: Ngạo Tuyết Phái is a small school of sword cultivators sworn to Tùng Đào Cung, founded in 1105 by a swordsman who learned his art watching the plum bloom through the snow. Its plum-blossom sword forms are quick and light.

285.name: Lang Hồi Cương
285.look: A forested knoll above the river, its moss cut by wolf trails and its foot littered with gnawed deer bones.
285.lore: Grey wolves have come back to this knoll in the centuries since the white wolf king fell. The villagers of Bạch Lang say the year they leave the den's boulders grey, the wolves will come down.

286.name: Kiêu Minh Lâm
286.look: A dim stand of old oaks between the lakes, hung with owl pellets and silent by day.
286.lore: Spirit owls with wings as wide as a boat hunt here at night and take lambs and dogs. Ba Quang's fishermen will not row past it after dark.

287.name: Cựu Tân Trấn
287.look: Stone footings and a broken quay on the shore, half buried in sand and shingle, with sea grass growing in the old streets.
287.lore: A small port that ferried goods along the coast from 420. In 968 a storm tide drove over the quay and took half the town; the rest moved inland to the lakes of Ba Quang.

288.name: Hạc Tức Mạch
288.look: A hollow in the woods where the pines grow twice as thick as their neighbours and the moss is bright green even in winter.
288.lore: A small vein (linh mạch) whose qi (linh khí) runs to Wood. Cửu Cao's riders rest tired cranes here, and the birds sleep a whole day after.

289.name: Lão Du Lâm
