289.look: A line of old elms along the edge of the steppe, bent away from the wind, with deer trails worn through the grass beneath.
289.lore: The elms shelter Lộc Uyển's deer from the steppe wind in early spring. Villagers gather the elm seed in famine years and grind it into cakes.

290.name: Bạch Lộc Quán
290.look: Low moss-grown halls on a wooded rise, their roofs fallen in, with a stone deer standing headless in the court.
290.lore: Hermits who fed the wild deer founded this small abbey in 370 and asked the Pivot to ban hunting in the meadow, which it did in 380. Its last master died in 612 without a disciple, and the halls were left to the deer.

291.name: Hàn Sam Lâm
291.look: Dark firs stand close on low ground behind the shore, their roots in black volcanic grit.
291.lore: The woodcutters of Đỗ Quyên cut their planks here and leave the azalea slopes alone. Old trees still carry scorch marks from the eruption.

292.name: Dã Liễu Lâm
292.look: A tangle of grey willows and firs fills the valley floor, bare branches hung with straw bird shelters.
292.lore: The orioles of Hoàng Oanh roost here in winter. The village cuts willow for baskets only in spring, after the birds have gone.

293.name: Hoàng Thổ Mạch
293.look: A low mound of yellow earth among the fish ponds, where the grass grows thicker than anywhere in the desert.
293.lore: An Earth vein lies under the pond fields. The villagers say it is why their fish grow so fat.

294.name: Lục Ba Đàm
294.look: A clear spring-fed pool among grass, its surface rippling green with lotus leaves.
294.lore: This is the largest of the Liên Đường ponds and the source of the rest. Dạ Quang's riders water horses at its lower end only.

295.name: Mục Thảo Mạch
295.look: A meadow on the steppe where the grass stays green even in drought, crossed by horse trails.
295.lore: A Wood vein lies under the meadow. Mã Minh's herders graze their best mares here.

296.name: Ngân Hùng Cương
296.look: A forested rise with great dens dug under the roots, and white fur caught on the bark.
296.lore: White bears from Vô Tung Lâm come here to den. In 1180 hunters took one alive and sold it in Mộc Lan.

297.name: Thoa Lạp Trấn
297.look: Burned stone foundations on the shore, overgrown with fir saplings.
297.lore: Hàn Giang Môn's fishers built this town around 320, named after their founder's rain cape and hat. It burned in the War of the Frost Coast in 498.

298.name: Lão Sam Lâm
298.look: Huge old firs close over the inlet, and the forest floor is deep with needles.
298.lore: Lâm Ẩn's children learn to track here. The firs are so tall that village smoke barely clears them.

299.name: Tầm Tung Viện
299.look: A ruined timber hall in the firs, with tracks of every beast carved into its stone threshold.
299.lore: Students of the hermit who taught Lâm Ẩn's children founded this academy in 800. In 1040 its masters went into Vô Tung Lâm together and did not come back.

300.name: Thanh Ly Lâm
300.look: A thick wood of fir and alder behind the reed marsh, where the trunks are scored with claw marks at shoulder height.
300.lore: Blue-grey spirit lynxes hunt marsh birds and deer here, and their coats fetch a high price in Liên Giang. Lô Hoa's reed-cutters never go in alone at dusk, and they hang reed bells at the wood's edge to hear the cats pass.

301.name: Ôn Bối Trì
301.look: A shallow warm pool in the grass behind the dunes, its bottom white with old shells.
301.lore: The shell-gatherers of Bối Sa soak their cracked hands here after the cold season. They throw in one shell from every catch, so the floor rises a little every year.

302.name: Cự Ngao Chử
302.look: A flat of rough grass and tide pools behind the shore, pocked with burrows wide enough to swallow a goat.
302.lore: Spirit crabs with claws as long as an arm come up out of the surf to burrow here. Their shells are hard enough to turn a blade, and the fishers of Lãng Thạch sell them to armourers on the mainland.

303.name: Phục Mãng Cương
303.look: A warm bare dune ridge beyond the willow rows, its sand marked with long curving trails.
303.lore: Sand pythons as thick as a man lie buried in the warm sand and take what walks over them. The villagers of Dương Liễu say the willows are the only thing the snakes will not cross.

304.name: Vũ Tễ Tuyền
304.look: A steaming pool in open grass that clouds over in wet weather and runs clear as glass when the rain stops.
304.lore: The islanders read the weather by it: when the pool clears, the storm is over. Fishers of Tình Sa will not put out until they have seen it clear.

305.name: Quế Ảnh Mạch
305.look: A grove of old cassia trees in the forest above the cove, where the moonlight falls through the leaves in sharp silver patches.
305.lore: A spirit vein of Wood qi runs under the cassias, strongest on moonlit nights. Lạc Hà's disciples who come over to the island sit here when the moon is full and say the sea is quieter in their meridians.

306.name: Ẩn Canh Mạch
306.look: A small wood behind the scholars' gardens, its floor soft with leaf mould and a stone seat at its centre.
306.lore: A Wood vein runs under the wood, gentle enough for those who come to cultivation late. Retired scholars of Nhạn Thanh sit here after their morning in the fields, and a few have reached Luyện Khí in old age.

307.name: Yến Ngữ Thang
307.look: A warm pool in the fields edged with reeds, crowded each spring with swallows dipping and calling.
307.lore: The swallows of Yến Quy bathe here before they nest. The farmers say a year when they bathe late is a year to plant carefully.

308.name: Ôn Tân Trì
308.look: A steaming pool on the wet shore beside the old ferry posts, lower than the sea at high tide but never flooded by it.
308.lore: The ferrymen of Chu Tân thaw out here after winter crossings. The tide rises all around it and stops at its rim, and no one knows why.

309.name: Hàn Thú Thang
309.look: A walled hot spring in the grass inland of the reed harbour, with a small guardroom beside it.
309.lore: Lạc Hà built the guardroom when it raised the western watch, so the watchmen could warm themselves after a night on the tower. A watchman who leaves his post for the spring is made to bathe in the sea instead.

310.name: Hàm Thủy Thang
310.look: A hot salty spring in the grass behind the salt pans, its rim crusted white.
310.lore: Its water is saltier than the sea, and the salt-makers once boiled it for salt in winter. Now they soak their aching backs in it after the summer raking.

311.name: Triều Một Trấn
311.look: Low broken walls standing in shallow water on the grassy shore, visible only at low tide.
311.lore: Salt traders built the town on the shore in 350, before any sect held the plain. In 988 a storm surge broke its sea wall and drowned the lower streets, and its people moved up the coast to Diêm Điền. At low tide the salt-makers still walk out to its gate.

312.name: Hoa Ổ Viện
312.look: Burned walls and a fallen gate on the steppe shore, with a few old peach trees still growing in the empty courtyard.
312.lore: Lạc Anh Phái built this hall in 280 to graft its peach trees. When Lạc Hà and Thính Vũ fought over the empty Petal Shore it burned with the orchards in 618, and no one rebuilt it. The peach trees in its courtyard still flower each spring.

313.name: Chu Hoa Mạch
313.look: A wood by the brook where red flowers grow on the forest floor all year.
313.lore: A Wood vein runs under the wood, named for the old line about vermilion blooms by the water. Thiên Bảo's apprentices rest here between rinsings.

314.name: Độc Phong Nguyên
314.look: Open grass by the brook head where the air hums and grey paper nests hang from every bush.
314.lore: Spirit hornets as long as a thumb nest here, and a dozen stings can kill. The villagers of Khê Đầu smoke them back from the spring each summer.

315.name: Quần Hầu Lĩnh
315.look: A bamboo ridge loud with chattering, where the canes bend under the weight of monkeys.
315.lore: Troops of spirit monkeys live in the bamboo and raid the fish racks of Hải Môn. They throw stones well enough to break a skull, and the fishers keep dogs.

316.name: Vong Ưu Tuyền
316.look: A clear warm pool in the grass behind the village, with a single stone bench beside it.
316.lore: The refugees of Vô Định Thành called it the spring of forgetting. The old ones bathe there in silence, and no one speaks while they are in the water.

317.name: Lạc Mai Lâm
317.look: A wood of wild plums along the river that turns white with blossom before the snow is gone.
317.lore: Its petals float down to the flower brook each spring and catch on the lovers' fence. The village's old women say a slip that catches in the plum petals is the luckiest of all.

318.name: Sảng Lại Lâm
318.look: A forest on the hills where the wind through the hollow branches sounds like many flutes.
318.lore: Its name comes from the old line about clear pipes sounding and a clean wind rising. The silver panners of Ngân Than say the forest keeps the count when their singers tire.

319.name: Yển Tùng Lâm
319.look: A wood of low, wind-bent pines behind the dunes, their crowns all leaning away from the sea.
319.lore: The sea pines shelter the sweet grass meadow from the salt wind. The grass cutters of Phương Thảo say that the day the pines fall the grass will lose its scent.

320.name: Cam Lộ Tuyền
320.look: A warm spring in the grass above the river, its water sweet enough to drink.
320.lore: The boatmen of Thủy Khẩu fill their jars here before going downriver. Lạc Hà's cooks send for it to brew the tea of the evening rites.

321.name: Thiết Đề Nguyên
321.look: Open steppe beyond the incense groves, beaten bare in long tracks by a running herd.
321.lore: A herd of wild spirit horses with hooves hard as iron runs here and tramples anything in its way. Mộc Hương's woodcutters stay inside the groves when they hear it.

322.name: Khô Tỉnh Trấn
322.look: Mud-brick walls on the steppe around a deep stone well, dry to the bottom, with empty houses roofless around it.
322.lore: A caravan halt that grew into a town around its well from 530. The well failed in the drought of 940, and the people left for the river.

323.name: Bàn Căn Mạch
323.look: A dip in the steppe where great roots break the surface in coils, though no tree stands near.
323.lore: Its qi (linh khí) runs to Earth and Wood. The villagers of Thụ Âm say these are the roots of their great tree, and that the tree drinks from the vein.

324.name: Thanh Lưu Mạch
324.look: A spring in the grass above the mills, so clear that its pebbles seem to float.
324.lore: A small vein (linh mạch) whose qi (linh khí) runs to Water. The millers say their wheels turn smoother on the stream it feeds, and they never let cattle drink at its head.

325.name: Kim Tuệ Mạch
325.look: A riverside field where the wheat always ripens first and stands tallest.
325.lore: Its qi runs to Earth and Wood. The village threshes the first sheaf from it before any other, and seed from this field is traded for twice its weight in common grain.

326.name: Thạch Hôi Khoáng
326.look: A white limestone quarry by the sea, with kilns burning shell and stone into lime.
326.lore: Its lime makes the mortar of Tinh Hán's walls and the packing between the ribs of the bone reef. The burners' eyes are always red, and they wash them in sea water each evening.

327.name: Quy Bối Sơn
327.look: A low, humped hill of grey rock on the shore, shaped like a turtle's back, its seaward side white with spray.
327.lore: It shelters Châu Bạng from the sea wind. Its qi runs to Water, calm and slow, and divers sit on its crown before the season to steady their breath.

328.name: Đào Hoa Thang
328.look: A warm pool in the grass below the peach orchard, its surface covered with pink petals every spring.
328.lore: The villagers of Đào Khê bathe here after the peach harvest. Like the orchard above it, no one sings at the pool.

329.name: Noãn Ba Tuyền
329.look: A shallow warm spring on the floodplain, ringed by a low mud wall that the autumn flood tops every year.
329.lore: When the flood comes, the warm water spreads over the plain and the fish crowd to it, and Hà Loan's boat traders call it their best season.

330.name: Bách Vũ Các
330.look: On the jungle edge above the floodplain, a tall pavilion of red timber stands among great netted aviaries, loud with peacocks, pheasants and messenger birds.
330.lore: A minor sect of spirit bird keepers sworn to Phượng Minh Cung, founded in 1110 by bird catchers who said that all birds bow to the phoenix and so should serve its palace. It raises messenger birds for the palace and sells feather fans and talisman feathers; it is one of the younger vassals of the south and still eager to prove itself.

331.name: Tử Trúc Lâm
331.look: A grove of dark purple-stemmed bamboo, so dense that it is dim at noon and rustles without wind.
331.lore: Trúc Thực Viên cuts the purple cane for the basket walls of Bích Lãng, since it rots slower than any other in salt water.

332.name: Trúc Địch Viện
332.look: Roofless halls by the river among the bamboo, their walls pierced with rows of small round holes like the stops of a flute.
332.lore: A flute school of Cửu Thiều Cung where its disciples learned the bamboo pipes. When the palace made its last stand in 340 the students went up to the palace's last stand and did not come back, and the school was never reopened.

333.name: Hòa Miêu Mạch
333.look: A patch of dry steppe beyond the paddies where grass grows green in the driest month.
333.lore: A Mộc (wood) vein under the dry ground. Thủy Điền's farmers raise their first seedlings here before planting them out.

334.name: Thanh Âu Nhãn
334.look: A small clear spring in the oak woods behind the marsh, where gulls come to drink and bathe.
334.lore: A Thủy (water) vein rises here. The old divers' families say the pearls of Châu Lệ came from the same water.

335.name: Ngọc Quản Trấn
335.look: Low walls in the oak woods at the foot of the hills, with a carved stone stage still standing in the old square.
335.lore: A town of Cửu Thiều Cung where jade pipes were cut and played. When the palace fell its people left within a year, like those of Vân Môn, and the woods took it.

336.name: Kim Diệp Mạch
336.look: A low grassy mound near the river, ringed by young ginkgo trees that turn gold before any others.
336.lore: A Mộc (wood) vein. The villagers say the great ginkgo of Ngân Hạnh draws its long life from it.

337.name: Vọng Triều Đường
337.look: A walled hall of grey stone on the steppe shore, with a tall lantern tower facing the sea and the burned piers of Châu Lệ.
337.lore: A minor sect founded in 790 by survivors of the pirate years, sworn to Phượng Minh, which keeps watch on the eastern gulf and lays sea-ward formations against storms and raiders. Its lantern burns every night over the old oyster beds, and its head swears no harbour on this coast will burn again.

338.name: Bạch Nhạn Huyệt
338.look: A shallow hollow in the steppe where the snow geese land each spring, the grass pale and stiff.
338.lore: A Kim (metal) vein lies under the hollow. The fishers say the geese come for it, not for the plum blossom.

339.name: Ngưu Dục Trì
339.look: A broad warm pool in the steppe, its banks trodden bare by hooves.
339.lore: Hoàng Ngưu's herders wash the ox with painted horns here before walking it round the corral on the first day of spring.

340.name: Thảo Tâm Nhãn
340.look: In an open meadow a round patch of grass stays bright green through the dry months, and at its centre a small clear spring wells up without a sound.
340.lore: A minor spirit eye of Wood (Mộc) qi a short walk from the bridge at Kiều Bạn. Travellers resting at the bridge come to sit by it, and the village charges a copper for the privilege.

341.name: Long Nhãn Lâm
341.look: Tall old longan trees, their trunks split and hollow with age, stand widely spaced across the grassland like an orchard gone wild.
341.lore: The ferry village says the first ferryman of Bình Độ planted it, and no one owns it now. In summer the whole village picks the fruit together and dries it for the markets of Thu Trì.

342.name: Ôn Vũ Thang
342.look: In the jungle above the flower fields a steaming pool lies among ferns, and when rain falls on it the drops hiss and raise a thin warm mist.
342.lore: The beekeepers of Hoa Điền bathe here to ease the stings of the season, and the water is said to draw out venom. Hồng Đậu Trang has offered twice to buy the spring, and the village has refused twice.

343.name: Tân Lang Lâm
343.look: Ranks of tall, slender areca palms rise out of the meadow grass, their crowns so high that the rain reaches the ground long after it starts.
343.lore: The villagers of Yên Kiều cut areca nuts here to chew with betel leaf, and Hồng Đậu Trang, which owns the grove, sends each guest a lacquered box of them on arrival. Those who chew the manor's nuts say they taste faintly of beans.

344.name: Tiêu Đồng Lâm
344.look: Above the rice terraces stands a wood of paulownia trees, nearly every trunk split and blackened by lightning yet still in leaf.
344.lore: Lightning finds these trees every storm season, and wood that has been struck and lived holds Wood qi with a spark of thunder in it. The zither makers of Không Mông pay the most for the charred ends, which they say give the truest note.

345.name: Hoàng Phong Cốc
345.look: A shallow bamboo valley where paper nests the size of rain barrels hang from the stems, and the air hums from end to end.
345.lore: Spirit-touched hornets as long as a thumb nest here, led by a queen no one has seen. The villagers of Song Khê smoke out a nest each autumn for its grubs and wax and are stung for their trouble.

346.name: Kích Cổ Đường
346.look: On open grass stand the stone footings of a round hall, its floor cut with rings of empty sockets where great drums once stood.
346.lore: Kích Cổ Đường was a small school of drummers sworn to Khải Lôi Môn, whose drums answered the Gate's thunder at every festival. When the Gate fell in 480 the school had no one left to answer, and its last drummers scattered two years later.

347.name: Địch Trúc Lâm
347.look: On the slope above the ferry, slender bamboo with dark purple stems grows in a dense grove, glossy after rain.
347.lore: The flute makers of the south cut their best stems here. The ferry village cuts only in the dry months, saying a stem cut in rain will always sound wet.

348.name: Hắc Đàn Mộc
348.look: A few great ebony trees stand alone in the river meadows, each blackened from crown to root where lightning has run down it.
348.lore: The struck ebony is harder than iron and holds a trace of thunder. Hà Châu will not cut a living tree, and takes only the limbs the storms bring down.

349.name: Hoàng Cúc Thang
349.look: A warm pool at the village edge, banked so thick with yellow chrysanthemums that its steam smells of them.
349.lore: The villagers soak chrysanthemum heads in it for a tea they sell to Phượng Minh for the autumn rites.

350.name: Tang Căn Mạch
350.look: The dusty caravan yard under the great mulberry, where the ground stays cool even at noon.
350.lore: A Mộc (wood) vein runs under the yard. Carters say it is why the old tree never ages.

351.name: Cự Giải Chử
351.look: A flat grassy shore between the lake and the dunes, riddled with burrows and littered with broken shells as big as shields.
351.lore: Spirit crabs with claws that can snap an oar live in the burrows. Hồ Tâm's villagers trap the small ones and leave the old ones alone.

352.name: Thủy Tùng Lâm
352.look: A grove of tall water pines on the wet grass by the river, their knobbed roots rising out of the mud like rows of kneeling stones.
352.lore: Lô Châu's reed cutters take its wood for the stilts of their houses, since water pine does not rot in the marsh. When the village was rebuilt in 782, every new stilt came from this grove, and the stumps are still counted as its founders.

353.name: Lục Âm Lâm
353.look: A deep broadleaf forest just inland of Yên Ba, where the blue-green haze hangs under the canopy all morning.
353.lore: The city's carpenters and charcoal makers work its edges under licence from Thúy Vi. Children of Yên Ba are told the mist in the trees is the sect's breath.

354.name: Lãnh Sam Lâm
354.look: Dark firs stand close on the low ground by the ford, snow caught in their branches long into spring.
354.lore: Ferrymen cut ford poles and boat timber here. Under Tùng Đào the firs were tapped for resin, and the old scars still show on the trunks.

355.name: Lô Khẩu Trấn
355.look: Rotted wooden quays and the stumps of house posts stand in a reed marsh on the coast, with a stone shrine above the water.
355.lore: A fishing town at a reedy inlet, it emptied when its fishers left for the hills under Tùng Đào's resin tax from 674. With no one to dredge it, the marsh took the quays.

356.name: Thạch Thượng Tuyền
356.look: A clear spring runs over flat river stones under pines just outside Tùng Gian Thành, and at night the moon shines through the pines on it.
356.lore: A spirit vein of Water qi feeds the spring, named for Vương Duy's line of the clear spring that flows over the stones. Townsfolk fetch its water for the Night of a Thousand Pines.

357.name: Đào Âm Mạch
357.look: A pine-covered hill above the city where the wind in the crowns roars like surf, and the ground underfoot trembles faintly with it.
357.lore: A spirit vein of Wood qi runs under the hill. The townsfolk of Đào Thanh climb up on windy evenings to hear the pines.

358.name: Thần Hi Lâm
358.look: An oak and beech forest on the east side of Khai Dương, so open that the first light runs far under its trees.
358.lore: Khai Dương's bakers gather their kindling here before dawn. The city keeps it as a common wood, and no one may fence it.

359.name: Trấn Sa Đường
359.look: A walled compound of pale mud brick on a rise in the steppe, with a sabre yard and a long stable.
359.lore: The caravan guard families of Trường Vân founded this hall in 1125, after Dạ Quang Môn was made to guard the caravans. They train guards in sabre and desert craft, and they watch Dạ Quang's riders more closely than the road.

360.name: Quy Vân Mạch
360.look: A low rise on the steppe where morning mist gathers and lingers until noon.
360.lore: An Earth vein lies under the rise, and its qi draws the mist. Trường Vân's guards say the long clouds over the mountains come home here.

361.name: Lãnh Giang Phái
361.look: Timber halls stand on the bank above the river mouth, and in winter a line of holes runs across the river ice with disciples sitting motionless beside them.
361.lore: Liên Giang's fishers founded this school in 1140 to revive Hàn Giang's ice-hole cultivation under Băng Tâm's licence. Its disciples still leave a fish on Hàn Giang's fallen gate after a good catch.

362.name: Bạch Âu Đường
362.look: A burned hall on the shore, its seaward wall gone and gull nests in the rafters.
362.lore: A small sect of sea cultivators founded this hall in 640. Thôn Hải Môn's pirates burned it in 779, two years before the Pirate Purge destroyed them.

363.name: Dạ Vũ Tuyền
363.look: A spring among the riverside firs that wells up highest on rainy nights.
363.lore: A Water vein rises here. Liên Giang's people say a child bathed in it will never drown.

364.name: Nhàn Vân Quán
364.look: A low abbey of grey roofs on the steppe shore, its long open galleries hung with silk scrolls of clouds that seem to drift when the sea wind moves them.
364.lore: Painters who came to Đàm Ảnh Thành for its pool founded the abbey in 905, under Lạc Hà Tông, and learned to paint with qi in the ink. Their scrolls can hold a reflection, hide a doorway or show a cloud that is not there. Every disciple must first paint the pool of Đàm Ảnh well enough that a heron tries to land on it.

365.name: Tinh Di Mạch
365.look: A hollow in the grass with a ring of still, dark pools, in which the stars can be seen to move across the night.
365.lore: A Water vein runs under the land here, and the painters of Đàm Ảnh say it feeds the stillness of the city's pool. Its name comes from the old line about things changing and stars moving through the autumns.

366.name: Lạc Nhạn Hồ
366.look: A broad shallow lake in the grass with level sandy shores, covered each autumn with wild geese.
366.lore: The geese that fly in formation over Nhạn Thanh come down here to rest each autumn. As in the city, no one may shoot a goose on the lake, and the herders say the geese know it.

367.name: Nhạn Trận Môn
367.look: A walled gate seat on the steppe shore, its parade ground marked with lines of white stones in the shape of a goose formation.
367.lore: Survivors of Chiết Kích Nguyên founded the gate in 806 under Lạc Hà Tông, swearing that Lạc Hà's disciples would never again fight in loose order. Its disciples drill in formations modelled on the flight of the wild geese, and every spring they drill the plain's levies. Their banner shows a goose formation breaking off at the cold.

368.name: Tử Trúc Mạch
368.look: A grove of purple-stemmed bamboo in the hills behind the city, its canes dark as old lacquer.
368.lore: A Wood vein runs under the grove, and its bamboo grows purple only here. The armoury of Tử Điện cuts it for arrow shafts and keeps a guard on the grove.

369.name: Triều Tịch Mạch
369.look: A pool in the steppe near the shore that rises and falls with the tide, though it does not touch the sea.
369.lore: Its qi runs to Water. Tinh Hán's formation masters know of it but have never drawn on it, saying a vein that keeps the sea's time will not keep a city's.

370.name: Cửu Tấu Mạch
370.look: A low ring of standing stones on the steppe outside the city, the grass inside it scorched brown.
370.lore: A Hỏa (fire) vein. Lai Nghi's musicians say it warms when the welcome is played nine times at dawn; no one has proved otherwise.

371.name: Quế Hương Thang
371.look: A cluster of hot pools steams in the jungle under cassia trees, whose fallen bark floats on the water and scents the whole hollow.
371.lore: Buyers for the Night Rain Market come up from Thu Trì to bathe here by day, before the market opens at dark. The bathhouse keeper, like the innkeepers below, never asks a name.

372.name: Vũ Linh Đường
372.look: On a grassy hill above Thu Trì a long, low hall stands under deep eaves hung with hundreds of small bronze bells on chains, each ringing its own note as the rain strikes it.
372.lore: Vũ Linh Đường is a small school of array-makers (trận pháp sư) who build bell-and-chain warning arrays for the Tower's walls and roads; its founder was a smith who cast rain-chains for the Tower. It keeps the warding bells on the walls of Thu Trì Thành, and its disciples can tell from the bells alone where the rain, or a stranger, is falling.

373.name: Vi Vũ Tuyền
373.look: In the meadow above Không Mông a clear spring rises in a stone basin, and a fine drizzle hangs over it even when the valley is dry.
373.lore: A Water (Thủy) vein shared, by long custom, between the Tower's resident disciples and the city's painters. The painters wet their ink stones here and say the drizzle never ruins a picture.

374.name: Thải Vũ Mạch
374.look: A low grass rise outside the city walls, where a small shrine holds a red feather under glass.
374.lore: A Hỏa (fire) vein. The city says Hùng Phần Vũ first sat here as a boy, and its young come to sit where he sat.

375.name: Dưỡng Mộc Tuyền
375.look: A clear spring rises in a ring of unusually tall trees below the market stair, its runnels feeding terraced herb plots.
375.lore: Wood qi rises with the water, and herbs watered from it grow fast and strong. Lam Yên's herb growers share its water by an old rota.

376.name: Tuần Tùng Đường
376.look: On a pine-covered hill above the road, a long timber hall with a watchtower at each end, bows racked under the eaves and wolf pelts on the walls.
376.lore: Tuần Tùng Đường is a young sect of road wardens sworn to Tùng Đào Cung, founded after wolves followed the caravans to Tùng Hạ Thị in 1190. Its wardens guard the caravans through the pine sea with staff and bow, and take their fee in coin and salt.

377.name: Tùng Âm Mạch
377.look: On a hill above the ring market, a stand of pines sings in even the lightest wind, and the ground under them is warm.
377.lore: A spirit vein of Wood qi runs under these pines, and pilgrims to the palace stop here to listen first. Tùng Đào's disciples say it is the vein that makes the pines sing.

378.name: Bạch Dương Lâm
378.look: A wood of tall white poplars on the dunes behind the sand flats, their leaves flickering silver in the sea wind.
378.lore: The poplars hold the dunes against the wind and keep the sand off the washing cradles. The gold-washers gather firewood here.

379.name: Bình Minh Hồ
379.look: A small lake in the mountains above the market, its still water catching the first light.
379.lore: Travellers leaving at dawn stop here for a last look. The lake is named from the poem: at dawn I see my guest off.

380.name: Phiêu Bồng Quán
380.look: A small roofless abbey on the steppe point, its walls whole but its doors gone and its courtyard full of wind-blown grass.
380.lore: Wanderers who would not settle founded a small school here in 860 and taught that a cultivator should belong to no place. In 1102 its last master died with no disciple willing to stay, and he left its books to Bình Thủy Môn. The abbey has stood empty since, and travellers waiting for the ferry still sleep in it.

381.name: Bình Tung Mạch
381.look: A shallow green pond in the grass behind the market, its surface thick with duckweed that drifts in rings with no wind to move it.
381.lore: A Water vein lies under the pond, and its qi wanders like the duckweed, never strongest in the same place two days running. Bình Thủy's disciples say it suits their sect better than any steady vein would.

382.name: Hạt Vĩ Cương
382.look: A dry steppe ridge whose rocks are pocked with burrows and littered with cast-off shells.
382.lore: Spirit scorpions as long as a forearm live here. The venom gatherers of Vật Hoa Thị catch them at night with lamps and sell the venom to alchemists.

383.name: Trường Châu Mạch
383.look: A long sandy isle in the shallows above the market, its steppe grass thick and green.
383.lore: An Earth vein lies under the isle, named for the old line about the long isle of the prince. The cranes of Hạc Đinh roost here at night, and the sect's disciples wade out to cultivate among them.

384.name: Hoàng Đồng Khoáng
384.look: A small mine of brassy, glittering ore high on the mountain, with a casting shed at the path's foot.
384.lore: Its copper is cast into the bronze weights of Thiên Quyền Thị. A weight cast here is tested against the standard before it leaves the shed.

385.name: Thạch Quyền Phong
385.look: A squat, flat-topped mountain above the market, shaped like the weight of a steelyard.
385.lore: The market's weighers say it is the counterweight that keeps the heart in balance. Its qi runs to Earth.

386.name: Minh Cầm Phong
386.look: A sharp grey peak above the market, its face cut by long straight cracks like the strings of a zither.
386.lore: In a high wind the cracks hum, and Thiều Âm's makers climb it to tune by the sound. Its qi runs Kim (metal), hard and ringing.

387.name: Hắc Tích Khoáng
387.look: Low tunnels open at the foot of a mountain wall above the river, with heaps of dark, heavy tin ore by the sluices.
387.lore: Tin has been dug here since 720 and is sold in Hạnh Hoa Thị for the bronze of the Tower's rain-chains. The ore is washed in the river, and the water below the mine runs grey.

388.name: Quy Nhạn Phong
388.look: A red-brown badland peak above the apricot market, its crest notched like a gate.
388.lore: Wild geese fly through the notch each spring and autumn, and the market of Hạnh Hoa sets its seasons by them. Its rock holds Earth (Thổ) qi.

389.name: Thạch Môn Trại
389.look: Two tall stone gate pillars stand alone on a mountain saddle over the road, with the outlines of a stockade wall in the grass around them.
389.lore: Khải Lôi Môn built the stockade to guard its western road, and the Tower kept it after the Gate fell. Once the Pivot's judgement on the Petal Shore had settled the west, the Tower let its garrison go, and only the gate pillars stand.

390.name: Bách Điểu Lâm
390.look: A low pine and birch wood behind Quy Điểu Trấn whose every branch is crowded with birds in autumn, the ground white with droppings and feathers.
390.lore: The homing flocks rest here before settling on the town's nest poles. Fowlers take only what the town allows, and a feather-gatherer who robs a nest is fined a pearl.

391.name: Địch Thanh Viện
391.look: On a wooded hilltop the roofless halls of a small academy stand among trampled walls, flutes of bone still lying in the grass.
391.lore: A sect of flute cultivators founded by herders' children, sworn to Thúy Vi, who learned to call beasts as the herders called their flocks. In 1012 its master's flute drove a herd of spirit cattle mad, and they trampled the halls; the survivors went back to the folds of Mục Ca.

392.name: Bàn Căn Huyệt
392.look: In a wooded hollow the roots of a few huge old oaks coil over one another into a knot as tall as a house.
392.lore: Wood qi pools in the knot of roots, and Thúy Vi keeps the hollow for disciples posted to Mục Ca. Herders will not graze their flocks near it, saying the roots move at night.

393.name: Sam Ảnh Lâm
393.look: Dark straight firs stand close behind the white beach, so their shadows reach the sand in the afternoon.
393.lore: The Thẩm clan cuts net poles and boat timber here and nowhere else. Strangers asking about the hidden valley's stream are often seen walking its paths, looking at the brooks.

394.name: Kỳ Bàn Phong
394.look: A flat-topped rocky peak above the cypress town, its summit crossed by natural cracks in a square grid.
394.lore: Earth qi gathers in its stone, and Không Sơn's students are said to have laid out the cypress grid by copying its cracks. Players climb it to play a game on the summit.

395.name: Hồi Âm Cốc
395.look: A deep limestone valley opens onto the coast, its walls so close that every shout comes back three times.
395.lore: The woodcutters of Tiều Ca sing here freely, for it lies below the boundary stones. Their songs echo up the gorge and, they say, reach the old academy anyway.

396.name: Phàn Thạch Khoáng
396.look: Pale altered rock on a volcanic shoulder is cut into pits, with leaching vats and white crusts below them.
396.lore: Miners dig alum stone and boil it for dyers and tanners along the coast. Thúy Vi's alchemists buy the purest crystals to clear their pill waters.

397.name: Cự Thát Chử
397.look: Low sandbars in a river bend below Lộc Minh, littered with fish bones and slick slides into the water.
397.lore: Otters as long as boats hunt the river bend and steal from the ferry nets. Lãng Đào's ferrymen toss them a fish as they pass, and the otters let them by.

398.name: Luyện Thiết Trấn
398.look: On a hillside above the river, the slumped stone bellies of old smelting furnaces stand among pines, slag heaps grown over with moss.
398.lore: This town smelted iron for Tùng Đào, and its furnaces made much of the chain for Thiết Tỏa Quan. After the War of the Pivot the palace stopped buying iron, and within a generation the town was empty.

399.name: Trúc Căn Mạch
399.look: A bamboo grove on a hillside above Cổ Độ grows taller and greener than any around it, its stems creaking in the still air.
399.lore: A spirit vein of Wood qi runs under the grove, and its bamboo grows a man's height in a night in spring. The smiths of Cổ Độ cut their tongs' handles from it.

400.name: Cự Miết Chử
400.look: Muddy shoals in a slow bend of the river, where flat leathery shells as wide as doors bask in the sun and slide into the water at a footstep.
400.lore: Giant softshell turtles live in the bend and snap at the oars of passing boats. Hà Bạn's fishermen go wide of the shoals, and alchemists pay well for a shell.

401.name: Cựu Hà Trấn
401.look: On a dry rise, the silted streets of a small town lie under grass, with a stone landing stair that ends in a meadow.
401.lore: A town on the old course of the river, left dry when the river changed course. Its people moved to the new bank, and Hà Bạn Trấn grew there.

402.name: Thử Vương Cương
402.look: A knoll riddled with rat holes the width of a man's arm, its grass stripped and grain husks heaped at the burrow mouths.
402.lore: Giant rats live here and raid the granaries of Lâm Hạ whenever a staddle cracks. The town's rat-catchers hunt them with terriers and smoke.

403.name: Khê Sam Lâm
403.look: Straight red-barked firs stand in the shallows of the green brook, their roots knotted like knees above the water.
403.lore: Bích Khê Trấn forbids felling these firs, since their roots hold the brook bed where the jade pebbles lie. Carvers say the best stones are found where the knees are thickest.

404.name: Cổ Bách Lâm
404.look: A dark wood of ancient cypresses north of Thanh Bách Thành, their trunks twisted and grey and their scent heavy in the air.
404.lore: Thanh Bách cuts its coffin wood here, one tree for each official who dies in office. The oldest trees are tied with red cord and may never be cut.

405.name: Hào Trư Cương
405.look: A low forested rise where the bark of every trunk is torn and black quills as long as arrows lie in the leaf litter.
405.lore: A spirit porcupine the size of an ox lives here and throws its quills like darts. Hòe Âm's hunters buy the quills for fletching and never go for the beast itself.

406.name: Tầm Kiếm Đường
406.look: A long timber hall with a stone hearth stands on a wooded bluff over the sea, its walls hung with mountain maps marked in red.
406.lore: A Tiêu-clan hunter turned away from Lê Hoa Am's gate founded this hall in 1162 to take the men the hermitage will not. Its members hunt, guide and search the mountain for the sealed cave of 930, and Lê Hoa Am tolerates them under Băng Tâm's licence.

407.name: Ôn Thạch Thang
407.look: Warm water fills a ring of smooth stones in the steppe, steaming in the cold mornings.
407.lore: Hồi Lan's merchants bathe here to wash off the road. The spring's mild Fire qi is good for joints stiffened by the desert cold.

408.name: Xuân Hàn Lâm
408.look: A forest of fir and wild magnolia, where snow lingers among the white blossoms in spring.
408.lore: Mộc Lan's people come here in spring to see the magnolias. The cold lingers longest in this wood.

409.name: Hiểu Lộ Mạch
409.look: A meadow on the coastal steppe that is soaked with dew every dawn, even in the dry months, its grass greener than the land around it.
409.lore: A Wood vein lies under the meadow and draws the dew. Kê Minh's herders graze their lambs here, and they drive them out at the first cockcrow so the grass is still wet when they eat.

410.name: Sài Quần Nguyên
410.look: Open red-earthed grass above the cliffs, crossed by worn trails and littered with old bones.
410.lore: Packs of rust-red spirit dholes hunt the grass inland of Xích Ngạn, the colour of the rock they run over. The townsfolk drive their goats in at dusk and keep fires on the cliff stair.

411.name: Vọng Phàm Quán
411.look: A broken hall of red stone on the steppe headland, its roof fallen in and a stone platform facing the open sea.
411.lore: Cô Phàm Các built this watch hall in 430 for its watchers to call the fleet home. After the fleet was lost in 705 the last watchers kept the vigil for three more years, then went down to Xích Ngạn and did not come back. The townsfolk say a lamp is sometimes seen on the platform on stormy nights.

412.name: Lục Âm Mạch
412.look: A dim stand of jungle behind the town where the canopy closes overhead and the air is cool and green even at noon.
412.lore: A Wood vein runs under the shade, and the sea swallows of Hải Yến hunt the insects that swarm over it at dusk. The town's nest harvesters rest here at midday and say they never grow sick.

413.name: Ngạc Bối Chử
413.look: Muddy jungle shoals on the river upstream of the city, where long grey backs lie motionless in the shallows.
413.lore: Spirit crocodiles bask here, some longer than a river boat. Triều Âm's boatmen keep to the far bank and throw them the fish offal from the market, which keeps them fat and lazy.

414.name: Di Hà Trấn
414.look: A ring of grass-grown walls on the coast with a stone river quay that now faces a dry meadow.
414.lore: Boatmen built the town in 430 on the plain's widest river, the same river that once ran past Chu Tân's ford. The river wandered away over the years, and by 860 the quay faced only grass and the last boatmen had left. Herders now shelter their flocks in its walls.

415.name: Thanh Miêu Mạch
415.look: A wood of young trees among the fields, where the seedlings always sprout a fortnight before the rest.
415.lore: A Wood vein runs under the wood, and the farmers of Thanh Điền bring their seed rice here to sprout. Mục Vân Trang lets them, as long as they keep their horses out.

416.name: Bảo Thụ Lâm
416.look: A wood of tall old trees between the fish ponds, their autumn leaves so bright they look lacquered.
416.lore: The city's first farmers left the wood standing as a windbreak for the ponds. Families of Thảo Đường call a promising child a jewel tree after it, from the old saying.

417.name: Dã Độ Trấn
417.look: Roofless houses on the grassy shore beside a silted landing, where a rotten ferry boat lies across the mud.
417.lore: Ferrymen founded the town in 500 on the coast creek. When Thảo Đường Thành rose in 680 its trade drew the ferrymen away, the landing silted, and by 712 only the boat was left. The coast says the boat turns on its own when the tide comes in.

418.name: Bạch Du Lâm
418.look: A wood of pale-barked elms on the grass upstream of the weir, cut in rows and growing back in rows.
418.lore: The fishers of Ngư Lương cut its elms for the weir's frames and replant one for each they fell. Each stretch of weir has its own rows of trees.

419.name: Bạch Miết Chử
419.look: Grassy shoals on the river where huge flat shells lie in the sun like stepping stones.
419.lore: Spirit soft-shelled turtles as wide as a door haul out here. Their bite takes off a hand, and the levee guards of Liễu Ngạn chase them back into the river when they come near the levee.

420.name: Huệ Phong Mạch
420.look: A hollow in the open grass where wild orchids grow and the breeze carries their scent toward the town.
420.lore: A Wood vein runs under the hollow, and the healers of Hòa Phong sit here before they treat the gravely ill. They say the breeze over it carries its qi to the sick.

421.name: Thạc Thử Cương
421.look: A low grassy rise behind the granaries, honeycombed with burrows as wide as a barrel.
421.lore: Spirit rats as large as dogs burrow here and raid the grain towers at night, as in the old song of the great rats. Every grain guild of Ngũ Cốc pays its own rat-catcher and blames the others' rats.

422.name: Phong Kiêu Lâm
422.look: A dark stand of old maples above the town where pellets and bones lie thick under the branches.
422.lore: Spirit owls as large as a child roost here and hunt the river land by night. They take rats from the granaries and the occasional lamb, and the townsfolk count the bargain fair.

423.name: Dã Tang Lâm
423.look: A tangled wood of wild mulberries on the river, purple with fallen fruit in summer.
423.lore: The poorest families of Tang Ma pick leaves here for their silkworms. Children come in summer to paint their door charms in the purple juice.

424.name: Minh Sa Các
424.look: The roof ridge of a pavilion standing out of a dune on the desert edge, its halls filled with sand to the eaves.
424.lore: A small sect that studied the humming of the dunes was founded here in 560. The dunes crept over its halls for three centuries, and in 893 its last disciples gave up digging and went to Thạch Kiều.

425.name: Kiều Cơ Mạch
425.look: A low swell of steppe where bare grey bedrock breaks through the grass in smooth domes.
425.lore: Its qi runs to Earth, solid and slow. The builders of Thạch Kiều's bridge are said to have cut its first stones here.

426.name: Xuân Thủy Thang
426.look: A warm, shallow spring in the grassland with stone troughs where oxen stand.
426.lore: Carters rest their oxen here after the ore road. The Ôn clan charges nothing for it, which surprises everyone who knows the clan.

427.name: Chân Kim Các
427.look: A two-storey stone pavilion in a forest clearing, its yard full of crucibles and its doors bound in bronze.
427.lore: Assayers and refiners of spirit ore founded this pavilion in 980 beside Song Kiều's open scales, sworn to Thiên Xu. They test and refine ore for the mines of Ngọc Hành, and their stamp on an ingot is taken at Thiên Quyền Thị without a second weighing.

428.name: Hải Ôn Tuyền
428.look: A warm spring bubbling up among rocks at the edge of the wheat, where its water runs out into the gulf.
428.lore: The wheat farmers of Mạch Điền soak here after harvest, and the water tastes faintly of salt.

429.name: Kim Trúc Lâm
429.look: A hill forest of golden-yellow bamboo above the port, the canes glowing in the evening light.
429.lore: Thanh Khê's shipwrights cut its canes for masts and lantern poles; every lantern on the harbour wall hangs from golden bamboo.

430.name: Cựu Khê Trấn
430.look: Grass-grown walls in the bamboo above the port, with a row of small grave mounds outside the gate.
430.lore: A town of bamboo cutters built ten years after the port, emptied by a fever in 812 that killed half its people before Lễ Tuyền's healers came. The survivors moved down to Thanh Khê and never went back up.

431.name: Dã Trư Lâm
431.look: Oak forest with its floor torn up in long furrows and the trunks rubbed bare and muddy.
431.lore: Spirit boars with tusks like sickles live here and raid the rice at harvest. Hoàng Vân's keepers pay a bounty for every pair of tusks.

432.name: Minh Kính Hồ
432.look: A still lake in the woods behind the rice fields, reflecting the hills so exactly that the shore line is hard to see.
432.lore: The Vương of Đạo Hương paint it on their betrothal letters; the one sent to the Tạ in 1199 bore it too.

433.name: Bạc Hà Đàm
433.look: A spring-fed pool in the meadows, its shallow edges thick with wild mint.
433.lore: Lễ Tuyền's herb growers draw water for the beds from it, and the meadows smell of its mint after rain.

434.name: Thạch Ma Trấn
434.look: Half-buried walls in a landslide scar on the hillside, with round millstones lying among the rubble.
434.lore: A quarry town that cut millstones for the rice mills of the plain. In the great rains of 1062 the hillside slid and buried it in a night; the survivors went down to Lục Dã.

435.name: Mãng Đằng Lâm
435.look: A dark patch of broadleaf forest north of the drying yards, so thick with hanging vines that it is hard to tell which of them are moving.
435.lore: Spirit-touched rock pythons as long as a ferry raft lair here and slide out onto Bình Dã's warm yard on the rare dry nights. The yard-keepers sweep it with long poles before dawn.

436.name: Trúc Ẩn Viện
436.look: Deep in a bamboo grove, a walled compound of grey-tile halls stands roofless, its courtyards grown solid with bamboo that has split the paving.
436.lore: Trúc Ẩn Viện was a small righteous (chính đạo) school of scholars and zither players under the Tower's lordship. When the Night Rain Edict opened the Tower to the ma đạo arts, its masters packed their books and walked north in 906, and the bamboo took the halls they left.

437.name: Thanh Hoàng Lâm
437.look: Along the river near Xuân Thảo Thành, giant bamboo grows so straight and close that from the water it looks like a green wall.
437.lore: The city cuts its scaffolding and water pipes here, and every pole taken must be replaced with a planted shoot. Charred stumps from the Petal Shore fighting still stand among the bamboo.

438.name: Hải Khí Nhãn
438.look: On the dry steppe behind Lãng Hoa a shallow salt hollow glitters white, and the air over it smells of the sea though the shore is out of sight.
438.lore: A small spirit eye of Water (Thủy) qi carried inland on the sea wind. The salt-boilers of Lãng Hoa say it is where the spray flowers go when they vanish.

439.name: Lân Giáp Cốc
439.look: A bamboo hollow behind the town honeycombed with burrows, the earth around them scored by heavy claws and littered with shed scales.
439.lore: Pangolin-kind beasts with spirit-hard scales burrow here and dig up the anthills of the coast. Xuyên Lâm's guides teach their apprentices to roll one over with a staff without being cut.

440.name: Lôi Trúc Lâm
440.look: A low coastal grove of thick-stemmed bamboo, where new shoots stand in dense ranks after every storm.
440.lore: Thunder bamboo sprouts at the sound of the first spring thunder, and its shoots hold a spark of it. Phong Đăng digs the shoots for the table and sells the oldest stems to the Tower's smiths for quenching rods.

441.name: Cốc Vũ Quán
441.look: On a bamboo hill above Phong Đăng an open-sided abbey stands beside a stone rain altar, and bamboo gutters carry water from its roofs down to small terraces of spirit rice.
441.lore: Cốc Vũ Quán is a small school that calls the rain for the farmers of the south and grows spirit rice (linh mễ) on its terraces. Each year it sends a priest to bless the first cart on Phong Đăng's great steelyard, and it has kept clear of the Tower's ma đạo arts without ever refusing them aloud.

442.name: Bàn Thạch Huyệt
442.look: A flat shelf of bedrock in the grass behind the harbour, with a ring of old fleet mooring stones set round it.
442.lore: A Thổ (earth) vein lies under the rock. Sailors say it is why the old jetty stood for four centuries.

443.name: Xích Nhưỡng Mạch
443.look: A field of rust-red earth among the mulberry rows, warm underfoot on cold mornings.
443.lore: A Thổ (earth) vein touched with fire. The silk women say it is what puts fire in the thread.

444.name: Tuyết Báo Cương
444.look: A low wooded knoll above the bogs, its rocks scored with claw marks and the snow around it trampled into tracks that lead nowhere near the village.
444.lore: Snow leopards den among its rocks, kin, the herders say, to the spirit beast Hàm Nguyệt Trang hunted across the ice in 610. Herders keep their reindeer well away from it.

445.name: Ngưng Yên Nhãn
445.look: A small round hollow in the pines behind Hàn Yên Thôn, where a thin column of mist rises and hangs frozen in the air on still winter days.
445.lore: A small spirit vein of Water qi, cold and clear, wells up here; villagers say it is why the village smoke freezes. Hàm Nguyệt Trang's disciples come to sit in its mist.

446.name: Ôn Thủy Mạch
446.look: A line of snow-free ground runs through the pines behind Noãn Ốc Thôn, steaming faintly, with green moss even in midwinter.
446.lore: A spirit vein of Water qi runs here with a faint warmth in it, and it feeds the hot spring found under the snow in 1015. Old cultivators who soak at Noãn Ốc say the vein, not the spring, is what eases their bones.

447.name: Hải Tùng Lâm
447.look: A strip of twisted sea pines grows on the sandy shore below the black-walled wheat fields.
447.lore: The farmers of Mạch Lãng planted the first rows to keep the salt wind off their wheat, and the forest has grown on by itself. Its pine cones are roasted at the harvest feast.

448.name: Khuynh Mộc Lâm
448.look: On the windy headland every tree leans inland at the same angle, like a crowd bending away from the sea.
448.lore: The pilots of Phong Phàm say the trees lean a little further before a storm. Young pilots are sent to sit under them for a season to learn the wind.

449.name: Hỏa Ti Trấn
449.look: Blackened walls on a steep slope above the vent field, with rows of stone reeling basins standing in the roofless halls.
449.lore: Xích Thành Môn's town of fire-silk spinners, where the thread for the Xích Hà Kỳ was reeled from the vents. It burned in the fighting of 590 when Phượng Minh destroyed the gate, and no one has spun fire-silk there since.

450.name: Lệ Thạch Khoáng
450.look: A grey quarry of fine sandstone high on the mountain, its slabs split and stacked by the path to the valley.
450.lore: Phất Y Cốc's whetstones are cut here. Every disciple cuts and dresses his own first stone, and carries it until it is worn through.

451.name: Triều Phượng Đỉnh
451.look: The highest summit of the palace ridges, a bare red crest above the wutong where flocks of birds circle at dawn.
451.lore: The saying is that a hundred birds come to pay homage to the phoenix, and here they do circle every morning. Its qi runs strong Hỏa (fire), and Phượng Minh's elders keep its crest for themselves.

452.name: Minh Cổ Bảo
452.look: A broken stone fort on a shoulder of the ridge, its drum tower split and its gate choked with fallen wutong leaves.
452.lore: Cửu Thiều Cung's guard fort on the ridge road, whose drums warned the palace when Thiên Xu came south. It fell in 340 in the War of the Nine Shao, and Phượng Minh has left it as it fell.

453.name: Long Tu Lâm
453.look: A high jungle of giant banyans whose hanging roots have grown into trunks, so that one tree stands like a grove.
453.lore: The paths through it run along the roots, never on the ground. Rattan cutters say one banyan here has swallowed a whole hut, and that its roof can still be seen inside the trunk.

454.name: Thanh Đằng Thôn
454.look: Stilted houses in a jungle clearing, their walls woven of split rattan and bundles of green cane stacked under every floor.
454.lore: The villagers cut the rattan of the inland jungle and weave the baskets, ropes and fish traps the coast towns buy. A child here learns to split cane before it learns to count.

455.name: Kỳ Nam Lâm
455.look: An old jungle of tall pale-barked trees, many tied with knots of red cord and scarred where resin has been cut.
455.lore: The finest agarwood, kỳ nam, forms only in old wounded trees here, and a single piece can buy a house. Each gatherer marks his trees with red cord, and the cords are older than most of the gatherers.

456.name: Trầm Hương Trấn
456.look: A small walled town on the jungle shore whose air is heavy with incense smoke from the resin sheds along its quay.
456.lore: The town lives by the agarwood of the jungle behind it, graded and sold by weight in its sheds. Its best kỳ nam goes to Lạc Hà Tông's meditation halls, and a merchant who sells false agarwood here is banished from the island.

457.name: Ba Tiêu Lâm
457.look: A thicket of wild plantains on the coastal grass, their broad torn leaves rattling in the sea wind.
457.lore: The wild plantains feed the village in lean years, and rain on the leaves can be heard from the beach. Children are sent to gather the fruit and told never to go past the last tree.

458.name: Xướng Vãn Thôn
458.look: A fishing village of thatched houses on a grassy shore, its boats drawn up in a long row with their bows toward the sunset.
458.lore: Its boats come in singing at dusk, as fishing boats do all over Lạc Hà's lands. In 803, when the boats fell silent after Chiết Kích Nguyên, the village kept silent for a year, and it still sings one verse fewer than its neighbours.

459.name: Phi Hồ Lâm
459.look: A patch of jungle whose trees hang thick with dark folded shapes by day, and roar with wings at dusk.
459.lore: Spirit fruit bats as broad as eagles roost here in thousands and strip the island's orchards at night. A bitten hunter runs a fever for a month, and the villagers leave the roost alone.

460.name: Hồng Thụ Thôn
460.look: Houses on stilts among the mangrove roots, joined by plank walks, with charcoal kilns smoking on the firmer ground behind.
460.lore: Its people catch mud crabs, gather shellfish and burn mangrove charcoal for the island's smiths. They cut only every third tree, so the mangrove will keep the sea out.

461.name: Nịch Tùng Lâm
461.look: A drowned forest below the level of the sea, where straight water pines stand knee-deep in black water beside the mangrove.
461.lore: The wood of the water pine does not rot, and the boatwrights of Lan Chu pay well for it. Cutters go in only at low tide, by boat, and leave before the water rises.

462.name: Phương Lân Thôn
462.look: A fishing village on a low shore with a single long boat shed shared down the middle by two clans.
462.lore: Two fishing clans have shared the village since it was founded and have never once gone to the elders with a quarrel. The island says it is the only village where a borrowed net always comes back mended.

463.name: Nam Minh Thôn
463.look: A small fishing village on the jungle point, facing a sea so deep it shows dark blue right up to the rocks.
463.lore: Its fishers take the deep-water fish no one else on the island can reach. They never go inland, since the mist leopards of Vụ Báo Lâm hunt the paths behind the village.

464.name: Hải Khúc Trấn
464.look: The tops of walls and a gate arch sticking out of drifted sand on a grassy coastal hill, the lanes between them filled to the windowsills.
464.lore: Fishers built the town on a bend of the coast in 430. Storm after storm blew the beach sand up the hill into its wells and lanes, and in 748 the last families left it. Two years later the people of Dương Liễu began planting willows on their own dunes, so that the same would not happen to them.

465.name: Tà Dương Mạch
465.look: A low grassy rise where the evening light falls level across a field of warm, ochre stones.
465.lore: An Earth vein runs under the rise, strongest in the hour of the evening glow, which suits Lạc Hà's arts. The sect's disciples on the island come here at dusk to cultivate.

466.name: Tang Du Thôn
466.look: A few stone houses on the steppe shore, their doors all turned to the sunset and goat pens on the slope behind.
466.lore: The village is named for the old saying that the setting sun among the mulberries and elms is late, but not too late. Its people keep goats and fish, and old islanders come here to live out their last years facing the evening.

467.name: Hào Trư Lĩnh
467.look: A forested ridge whose paths are littered with black and white quills as long as a forearm.
467.lore: Spirit porcupines den here and can shoot their quills across a clearing. The talisman makers of the mainland buy the quills as pens, and the hunters who gather them wear buffalo-hide coats.

468.name: Ngưu Đẩu Thôn
468.look: A hill village of grey roofs on open grass, its buffalo pens ringed with stone walls.
468.lore: The villagers raise water buffalo and name their herds after the stars of the Ox and the Dipper, which stand over the hills in autumn. The old line says a dragon light once shot up toward those stars, and the village children still watch for it.

469.name: Tham Tuyền
469.look: A small hot spring in a cleft of the grassy hills, its water bright and sweet-smelling.
469.lore: The old saying holds that whoever drinks from the spring of greed turns greedy, and that a clean heart only finds it refreshing. The villagers drink from it only at weddings, to show the families have nothing to hide.

470.name: Mộ Sơn Thôn
470.look: A village of tea terraces on a grassy hillside that turns purple at dusk.
470.lore: Its villagers grow tea and graze cattle on the hilltops. They pick the tea only in the hour before sunset, and Lạc Hà's disciples say it is the only tea that tastes of the evening glow.

471.name: Tẩy Trần Tuyền
471.look: A warm spring in the grass a short walk from the ferry road, with a bathhouse of bamboo built over it.
471.lore: Travellers fresh off the strait crossing wash the road off here before going on. Bình Thủy Môn pays for the bathhouse, and a newcomer's first bath is free.

472.name: Vọng Hương Thôn
472.look: A fishing village on the strait coast, its racks of drying cuttlefish lined up facing the mainland across the water.
472.lore: The villagers dry cuttlefish and sell it to ferry passengers, many of them homesick. On clear days the mainland can be seen from the beach, and the old men sit and look at it.

473.name: Bích Lân Lâm
473.look: The deepest groves of the bamboo forest, where green shapes lie along the canes and drop at a footstep.
473.lore: Spirit bamboo vipers as green as the canes live here, and their bite stops a heart in minutes. Cutters wear buffalo-hide leggings and tap the canes ahead with a long pole.

474.name: Lục Trúc Thôn
474.look: Bamboo houses deep in a bamboo forest, with paper pulp vats steaming in the clearings.
474.lore: Its people cut bamboo for houses and rafts, dig shoots in spring and make a coarse paper that Nam Phố Đường buys for practice talismans. The old line about green bamboo in a garden is painted over the village gate.

475.name: Vạn Can Lâm
475.look: An endless bamboo forest whose canes stand so close that the light inside is green and the wind sounds like rain.
475.lore: No one has walked to its far edge, and cutters work only its rim. Bình Thủy's disciples train their footwork on the canes, running along the tops without touching the ground.

476.name: Phù Can Thôn
476.look: A coastal village where bamboo rafts are lashed together on the beach and stacked cane floats moored in the shallows.
476.lore: Its villagers build rafts and fish traps and float cut bamboo along the shore to the towns. A raft here is lashed with rattan from Thanh Đằng and lasts three seasons.

477.name: Bạo Ngưu Nguyên
477.look: Open grass behind the boatyards, churned into wallows and grazed short by heavy beasts.
477.lore: Wild spirit buffalo with horns hard as iron graze here and charge anything that comes near their calves. The town's carters drive them off with drums before the timber carts go through.

478.name: Lan Chu Trấn
478.look: A small walled town on a calm shore whose slips are crowded with half-built fishing boats, each with an orchid carved on the prow.
478.lore: The town builds the light fishing boats of Cô Vụ Đảo from bamboo and water pine. The orchid on each prow is the builder's mark, and a boat without one will not be bought.

479.name: Hải Quy Chử
479.look: A stretch of grassy shore pitted with great sand nests, each as wide as a cart.
479.lore: Spirit sea turtles come ashore each year to lay their eggs, and the mothers bite through a boat's side. The villagers of Đê Hạ keep away until the young have gone to sea.

480.name: Đê Hạ Thôn
480.look: A village of rice fields and fish ditches below a long earth dyke, the sea higher than its roofs at high tide.
480.lore: Its people grow rice and raise fish behind the dyke and send every household to mend it after a storm. A crack in the dyke is called before a fire.

481.name: Phong Vương Mạch
481.look: A high knoll in the jungle where the canopy closes into one green roof, humming with large slow bees.
481.lore: A Wood vein runs under the knoll, and the bees over it are larger and calmer than anywhere else on the island. The honey hunters of Phong Sào leave its combs alone and say the vein belongs to the bees.

482.name: Phong Sào Thôn
482.look: A village in a jungle clearing, its houses hung with wax combs and long bamboo ladders leaning on the tallest trees.
482.lore: Its villagers climb the jungle giants to take wild honey and wax, which they trade to the alchemists of Hải Yến. A honey hunter sings to the bees as he climbs, and no one else may use his song.

483.name: Ẩm Câu Tuyền
483.look: A steaming spring in a dip of the steppe, its overflow running into a long stone trough.
483.lore: The herders water their flocks here in winter when the ponds freeze. Mục Vân's couriers always stop to water their horses, and the trough's stones are worn by hooves.

484.name: Bạch Thảo Thôn
484.look: A herding village on the steppe shore, its sheep pens of piled stone and the autumn grass around it bleached white.
484.lore: Its herders run sheep on the pale grass and fish the shore in winter. Their wool goes to Nhạn Thanh and is said to be the whitest on the plain.

485.name: Nhất Sắc Mạch
485.look: A flat grassy shore where on calm evenings the sea and the sky turn the same colour and the horizon disappears.
485.lore: A Water vein runs under the shore, named for the line in which the autumn water and the endless sky are one colour. Lạc Hà's disciples cultivate here at the hour of the evening glow.

486.name: Thanh Phong Trấn
486.look: A small walled town on the steppe shore, its wool sheds open to the sea wind.
486.lore: The town ships wool and hides along the plain coast. Its name comes from the old line about clear breezes rising, and the merchants say the breeze keeps the moth out of their wool.

487.name: Khoáng Dã Mạch
487.look: A bare rise in the steppe where the grass grows short and the ground hums faintly underfoot.
487.lore: An Earth vein runs under the rise, steady and broad. Mục Vân's couriers break their journeys here to cultivate an hour before riding on.

488.name: Song Tỉnh Thôn
488.look: A cluster of felt tents and stone pens around two deep stone wells in the open grass.
488.lore: The herders move between the two wells with the seasons and never let one run dry. A quarrel over water here is settled by the oldest woman of the village.

489.name: Hắc Thứu Đài
489.look: A grassy terrace of high ground streaked white with droppings, where huge black birds sit hunched on the rocks.
489.lore: Spirit vultures nest here and take lambs and sick sheep from the herds. Herders say they gather over any flock that is about to suffer a loss, and drive their sheep home when they see them.

490.name: Vãn Chu Thôn
490.look: A fishing village on the grassy coast where the boats put out at sunset, each with a lamp at the stern.
490.lore: Its fishers go out in the evening and come home singing in the dark, guided by the lamps. In 803 they stayed ashore, and they still stay ashore on that dusk every year.

491.name: Chung Phàm Trấn
491.look: A small walled town on a high steppe spur over the sea, its water tanks cut into the rock.
491.lore: It is the last stop for boats going out to the far west, and it sells them water, salt fish and rope. Its people claim the sunset is nearer to them than to anyone on the continent.

492.name: Liệt Mã Cương
492.look: An open grassy ridge high above the coast, its turf torn by hooves.
492.lore: Wild spirit stallions run here and kill any horse that strays into their herd. Mục Vân's horse-breakers come each year to try to take one, and come back with fewer riders than they took.

493.name: Bình Sa Thôn
493.look: A village on flat sands at the shore, its houses raised on low mounds against the spring tides.
493.lore: Its villagers fish the shore flats and herd sheep on the grass behind. Geese come down on the level sand each autumn, and the village holds a feast when the first ones land.

494.name: Bình Vu Mạch
494.look: A wide patch of open grass that turns green weeks before the rest of the plain each spring.
494.lore: A Wood vein runs under the level grass, gentle and wide. The farmers of Hòa Lũng plant first beside it and say the vein wakes the plain.

495.name: Hòa Lũng Thôn
495.look: A farm village on the coastal grass, its fields raised on long ridges with ditches between.
495.lore: Its farmers grow rice and millet on ridges that stand above the floods. The village sends its grain by cart to Thảo Đường Thành.

496.name: Phù Dao Quán
496.look: Empty halls of grey stone on the open steppe, their doors banging in the wind and the courtyard drifted with dust.
496.lore: A small school sworn to Lạc Hà Tông founded the abbey in 760 to cultivate on the open steppe. The cold year of 1120 killed its herds and its old master, and in 1121 its few disciples went to serve Mục Vân Trang. Herders shelter in its halls in storms.

497.name: Thiên Cao Mạch
497.look: A broad rise of steppe under an enormous sky, with a single stone cairn on its crown.
497.lore: An Earth vein runs under the rise, named for the old line in which heaven is high and earth far-reaching. The disciples of Phù Dao Quán cultivated here, and their cairn still stands.

498.name: Thán Ổ Thôn
498.look: A village of black-roofed huts in a wooded hollow, its charcoal mounds smoking under turf.
498.lore: Its people burn charcoal in the woods and carry it to the towns of the plain. Each family has its own wood and cuts it in turn so the trees grow back.

499.name: Ngư Hỏa Trấn
499.look: A broken sea wall and roofless houses on a grassy shore, with rows of rusted lamp hooks along the old quay.
499.lore: Fishers built the town in 610, and its boats fished at night by lamplight. The great storm of 870 broke its sea wall and sank its fleet in the harbour, and the survivors moved to Di Tân. Fishers still see lights on the water off the old quay.

500.name: Thanh Vân Mạch
500.look: A high forest shoulder above the coast where the clouds come down through the trees.
500.lore: A Wood vein runs under the forest, named for the old line about never letting the will for the blue clouds fall. Lạc Hà's young disciples are sent here to cultivate before their first trial.

501.name: Di Tân Trấn
501.look: A small walled harbour town on the grassy coast, its harbour so packed with coast boats that one can walk across it.
501.lore: Its name comes from the old line about boats crowding the ford. It is the busiest harbour on the plain coast after Nhạn Thanh, and its harbour master settles mooring quarrels by lot.

502.name: Thảo Lang Nguyên
502.look: Rolling high grass where the wind shows long tracks through the blades and old wolf dens open on the slopes.
502.lore: Spirit wolves the colour of dry grass hunt here and are hard to see until they move. In winter they come down on the flocks, and the herders sleep beside their sheep with fire pots.

503.name: Mục Địch Thôn
503.look: A herding village of felt and timber on open grass, its flocks moving around it to the sound of bamboo flutes.
503.lore: Its herders call their flocks with flutes, each family with its own tune. A sheep that answers the wrong tune is given back without a word.

504.name: Trường Phong Mạch
504.look: An open grassy rise inland of the town where the wind never stops and the grass lies flat.
504.lore: An Earth vein runs under the rise, and the wind over it is said to carry the qi far across the plain. Travellers staying at Phùng Nghênh come up to cultivate before setting out.

505.name: Phùng Nghênh Trấn
505.look: A small walled town on the grassy coast whose main street is nothing but inns, each with a lantern at the door.
505.lore: Its name comes from the old line about welcomes from a thousand miles away. The town's custom is that no stranger sleeps outside, and the innkeepers take turns to house those who cannot pay.

506.name: Vụ Liệt Mạch
506.look: A high steppe shoulder where the morning mists lie in long even ranks along the slope.
506.lore: An Earth vein runs under the shoulder, and its qi holds the mists in place until noon. Lạc Hà's disciples climb up to cultivate in the mist.

507.name: Thu Tân Thôn
507.look: A fishing village on the bay shore below bare hills, its boats drawn up on a gravel beach.
507.lore: Its villagers fish the bay in autumn when the water runs clearest and graze goats on the hills the rest of the year. The bay is said to be most like its name here.

508.name: Thúy Bình Mạch
508.look: A grassy rise backed by a wall of jungle that stands like a green screen.
508.lore: A Wood vein runs under the rise. The villagers of Đào Ẩn say their trees fruit best on the side facing it.

509.name: Đào Ẩn Thôn
509.look: A village in a jungle clearing ringed by longan orchards, heavy with brown fruit in summer.
509.lore: Its villagers grow longans and dry them on bamboo trays for the bay cities. Wild peaches from the old Petal Shore orchards grow among their trees.

510.name: Ngư Võng Thôn
510.look: A fishing village on the jungle shore where nets hang drying on poles all along the beach.
510.lore: Its villagers fish with nets and burn back the edge of Thiên Chu Lâm each spring. They say a spider web and a net are the same thing, and that the village must stay quicker.

511.name: Lưu Thủy Mạch
511.look: A spring-fed stream in the grass that runs clear and full even in the driest summer.
511.lore: A Water vein feeds the stream, named for the old tune of flowing water. Musicians of the bay come to play beside it.

512.name: Hoàng Long Trấn
512.look: A small walled town on the flat coast whose slipways hold half-carved dragon prows painted yellow.
512.lore: Its name comes from the old line about ships with blue bird and yellow dragon prows. Its carvers make the prows for the bay's ships, and a ship launched without one is thought unlucky.

513.name: Ngọc Lộ Thang
513.look: A warm spring in the grass whose steam leaves beads of dew on the reeds around it.
513.lore: The bead-drillers of Châu Liêm bathe their tired eyes in the water. They say it keeps an old driller's sight sharp.

514.name: Châu Liêm Trấn
514.look: A small walled town on the bay coast whose doorways all hang with curtains of shell beads that click in the wind.
514.lore: Its drillers string shell beads into curtains for the rich houses of the bay, after the old line about pearl curtains rolled up at dusk. A bride's curtain takes her family a year to make.

515.name: Ốc Thổ Mạch
515.look: A broad shelf of high steppe among the badlands where the soil lies deep and dark among bare red rock.
515.lore: A heavy Earth vein runs under the shelf, the only green ground for a day's walk. Thiên Bảo's prospectors cultivate here on their way through and never stay the night.

516.name: Mặc Thiết Khoáng
516.look: Adits cut into a high crag, their spoil heaps black against the red badlands.
516.lore: Miners dig black iron here in summer and carry it down on mules to Thiên Bảo's furnaces. In winter the mine is shut and the wind has it.

517.name: Trùng Tiêu Phong
517.look: A sheer grey peak above the badlands whose tip often stands above the clouds.
517.lore: Its name comes from the old line about peaks rising above the layered heavens. Its bare rock carries Metal qi, and Thiên Bảo's refiners climb it to temper blades in its cold wind.

518.name: Lam Ngọc Khoáng
518.look: A cold high working where blue-green jade shows in the rock face under a crust of frost.
518.lore: Jade cutters climb up each summer and work until the first snow. Thiên Bảo Trai buys every stone they bring down and sells the best at its auctions.

519.name: Tằng Loan Phong
519.look: A tall square-sided peak of pale rock, the highest in the bay's lands, standing above ridge after ridge.
519.lore: Its name comes from the old line about layered ranges rising green to the heavens. Its rock carries Metal and Earth qi, and few cultivators have climbed it.

520.name: Hoàng Tích Cương
520.look: A ridge of yellow rock in the steppe where great lizards lie motionless in the sun.
520.lore: Spirit lizards as long as a cart bask here and take stray goats and sheep. Their hides are sold to Thiên Bảo's armourers.

521.name: Liên Chu Thôn
521.look: A steppe village on a river where a bridge of boats lashed together carries the caravan road.
521.lore: Its villagers keep the pontoon bridge and take a small toll for Thiên Bảo Trai. When the river floods they cut the bridge loose and haul it back afterwards.

522.name: Dã Lư Nguyên
522.look: Open steppe crossed by dusty trails and the dung heaps of wild herds.
522.lore: Herds of wild spirit asses run here, fast as a horse and vicious. They kick riders from the saddle and kill ponies that stray into the herd.

523.name: Mã Độ Thôn
523.look: A steppe village by a shallow river ford, its corrals full of shaggy ponies.
523.lore: Its villagers breed hardy steppe ponies and sell them to the caravans. A caravan that buys its ponies here is said never to lose one to thirst.

524.name: Lưu Đan Trì
524.look: A hot pool in the steppe whose overflow runs down the rocks in a bright red stain.
524.lore: Its name comes from the old line about vermilion flowing from the pavilion's eaves. Its iron water stains the rocks red, and the fishers soak their sore joints in it.

525.name: Hàm Phong Thôn
525.look: A fishing village on the steppe coast where racks of split fish dry in a constant salty wind.
525.lore: Its fish dry in the salt wind in a single day, and the bay's caravans buy them for the road.

526.name: Kim Sa Tuyền
526.look: A warm spring in the steppe whose bed glitters with golden grains of mica.
526.lore: Prospectors once dug the spring for gold and found only mica. The herders of Bạch Dương water their sheep here in winter.

527.name: Minh Loan Các
527.look: A tall pavilion on the steppe shore, its eaves hung with hundreds of bronze bells that ring together in the sea wind.
527.lore: Bell-casters founded the pavilion in 960 under Lạc Hà Tông, after the old line about jade pendants and singing bells. Its disciples cast ward bells whose note drives off beasts and warns of attack, and every ship and caravan of the bay carries one. A disciple must cast a bell that rings true before learning any art.

528.name: Bạch Dương Thôn
528.look: A cluster of felt tents and stone pens around a deep well on the open steppe.
528.lore: Its herders run white sheep between the wells of the steppe and sell the wool at Vật Hoa Thị. They move camp by the stars.

529.name: Hoàng Điêu Đài
529.look: A rocky terrace on the high steppe where great eagles sit on the stones and the ground is strewn with bones.
529.lore: Spirit golden eagles nest here and take lambs and foals. Mục Vân Trang's riders have tried to tame their chicks and never succeeded.

530.name: Hà Khúc Thôn
530.look: A steppe village on a tight bend of the river, its fields laid out inside the loop.
530.lore: Its villagers farm the bend and fish the deep pools. When the river cuts a new bend, the village moves its fields and keeps its houses.

531.name: Bạch Lỗ Hồ
531.look: A shallow brine lake on the salt flats, ringed with white crust and too salty for any fish.
531.lore: The villagers of Xích Thổ rake salt from its shores and sell it to the caravans. Its water holds a body up like a raft.

532.name: Xích Thổ Thôn
532.look: A steppe village of red mud houses by a river, with salt carts lined up outside.
532.lore: Its villagers farm the red earth by the river and gather salt from the brine lake. They never take their flocks to the far heights.

533.name: Thiết Cốt Mạch
533.look: A ridge of dark badland rock where seams of grey metal stand out like bones.
533.lore: A Metal vein runs under the ridge, hard and cold. Lạc Hà's sword disciples cultivate here to temper their bodies before taking up a blade.

534.name: Than Đầu Thôn
534.look: A steppe village by a stretch of rocky river rapids, with a hauling path cut along the bank.
534.lore: Its villagers fish the rapids and haul the boats past them on ropes for a toll. The boatmen sing as they haul, and the songs are older than the village.

535.name: Sơn Tiêu Nhai
535.look: A high cliff of bare rock where red-faced apes sit on the ledges and hurl stones at anyone below.
535.lore: Spirit mountain apes live on the cliff and drive off hunters and climbers. They are said to remember a face and stone that person for years.

536.name: Hà Quang Tuyền
536.look: A hot spring on a steppe rise whose steam glows rose-red at sunset.
536.lore: Lạc Hà's disciples bathe here after cultivating at dusk. The herbalists of Yên Quang Các water their evening herbs from it.

537.name: Yên Quang Các
537.look: A pavilion of ochre walls on the steppe, surrounded by terraced herb beds that its disciples tend only at sunset.
537.lore: Alchemists sworn to Lạc Hà Tông founded the pavilion in 1065, after the old line about the haze and light congealing as the evening hills turn purple. They pick their herbs only in the hour of the evening glow and say the herbs hold the light. Lạc Hà's disciples buy most of its pills.

538.name: Lô Địch Thôn
